items.chapter: Introduction to the Indian Capital Market
items.title: NISM VI Indian Capital Market Basics: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on India's capital market for NISM Series VI: primary vs secondary market, MIIs, SEBI's role, ASBA/UPI issues and who does what.
items.intro: This opening chapter of the Depository Operations exam maps the capital market so that later chapters make sense. Expect direct questions on the difference between primary and secondary markets, which institution is a market infrastructure institution, what SEBI regulates, and how investors apply in public issues. Most items test roles: who raises money, who trades, who clears, who holds the securities.

points.heading: Two halves of the market
points.text: The primary market is where securities are created and sold for the first time, so money flows from investors to the issuer (IPO, FPO, rights issue, private placement). The secondary market is where existing securities change hands between investors on a stock exchange; the company receives nothing when you buy its shares from another investor on NSE or BSE.

points.heading: Market infrastructure institutions
points.text: Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are called MIIs because the whole system runs through them. The exchange matches orders, the clearing corporation guarantees and settles trades, and the depository (NSDL or CDSL) holds securities electronically and moves them between accounts. All three are regulated by SEBI and are expected to put public interest ahead of profit.

points.heading: SEBI and other regulators
points.text: SEBI, set up under the SEBI Act, 1992, protects investors and develops and regulates the securities market. RBI regulates government securities, money markets and foreign exchange, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs administers the Companies Act. In GIFT City, IFSCA is the unified regulator. A question asking who registers a depository participant always points to SEBI.

points.heading: Intermediaries
points.text: Key SEBI-registered intermediaries include stock brokers, depository participants, merchant bankers, registrars and share transfer agents (RTAs), bankers to an issue, custodians, portfolio managers, investment advisers and credit rating agencies. Each needs registration and must follow a code of conduct. A DP, for example, cannot operate without being registered with SEBI and admitted by a depository.

points.heading: Raising money through ASBA and UPI
points.text: In public issues, investors apply through ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount): the bid money stays in the investor's bank account and is only blocked, not debited, until allotment. Retail and small individual bidders can use a UPI mandate through their broker, DP or RTA app. On allotment the blocked amount is debited; for unallotted bids the block is released.

points.heading: Instruments traded
points.text: Equity shares give ownership and variable returns; debt instruments such as debentures and bonds give fixed claims with interest; hybrids such as convertible debentures and preference shares sit between. Units of mutual funds, ETFs, REITs and InvITs and government securities can also be held and traded in demat form. Derivatives are contracts, not securities held in a depository.

points.heading: Why depositories matter
points.text: Before 1996, physical certificates caused bad deliveries, forgery, theft and long transfer delays. Depositories allow settlement by simple book entries, so ownership changes instantly at pay-out. Today listed securities must be held in demat form for transfer, which is why every trader needs a demat account with a DP alongside a trading account with a broker.

points.heading: Investor protection layer
points.text: Investor protection rests on disclosure (offer documents, continuous listing disclosures), segregation of client assets, settlement guarantees by clearing corporations, investor protection funds at exchanges and depositories, and grievance redress through SCORES and online dispute resolution. Remember these as the safety net that surrounds the trading and holding system.

points.heading: Trading and demat account link
points.text: A trading account is opened with a stock broker to place orders; a demat account is opened with a DP to hold securities. Many brokers are also DPs, so investors often open both together, but they remain separate accounts with separate rights and obligations documents. Settlement moves securities between the demat account and the clearing corporation.

traps: Confusing exchange and clearing corporation: the exchange matches trades, the clearing corporation guarantees and settles them through novation.
Assuming the company gets money in the secondary market. Only primary market issues bring fresh funds to the issuer; secondary trades are between investors.
Thinking ASBA debits the bid amount on application. It only blocks the money; the debit happens after allotment is finalised.
Calling a depository participant a depository. NSDL and CDSL are the depositories; DPs are their agents who deal with investors.
items.recap: Primary market creates securities, secondary market trades them. Exchanges match, clearing corporations settle and guarantee, depositories hold electronically through DPs. SEBI regulates the securities market, RBI the money and G-sec markets. Public issue bids use ASBA or UPI so money is blocked, not debited, until allotment.

items.title: NISM VI Introduction to Depository: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM Series VI notes on what a depository is: NSDL and CDSL, Depositories Act 1996, registered vs beneficial owner, ISIN, fungibility and demat benefits.
items.intro: This chapter answers a simple question: what exactly does a depository do and why did India need one? Exam questions test the legal framework, the two depositories, the difference between registered and beneficial ownership, ISIN and fungibility, and the comparison with a bank. Learn the vocabulary precisely, because options often differ by a single word.

points.heading: Definition
points.text: A depository is an organisation that holds securities of investors in electronic form, at the investor's request, through registered depository participants. It also transfers ownership by book entry. The analogy is a bank: a bank holds money and transfers it between accounts; a depository holds securities and transfers them, without any physical movement of paper.

points.heading: The two depositories
points.text: India has two depositories: National Securities Depository Ltd (NSDL), set up in 1996 and promoted by IDBI, UTI and NSE, and Central Depository Services (India) Ltd (CDSL), promoted by BSE and banks and operational from 1999. Investors can hold accounts with either through any DP; inter-depository transfers are seamless.

points.heading: Legal framework
points.text: The Depositories Act, 1996 provides the legal basis, read with the SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, now the 2018 version, and each depository's bye-laws and business rules. The Act made ownership transfers by book entry legal and removed stamp duty on demat transfers at that time. Depositories must be registered with SEBI.

points.heading: Registered owner vs beneficial owner
points.text: For dematerialised securities, the depository is shown as the registered owner in the issuer's register of members, but only to effect transfers. The investor whose name appears in the depository's records is the beneficial owner and enjoys all rights: voting, dividends, bonus and rights entitlements. Exam options that give voting rights to the depository are wrong.

points.heading: ISIN
points.text: Each security admitted to a depository has a 12-character International Securities Identification Number, such as INE002A01018. In India, ISINs start with IN; the next character indicates the issuer type (E for companies, F for mutual funds). Different types of securities of the same company, such as partly paid shares, carry different ISINs.

points.heading: Fungibility
points.text: Securities in demat form are fungible: they have no distinctive numbers or certificate numbers, so any 100 shares of a company with the same ISIN are identical. This is why the depository can settle trades by changing balances without tracking specific certificates, and why distinctive numbers disappear after dematerialisation.

points.heading: Benefits over physical holding
points.text: Demat eliminates risks of loss, theft, mutilation, forgery and bad delivery; removes odd-lot problems; speeds up transfers and credits of corporate actions; and allows pledging with a few instructions. Investors can hold all securities in one account and get a single consolidated account statement. Costs such as courier and handling also fall.

points.heading: Depository vs bank
points.text: Both hold assets in accounts and transfer by instruction, but a depository cannot use, lend or pay interest on the securities it holds; it has no claim on them. A bank lends deposits and pays interest. Depository accounts can never be overdrawn, while banks permit overdrafts. Securities balances are held in trust for the investor.

points.heading: What can be held in demat
points.text: Equity and preference shares, debentures and bonds, government securities, mutual fund units, ETFs, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, REIT and InvIT units, sovereign gold bonds and warrants can all be held in demat form. Listed companies' shares must be in demat form for transfer, so physical shares need to be dematerialised before they can be sold on an exchange.

traps: Treating the depository as the beneficial owner. It is only the registered owner for transfer purposes; all economic and voting rights stay with the investor.
Assuming one ISIN per company. Each distinct class (fully paid, partly paid, different debenture series) gets its own ISIN.
Believing a depository can lend or invest client securities like a bank lends deposits. It merely records and transfers them.
Mixing up promoters: NSDL is associated with NSE, IDBI and UTI; CDSL with BSE.
items.recap: Depository = electronic custodian of securities, governed by the Depositories Act 1996 and SEBI regulations. Two depositories: NSDL and CDSL. Depository is registered owner, investor is beneficial owner with all rights. ISIN is the 12-character identifier; demat securities are fungible. Unlike a bank, a depository cannot lend or use holdings.

items.title: NISM VI Depository Business Partners: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on depository business partners for NISM VI: DPs, issuers and RTAs, clearing corporations, pledgee banks, eligibility and supervision.
items.intro: A depository never deals with investors directly; it works through a network of partners. This chapter explains each partner's job and how the depository keeps watch over them. Questions are typically 'who does this?' — who opens accounts, who confirms demat requests, who credits allotments, who supervises DPs — so build a clear mental map of the flows.

points.heading: Depository participant
points.text: A DP is the depository's agent and the investor's point of contact. It opens and maintains demat accounts, accepts instructions, sends statements and handles grievances. A DP must be registered with SEBI under the Depositories and Participants Regulations and admitted by the depository. One entity can be a DP of both NSDL and CDSL.

points.heading: Who can be a DP
points.text: Eligible categories include banks, financial institutions, custodians, clearing corporations, stock brokers, NBFCs and RTAs meeting net worth criteria prescribed by SEBI. Stock brokers and NBFCs face higher net worth thresholds than banks because they are not otherwise prudentially regulated to the same degree. Figures change, so learn the category list rather than exact amounts.

points.heading: Issuer and RTA
points.text: The issuer (the company) appoints a registrar and share transfer agent to maintain its records. The RTA is the depository's link to the issuer: it confirms dematerialisation and rematerialisation requests, executes corporate actions such as allotments and bonus credits, and reconciles the issuer's capital with the depository's records every quarter (reconciliation of share capital audit).

points.heading: Tripartite agreement
points.text: Before its securities can be dematerialised, an issuer signs a tripartite agreement with the depository and its RTA. Once the agreement is in place and the security is admitted, investors can convert physical certificates or receive allotments directly in demat form. Listed public issues require this arrangement with both depositories.

points.heading: Clearing corporation interface
points.text: The clearing corporation holds a pool or settlement account with each depository. On pay-in, securities move from the selling client's account (via block mechanism) to the clearing corporation; on pay-out, they move from the clearing corporation directly to the buying client's account. The depository simply executes these book entries on settlement instructions.

points.heading: Banks and pledgees
points.text: Banks and NBFCs participate as pledgees when investors borrow against securities. They hold demat accounts and accept or invoke pledges. Banks also act as clearing banks and DPs. The depository records the pledge so the pledged securities cannot be transferred without the pledgee's consent.

points.heading: Depository's supervision of DPs
points.text: Depositories inspect DPs periodically, require internal audits and concurrent audits of account opening and DIS controls, monitor complaints and can levy penalties or suspend DPs for violations. DPs must also submit compliance certificates and net worth certificates. SEBI in turn inspects the depositories.

points.heading: Rights and obligations document
points.text: The relationship between the beneficial owner and DP is governed by a standard rights and obligations document prescribed by SEBI, given to the client at account opening. It sets out charges, communication of changes, statements, grievance redress and the DP's duties. Fee changes must be notified to clients in advance.

points.heading: Information flow summary
points.text: Investor gives instruction to DP; DP enters it into the depository system; depository executes book entry; RTA confirms anything that changes issuer records; clearing corporation sends settlement obligations. Remembering this chain helps solve most 'who acts next' questions.

traps: Saying the investor deals directly with the depository. All requests go through the DP, which acts as the depository's agent.
Confusing the RTA's role with the DP's role in dematerialisation. The DP forwards the request; the RTA verifies certificates and confirms the credit.
Assuming a DP is registered only with the depository. SEBI registration is required, and admission by the depository is separate.
Forgetting that the pledgee, not the pledgor, accepts a pledge and can later invoke it.
items.recap: Depository works through partners: DPs face investors, RTAs represent issuers, clearing corporations route settlement, banks act as pledgees and clearing banks. DPs need SEBI registration and depository admission, follow the rights and obligations document and are audited and inspected by the depository. Issuers join through a tripartite agreement.

items.title: NISM VI Demat Account Opening Rules: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI revision notes on opening demat accounts: account types, KYC and IPV, joint, minor, HUF and NRI accounts, BSDA and nomination at account opening.
items.intro: Account opening is one of the most heavily tested areas of the Depository Operations exam. You need to know who can open which type of account, what documents and verification are needed, how many holders are permitted, and what the Basic Services Demat Account offers. Questions are often set as small scenarios: a minor, an HUF, an NRI or a company wants an account — what applies?

points.heading: Types of beneficial owner accounts
points.text: Accounts can be opened for resident individuals, NRIs (repatriable and non-repatriable), HUFs, minors, corporates, trusts, partnership firms, FPIs, banks and clearing members. Each type has its own sub-type in the depository system, which matters for tax, repatriation and settlement. A clearing member account is a business account, not a beneficial owner account.

points.heading: KYC and in-person verification
points.text: Every holder must complete KYC: PAN (mandatory except specified exemptions), proof of identity and address, and in-person verification by the DP's staff or via video-based KYC. KYC records are uploaded to a KRA so the investor need not repeat KYC with other intermediaries. Original documents must be verified against copies.

points.heading: Joint accounts
points.text: A demat account can have a maximum of three holders. The order of names matters: holdings in 'A and B' are different from 'B and A', so shares held in a different order cannot be credited without transposition. All holders sign the account opening form, and instructions generally need all holders' signatures unless a holder authorises otherwise.

points.heading: Minor accounts
points.text: A minor can only be the sole holder; joint holding is not allowed. The account is operated by a natural or court-appointed guardian whose details and KYC are recorded. A minor cannot nominate. When the minor turns 18, the account must be converted with fresh KYC of the now-major holder.

points.heading: HUF, corporate and NRI accounts
points.text: An HUF account is opened in the name of the HUF and operated by the Karta; coparceners cannot be joint holders. Corporates provide board resolutions and authorised signatories. NRIs need a repatriable or non-repatriable bank account (NRE or NRO) linked appropriately, and FEMA-compliant documentation. Partnership firms often hold through partners' names because a firm is not a legal person.

points.heading: Basic Services Demat Account
points.text: BSDA is a low-cost account for small individual investors with only one demat account across depositories, as sole or first holder. As of 2026, holdings up to ₹4 lakh attract no AMC and holdings between ₹4 lakh and ₹10 lakh a capped AMC (check current SEBI circular). The DP must offer BSDA to eligible clients and convert accounts automatically if eligibility changes.

points.heading: Nomination at opening
points.text: Individual sole or joint holders must either nominate or explicitly opt out through a declaration (with verification). SEBI's 2025 nomination framework allows multiple nominees (up to 10 as of 2026, check current rules) with percentage shares. Non-individuals such as companies, HUFs and societies cannot nominate.

points.heading: Documents given to the client
points.text: After opening, the DP gives the client a copy of the account opening form, rights and obligations document, tariff sheet, Do's and Don'ts and the client master report showing account details. A DIS booklet is issued on request only. Clients should verify their client master for correct bank details and nominee information.

points.heading: Linking bank account and contact details
points.text: Bank details are captured so that cash corporate benefits such as dividends reach the right account. Mobile numbers and email IDs are mandatory for alerts; SEBI requires them to be unique to a family. Incorrect contact details are a common cause of missed alerts and fraud, which is why DPs validate them at opening.

traps: Allowing a minor as a joint holder. A minor can only be the sole holder through a guardian.
Thinking an HUF can nominate or that coparceners are joint holders. The Karta operates the account and nomination is not available.
Believing holdings in 'A and B' and 'B and A' are interchangeable. The order of names is part of the account identity.
Assuming BSDA is available to anyone. It requires only one demat account, as sole or first holder, and holding value within the SEBI limit.
items.recap: Up to three holders; minors only as sole holder via guardian; HUF operated by Karta, no nomination. KYC with PAN and in-person or video verification, recorded with a KRA. BSDA for small investors with a single demat account and holdings within the SEBI limit. Individuals must nominate or opt out explicitly.

items.title: NISM VI Demat Account Operations: Revision Notes
items.description: Notes on demat account operations for NISM VI: DIS controls, online instructions, freezing, transposition, account closure and transaction statements.
items.intro: Once an account is open, the DP handles a stream of instructions and changes. This chapter is practical and scenario-heavy: how delivery instruction slips are issued and checked, how a client can freeze an account, what transposition means, how accounts are closed and how often statements must be sent. Know the safeguard behind each rule.

points.heading: Delivery instruction slips
points.text: A DIS is the client's written instruction to debit securities. DPs issue pre-numbered DIS booklets only on request, record the serial numbers against the account, and verify signatures and slip numbers before execution. Loose slips are given only with the account holder's personal presence or under strict controls, because blank slips are a classic fraud route.

points.heading: Online instructions
points.text: Clients can submit debit instructions electronically through depository platforms such as NSDL's SPEED-e or CDSL's easiest, or the DP's app, with two-factor authentication. Sell transactions on exchanges now use the block mechanism and e-DIS or DDPI authorisation, so a client's holdings are debited only for valid obligations.

points.heading: DDPI instead of POA
points.text: The Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction is a limited authorisation a client may give a broker, covering transfer for settlement of trades, pledges for margin, mutual fund transactions on exchange platforms and tendering in open offers. It replaced the broad power of attorney that earlier allowed misuse. DDPI is optional; clients can use e-DIS instead.

points.heading: Freezing and unfreezing
points.text: A client can freeze an account for debits, credits or both, or freeze specific ISINs or quantities, for example while travelling. Regulators and courts can also order freezes, and accounts with incomplete KYC may be frozen by rule. Unfreezing requires a request from the same authority that froze it.

points.heading: Change in details
points.text: Address, bank details and contact information can be changed on a signed request with supporting documents, after verification. Names can be changed after events such as marriage with proof. Changes are reflected in the client master and the client must be informed. A change of PAN is not normally permitted; PAN mismatch requires correction.

points.heading: Transposition
points.text: Transposition changes the order of names in a joint holding when all holders are alive, for example moving shares from 'B and A' to an account in 'A and B'. Physical certificates can be transposed during dematerialisation with a transposition-cum-demat form. Transposition differs from transmission, which happens only on death.

points.heading: Consolidation and closure
points.text: A client with multiple accounts in the same names and order can consolidate by transferring holdings, typically through an account closure request in which balances move to the target account. Closure with balances needs an instruction to transfer or rematerialise. Accounts with pending pledges, freezes or lock-in cannot be closed until these are cleared.

points.heading: Statements
points.text: DPs must send a transaction statement in any month with a transaction and a holding statement periodically, now usually through the Consolidated Account Statement issued by depositories for investors with a PAN-mapped account. If there are no transactions, a holding statement is still sent periodically, half-yearly through the CAS for accounts without activity (check current depository rules). Statements can be electronic if the client agrees.

points.heading: SMS and email alerts
points.text: Depositories send alerts directly to the registered mobile and email for every debit, pledge creation and certain other transactions. This lets the client catch unauthorised activity immediately. The client must keep contact details updated; using a broker's mobile number is not allowed.

traps: Confusing transposition with transmission. Transposition reorders living joint holders; transmission happens on a holder's death.
Assuming DDPI gives the broker unlimited control. It covers only specified purposes such as settlement and margin pledges.
Thinking DIS booklets are issued automatically with every account. They are issued on request, and their numbers are recorded against the account.
Believing an account can be closed while securities are pledged or frozen. These must be released first.
items.recap: DIS booklets are pre-numbered, issued on request and checked before execution. DDPI is a limited authorisation that replaced broad POAs. Clients can freeze debits, credits or specific ISINs. Transposition changes the order of living joint holders. Closure requires transferring balances and clearing pledges. Statements go monthly when there are transactions, and periodically (through the CAS) otherwise.

items.title: NISM VI Transmission and Nomination: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI transmission and nomination notes: who can nominate, multiple nominees, transmission with and without a nominee, joint holders and documents needed.
items.intro: When an account holder dies, the securities must pass to the right person with minimum delay. This chapter covers how nomination works, how transmission is processed in different situations and the documents required. Exam questions often describe a family situation — a sole holder with a nominee, a joint account where one holder dies, a minor nominee — and ask what happens.

points.heading: Who can nominate
points.text: Only individuals holding accounts singly or jointly can nominate. Non-individuals such as companies, HUFs, trusts, partnership firms and societies cannot. A guardian cannot nominate on behalf of a minor account holder. In joint accounts, all holders jointly make the nomination, and it applies only after the death of all joint holders.

points.heading: Who can be a nominee
points.text: Only an individual can be a nominee, including a minor represented by a guardian. A trust, company, society, HUF or Karta in that capacity cannot be a nominee. An NRI can be a nominee subject to FEMA rules. Under SEBI's 2025 framework, up to 10 nominees can be named with percentage shares (check current rules).

points.heading: Nominee's position
points.text: A nominee receives the securities on the holder's death, which gives the depository and DP a clean discharge. Whether the nominee is the ultimate owner or a trustee for legal heirs depends on succession law, and courts have generally treated the nominee as holding for heirs. Nomination is therefore a transfer mechanism, not a substitute for a will.

points.heading: Transmission with a nominee
points.text: The nominee submits a transmission request form, a copy of the death certificate attested appropriately and their own KYC. The DP verifies documents and transfers the holdings to the nominee's demat account, which must be in the nominee's name. No legal heirship documents are needed when a valid nomination exists.

points.heading: Joint account, one holder dies
points.text: If one of the joint holders dies, the securities are transmitted to the surviving holders by closing the account and moving balances to a new account in the survivors' names. The survivors submit the death certificate and a transmission request; nomination is not triggered because some holders remain alive.

points.heading: Sole holder without a nominee
points.text: When there is no nomination, the claimant must prove entitlement. Depending on value, depositories prescribe documents such as succession certificate, probate or letter of administration, or for smaller values an affidavit, indemnity and no-objection from other legal heirs. Value thresholds for simplified documentation are set by SEBI and depositories.

points.heading: Minor as nominee
points.text: A minor nominee is represented by a guardian, whose details are recorded at nomination. On transmission, securities are credited to the minor's demat account operated by the guardian. When the minor becomes major, the account must be updated with fresh KYC.

points.heading: Changing or cancelling nomination
points.text: Nomination can be changed or cancelled any number of times by the holders while alive, through a fresh nomination form. The latest valid nomination prevails. DPs must record nominations promptly and confirm them to clients, since an unrecorded change can lead to disputes.

points.heading: Transmission vs transposition
points.text: Transmission moves securities due to death of a holder, to nominees, survivors or legal heirs. Transposition reorders names among living holders. A common exam scenario mixes the two: if all holders are alive and only the order differs, it is transposition, not transmission.

traps: Allowing a company, trust or HUF to be a nominee. Only individuals can be nominees.
Assuming nomination in a joint account applies when the first holder dies. It operates only after all joint holders die; survivors take first.
Thinking a nominee needs a succession certificate. A valid nomination avoids those documents; they are needed when there is no nomination.
Treating a guardian of a minor account holder as able to nominate. A minor's account cannot have a nomination.
items.recap: Only individuals nominate and only individuals (including minors via guardian) can be nominees. Joint accounts: survivors get the holdings; nominees come in only after all holders die. With a nominee, a death certificate and KYC suffice; without one, legal heirship documents apply based on value. Transmission is on death; transposition is reordering living holders.

items.title: NISM VI Dematerialisation and Remat Process: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI dematerialisation notes: DRF submission, defacing, DP and RTA roles, rejection reasons, lock-in and partly paid shares, and rematerialisation steps.
items.intro: Dematerialisation converts physical certificates into electronic balances; rematerialisation does the reverse. The exam tests the sequence of steps, which party performs each step and the common reasons requests get rejected. Learn the process as a flow chart, because many questions describe a step and ask who acts next or what goes wrong.

points.heading: Starting a demat request
points.text: The client fills a Dematerialisation Request Form (DRF) and hands it to the DP with the physical certificates. The holder's names and their order on the certificates must match the demat account exactly. Separate DRFs are needed for different ISINs, for locked-in and free securities, and for fully and partly paid shares.

points.heading: Defacing the certificates
points.text: Before forwarding, the DP or client marks each certificate 'Surrendered for Dematerialisation' so that it cannot be misused if lost in transit. The DP checks the certificates, the DRF and the signatures, then generates a demat request number in the depository system.

points.heading: Electronic and physical legs
points.text: The DP sends the electronic request through the depository system and dispatches the physical DRF and certificates to the issuer's RTA. Both legs must reach the RTA; the electronic request alone cannot be confirmed without the certificates.

points.heading: RTA verification
points.text: The RTA verifies that the certificates are genuine, that the holder's name matches the register, that there are no stop-transfer orders and that the distinctive numbers are valid. On approval, it confirms the request electronically and the depository credits the holder's demat account. The RTA then updates the register to show the depository as registered owner.

points.heading: Rejection reasons
points.text: Common reasons are signature mismatch, name or order mismatch, certificates reported lost or under court order, fake certificates, wrong ISIN or a mismatch between the DRF and certificates. On rejection, the certificates are returned so the client can correct the problem and resubmit.

points.heading: Locked-in and partly paid shares
points.text: Locked-in shares can be dematerialised, but they are credited under a lock-in status with the lock-in release date and cannot be transferred until then. Partly paid shares carry a separate ISIN, so they cannot be clubbed with fully paid shares on the same DRF.

points.heading: Rematerialisation
points.text: A client wanting physical certificates submits a Remat Request Form to the DP. The DP blocks the quantity and forwards the request electronically; the RTA prints the certificates and dispatches them to the client, after which the depository debits the balance. Since transfers of listed shares require demat form, remat is uncommon.

points.heading: Timelines
points.text: SEBI and depositories prescribe tight timelines for each leg: the DP must forward documents promptly and the RTA must process within the prescribed period, typically measured in days. Delays are monitored through pending demat request reports and are a frequent grievance category.

points.heading: Transmission-cum-demat
points.text: Where a physical holder has died, the claimant can apply for transmission and dematerialisation in one step using a transmission-cum-demat form, saving the step of first getting physical transmission done. Similarly, a transposition-cum-demat form handles a different order of names.

traps: Thinking the DP confirms the demat credit. Only the RTA can confirm after verifying the certificates.
Clubbing locked-in and free shares, or fully and partly paid shares, in one DRF. Separate forms are needed because they are distinct ISINs or statuses.
Believing certificates need not be defaced. Defacing is done before dispatch to prevent misuse.
Assuming a name order mismatch can be ignored. Certificates in 'B and A' cannot be credited to an account in 'A and B' without transposition.
items.recap: Demat flow: client submits DRF and defaced certificates to DP, DP sends electronic request and physical documents to RTA, RTA verifies and confirms, depository credits the account. Names and order must match. Locked-in and partly paid shares go on separate forms. Remat reverses the flow with the RTA printing certificates.

items.title: NISM VI Demat Trading and Settlement: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on how demat accounts support T+1 settlement for NISM VI: block mechanism, pay-in, direct pay-out, off-market and inter-depository transfers.
items.intro: This chapter links the depository to the stock exchange. You must understand what happens in the demat account between the day a client sells or buys and the day settlement completes under T+1. Questions test timelines, the block mechanism for sell orders, direct pay-out, off-market transfer rules and inter-depository transfers, usually through short practical scenarios.

points.heading: T+1 cycle
points.text: Equity trades on Indian exchanges settle on T+1: a trade on Monday settles on Tuesday, skipping weekends and settlement holidays. A trade on Friday settles on Monday. An optional same-day (T+0) settlement has also been introduced for a limited set of stocks; the rolling T+1 cycle remains the default for most trades.

points.heading: Block mechanism for sales
points.text: When a client sells, the shares are blocked in the client's own demat account in favour of the clearing corporation, either through e-DIS (validated by the client) or through DDPI. On the pay-in day, the blocked shares are debited directly to the clearing corporation. If the trade is not executed, the block is released. This prevents misuse of client securities in a broker pool account.

points.heading: Pay-in and pay-out
points.text: Pay-in is when sellers deliver securities and buyers deliver funds to the clearing corporation. Pay-out is when the clearing corporation delivers securities to buyers and funds to sellers. Under direct pay-out, securities are credited straight to the buying client's demat account instead of passing through the broker's pool.

points.heading: Early pay-in
points.text: A seller can deliver securities to the clearing corporation before the normal pay-in, usually on trade day itself. Early pay-in reduces risk for the clearing corporation, so margins on that sale are exempted. With block mechanism, early pay-in is largely automatic.

points.heading: Unpaid securities
points.text: If a buying client has not paid in full, the broker may hold the securities in a client unpaid securities pledgee account and later pledge them as margin trading collateral or sell them after the prescribed period. The broker cannot simply keep client securities in its own account indefinitely.

points.heading: Off-market transfers
points.text: Transfers between two demat accounts that do not go through an exchange are off-market. The client must mention a reason code such as gift, sale outside exchange or transfer between own accounts, and stamp duty may apply. Off-market sale consideration must be disclosed, and DPs watch high-value or unusual transfers for suspicious activity.

points.heading: Inter-depository transfers
points.text: Securities can be moved between an NSDL account and a CDSL account through an inter-depository transfer instruction. The two depositories are linked electronically, so the credit happens on the same day. The client fills the target depository's DP ID and client ID correctly; mistakes are hard to reverse.

points.heading: Short delivery
points.text: If a seller fails to deliver, the clearing corporation conducts an auction to buy the shares for the buyer. If the auction fails, the trade is closed out at a price set by rules, generally the higher of the highest price in the period or a premium over the closing price. The defaulting seller bears the cost.

points.heading: Clearing member accounts
points.text: Clearing members hold pool and settlement accounts with depositories to handle settlement flows. Client securities must not be mixed with the broker's own holdings. Since the block mechanism and direct pay-out, client shares spend very little time outside the client's own account.

traps: Counting calendar days instead of trading days for T+1. Saturdays, Sundays and settlement holidays are skipped.
Assuming the broker's pool account receives client sale shares days in advance. Under block mechanism shares stay in the client's account until pay-in.
Treating an off-market transfer as needing no reason. A reason code is mandatory and stamp duty may apply.
Believing early pay-in increases margin. It reduces risk, so margin on that position is exempted.
items.recap: T+1 is the default cycle. Sales use block mechanism via e-DIS or DDPI; securities are debited at pay-in. Buyers get direct pay-out to their own accounts. Early pay-in exempts margins. Off-market transfers need a reason code and may attract stamp duty. Short deliveries go to auction, then close-out at the defaulter's cost.

items.title: NISM VI Pledge and Hypothecation in Demat: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI notes on pledging demat securities: pledgor and pledgee steps, closure, invocation, pledge vs hypothecation, margin pledge and re-pledge.
items.intro: Demat securities can be used as collateral without any paperwork moving between banks. This chapter covers who initiates and who accepts each step of a pledge, how a pledge is closed or invoked, how hypothecation differs, and the margin pledge framework that replaced broker-held collateral. Questions mostly test sequence and rights.

points.heading: Creating a pledge
points.text: The pledgor (the borrower) initiates the pledge through its DP, specifying the pledgee's account, ISIN and quantity. The pledgee (the lender, usually a bank or NBFC) then accepts or rejects it through its own DP. Only after acceptance are the securities marked as pledged; they stay in the pledgor's account but cannot be transferred.

points.heading: Closing a pledge
points.text: When the loan is repaid, the pledgor initiates closure and the pledgee confirms it. The pledge mark is removed and the securities become free again. A pledgee can also initiate closure on its own when it is satisfied that the loan is closed.

points.heading: Invoking a pledge
points.text: If the borrower defaults, the pledgee invokes the pledge, and the securities move from the pledgor's account to the pledgee's account. In a pledge, the pledgee can invoke without the pledgor's fresh consent, as per the loan agreement. This is the main protection a lender has.

points.heading: Pledge vs hypothecation
points.text: In depository terms, hypothecation gives the lender weaker control: invocation requires the hypothecator's confirmation, whereas a pledgee can invoke unilaterally. Hypothecation is used where the lender is comfortable with a lighter charge, such as some loans where securities are additional comfort rather than primary security.

points.heading: Margin pledge
points.text: Clients who want to give securities as margin for trading pledge them to their trading member in a margin pledge account. The trading member re-pledges to the clearing member, which re-pledges to the clearing corporation. The shares stay in the client's demat account throughout, ending the old practice of transferring them to the broker.

points.heading: Benefits during pledge
points.text: Corporate benefits on pledged securities, such as dividends, bonus and rights, flow to the beneficial owner (pledgor), because ownership does not change. Bonus shares may also be pledged automatically if the agreement provides. Voting rights also stay with the pledgor unless invoked.

points.heading: Loans against securities
points.text: Banks and NBFCs offer loans against shares, mutual fund units and bonds with a loan-to-value ratio, for example a loan of ₹5 lakh against shares worth ₹10 lakh (50% LTV). If the value falls, the lender makes a margin call; if not met, the pledge is invoked and shares sold. LTV caps are set by RBI for some categories.

points.heading: Pledge alerts
points.text: Depositories send SMS and email alerts on creation and invocation of pledges, so the client knows immediately if a pledge was created without consent. Clients should match these alerts with their loan or margin records.

points.heading: Locked-in and frozen securities
points.text: Locked-in securities can be pledged in specified cases, for example promoter shares pledged to banks for loans to the company, with the lock-in continuing. Frozen securities cannot be pledged until unfrozen.

traps: Getting the initiator wrong. The pledgor initiates creation; the pledgee accepts. The pledgee invokes.
Assuming pledged shares move to the lender's account at creation. They stay in the pledgor's account until invocation.
Treating pledge and hypothecation as identical. Hypothecation invocation needs the hypothecator's confirmation.
Thinking dividends on pledged shares go to the lender. They go to the beneficial owner, the pledgor.
items.recap: Pledgor initiates, pledgee accepts, pledgee invokes on default; closure by pledgor confirmed by pledgee. Shares remain in the pledgor's account until invocation and corporate benefits stay with the pledgor. Hypothecation needs the hypothecator's confirmation to invoke. Margin pledges flow client to trading member to clearing member to clearing corporation.

items.chapter: Special Services – Public Offering / Corporate Actions
items.title: NISM VI Public Issues and Corporate Actions: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on IPO credits and corporate actions in demat for NISM VI: record date, bonus and split maths, rights entitlements, mergers and buybacks.
items.intro: Public issue allotments and corporate actions reach investors' demat accounts automatically through the depository. The exam tests how this happens, the role of the RTA and record date, and simple calculations on bonus issues and splits. Remember a simple rule: securities benefits come to the demat account, cash benefits go to the bank account linked to it.

points.heading: IPO allotment credit
points.text: After the basis of allotment is finalised, the issuer's RTA uploads the allotment as a corporate action and the depository credits shares directly to successful applicants' demat accounts. The investor's DP ID and client ID from the bid are used, so incorrect details lead to failed credits. Listing usually follows on T+3 from issue closure (as of 2026).

points.heading: Record date
points.text: The record date is fixed by the company to determine which beneficial owners are entitled to a corporate benefit. The depository provides the RTA a list of beneficial owners as at the end of the record date. Because of T+1 settlement, an investor must buy at least one trading day before the record date to be on the list.

points.heading: Bonus issue
points.text: A bonus issue gives free shares from reserves. In a 1:2 bonus, a holder gets one new share for every two held: 100 shares become 150. Fractional entitlements are usually consolidated and sold, with proceeds paid in cash. Bonus shares come to the demat account; the share price adjusts downward proportionally.

points.heading: Stock split
points.text: A split reduces face value and increases the number of shares without changing total value. If a ₹10 face value share is split into ₹2, each share becomes five: 100 shares become 500, and price per share falls to roughly one-fifth. The old ISIN is replaced with a new one for the new face value.

points.heading: Rights issue and rights entitlements
points.text: In a rights issue, existing shareholders get the right to buy new shares, usually at a discount. Rights entitlements are credited in demat form with a separate ISIN, can be traded on exchanges or renounced off-market, and lapse if not exercised or sold before the deadline. Applications are made through ASBA.

points.heading: Mergers and amalgamations
points.text: When companies merge, shares of the transferor company are extinguished and the transferee's shares credited per the swap ratio, for example 3 shares of B for every 5 of A. The RTA executes this as a corporate action, and fractions are dealt with as per the scheme.

points.heading: Buyback through tender
points.text: In a tender offer buyback, shareholders tender shares through their broker; shares are blocked in the demat account, and accepted shares are debited while unaccepted shares are released. Cash goes to the linked bank account.

points.heading: Cash benefits
points.text: Dividends, interest and redemption amounts are paid through electronic transfer to the bank account linked to the demat account as per records on the record date. Updating the bank account in the demat client master is therefore essential; dividends are not credited to demat accounts.

points.heading: Debit corporate actions
points.text: Some corporate actions debit securities, such as redemption of debentures, reduction of capital or a reverse split (consolidation of shares). These are executed by the depository on RTA instructions, with the debit and corresponding payment or new credit happening together.

formulas: Bonus shares = shares held × (bonus number ÷ base number); e.g. 200 × 1/4 = 50 new shares.
Shares after split = shares held × (old face value ÷ new face value); e.g. 100 × 10/1 = 1,000.
traps: Thinking dividends are credited to the demat account. They go to the linked bank account; only securities go to the demat account.
Miscalculating bonus: a 1:2 bonus means one new for two held, so 100 becomes 150, not 300.
Buying on the record date and expecting the benefit. With T+1, you must buy at least one trading day before the record date.
Assuming rights entitlements cannot be traded. They are credited in demat form and can be sold or renounced before expiry.
items.recap: RTA executes allotments and corporate actions; the depository credits or debits accounts. Record date decides who is entitled; under T+1 buy a day earlier. 1:2 bonus = one free share per two held; split multiplies shares by old FV/new FV. Rights entitlements are tradeable demat credits. Cash goes to the bank account.

items.chapter: Special Services – Debt Instruments & Government Securities
items.title: NISM VI Debt and G-Secs in Demat: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI revision notes on debt securities in demat: bonds, CPs, CDs, G-secs, T-bills, RBI Retail Direct, and how interest and redemption are processed.
items.intro: Most debt securities in India now exist only in electronic form. This chapter covers corporate bonds and debentures, money market instruments and government securities, and how a depository handles interest payments and redemptions. Questions test features of each instrument, which must be in demat and how retail investors can hold G-secs.

points.heading: Corporate bonds and debentures
points.text: Listed corporate debt securities must be issued and held in demat form. Interest is paid on coupon dates to beneficial owners as per the record date, and principal is repaid on maturity. Debentures can be secured or unsecured, and convertible or non-convertible; most retail trading is in non-convertible debentures (NCDs).

points.heading: Commercial paper
points.text: Commercial paper is an unsecured short-term promissory note issued by companies, NBFCs and other eligible entities for maturities up to one year, at a discount to face value. CPs are issued only in demat form, and their issuance and holding are regulated by RBI, while listing comes under SEBI rules.

points.heading: Certificates of deposit
points.text: CDs are negotiable short-term instruments issued by banks and certain financial institutions at a discount, for tenors from 7 days to one year for banks. They must be in demat form. Unlike a fixed deposit, a CD can be transferred, but cannot be prematurely redeemed by the issuer except as permitted.

points.heading: Government securities
points.text: Central government dated securities and state development loans carry fixed or floating coupons and long maturities, while treasury bills are zero-coupon instruments of 91, 182 and 364 days issued at a discount. RBI acts as debt manager and maintains the Subsidiary General Ledger for banks and institutions.

points.heading: How retail investors hold G-secs
points.text: Retail investors can hold G-secs in their demat accounts through depositories, which hold them in a constituent SGL account with RBI on their behalf. Alternatively, the RBI Retail Direct scheme lets individuals open a gilt account directly with RBI and buy in primary auctions and on the NDS-OM secondary platform.

points.heading: Interest processing
points.text: For demat debt, the depository provides the list of beneficial owners as on the record date to the issuer's RTA or paying agent, which pays interest to the linked bank accounts. If the investor sells just before the record date, the buyer may receive the interest, with the price reflecting accrued interest.

points.heading: Redemption as a corporate action
points.text: On maturity, redemption is processed as a corporate action: the depository debits the securities from beneficial owners' accounts and the issuer pays the redemption amount to their bank accounts. Partial redemptions reduce face value per unit without changing the number of units.

points.heading: T-bill pricing example
points.text: A 364-day T-bill with face value ₹100 issued at ₹93.50 earns ₹6.50 at maturity. The discount yield is calculated on face value, while the investor's effective return is computed on the price paid: 6.50 ÷ 93.50 ≈ 6.95% for the year.

points.heading: Sovereign gold bonds
points.text: SGBs are government securities denominated in grams of gold, issued by RBI on behalf of the government, and can be held in demat form and traded on exchanges. They carry a fixed interest on the issue price in addition to gold price returns. New issuance has been paused, but existing tranches trade and are held in demat.

traps: Treating CPs as secured. Commercial paper is unsecured and backed only by the issuer's credit.
Assuming T-bills pay a coupon. They are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value.
Forgetting that redemption debits the demat account. It is a debit corporate action, with money paid to the bank account.
Thinking retail investors cannot hold G-secs. They can, via demat accounts (CSGL through depositories) or RBI Retail Direct.
items.recap: Listed corporate debt, CPs and CDs exist in demat form. G-secs are held by RBI in SGL accounts; retail can hold via depositories or RBI Retail Direct. T-bills are discounted zero-coupon instruments. Interest goes to beneficial owners on the record date; redemption debits securities and pays money as a corporate action.

items.title: NISM VI Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI): Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VI notes on foreign portfolio investors: DDP registration, Category I and II, KYC, custodians, the 10% individual limit and monitoring by depositories.
items.intro: Foreign portfolio investors are a major source of investment in Indian markets, and depositories play a key role in watching their limits. This chapter covers how FPIs register, their categories, the role of custodians and designated depository participants, and investment limits. Expect conceptual questions with a few numbers that you must recall exactly.

points.heading: What an FPI is
points.text: An FPI is a non-resident entity that invests in Indian securities as a portfolio investor rather than taking a controlling stake. Investment below 10% of a listed company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis is portfolio investment; at 10% or above, it is treated as foreign direct investment.

points.heading: Registration through DDPs
points.text: FPIs register with a Designated Depository Participant, which grants registration on behalf of SEBI. DDPs are SEBI-approved custodians that also act as DPs. Registration is permanent unless suspended or surrendered, subject to payment of fees at the prescribed intervals. The DDP also conducts KYC and ongoing due diligence.

points.heading: Categories
points.text: There are two categories. Category I includes government and government-related investors such as central banks and sovereign wealth funds, multilateral bodies, and appropriately regulated entities like pension funds, banks, insurers and asset managers from eligible jurisdictions. Category II covers all others, such as unregulated funds, family offices and individuals. KYC intensity is higher for Category II.

points.heading: Investment limits
points.text: A single FPI, or an investor group with common ownership, must hold less than 10% of a company's total paid-up equity. The aggregate limit for all FPIs is now the sectoral cap applicable to that sector, unless a company lowers it with shareholder approval. Limits are as of 2026; check current SEBI and RBI rules.

points.heading: Monitoring by depositories
points.text: Depositories monitor FPI holdings in each listed company and publish alerts when aggregate holdings approach the limit, after which further FPI purchases are restricted. When a single FPI group breaches 10%, it must divest the excess within a prescribed short period or have the investment reclassified as FDI.

points.heading: Custodians and settlement
points.text: FPIs appoint a SEBI-registered custodian that holds their securities and settles trades on their behalf. FPIs trade through brokers, and their trades are confirmed by custodians before settlement. Custodians also handle corporate actions, tax deductions and reporting for their FPI clients.

points.heading: PAN, bank and demat accounts
points.text: Every FPI needs a PAN, a demat account with a DP and a special non-resident rupee account with a designated bank for investment flows. Funds come in through banking channels in foreign currency and are converted to rupees; repatriation of sale proceeds and income is permitted after applicable taxes.

points.heading: Permitted instruments
points.text: FPIs can invest in listed equity, unlisted equity within limits, government securities, corporate bonds, units of mutual funds, REITs and InvITs, and exchange-traded derivatives within prescribed limits. Debt investment is subject to RBI's macro-prudential limits, and some government securities are fully accessible under the fully accessible route.

points.heading: Offshore derivative instruments
points.text: Some FPIs issue offshore derivative instruments such as participatory notes to overseas investors with Indian securities as underlying. Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs, subject to strict KYC and reporting. This is a frequent exam detail.

traps: Confusing FPI and FDI thresholds. Below 10% is portfolio investment; 10% and above is FDI.
Thinking SEBI processes FPI registration directly. DDPs grant registration on SEBI's behalf.
Assuming any FPI can issue participatory notes. Only Category I FPIs, subject to conditions.
Forgetting the aggregate limit now defaults to the sectoral cap, not the older 24% default.
items.recap: FPIs register through DDPs on SEBI's behalf; two categories, with Category I for government and regulated entities. Individual FPI or group holdings must stay below 10% of paid-up equity, aggregate up to the sectoral cap. Depositories monitor limits; breaches must be divested or reclassified as FDI. Custodians settle FPI trades; FPIs need PAN and demat accounts.

items.title: NISM VI Depository Investor Services: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on depository investor services for NISM VI: statements, CAS, SMS alerts, grievance escalation via SCORES and ODR, investor protection funds.
items.intro: The final chapter of the Depository Operations syllabus focuses on what investors are entitled to and how they can protect themselves. It covers statements and alerts, grievance redress, the online dispute resolution mechanism, investor protection funds and safe practices. Questions usually ask for the right escalation path, timeline or safeguard in a given situation.

points.heading: Consolidated Account Statement
points.text: Investors with a PAN get a single CAS from the depository that covers all their demat accounts and mutual fund folios. It is sent monthly when there are transactions, and half-yearly otherwise. The CAS shows holdings, transactions and the value of investments, making it easy to spot unauthorised activity.

points.heading: Alerts
points.text: Depositories send SMS and email alerts directly to the investor for debits, pledges and changes in key details. The investor should immediately contact the DP and depository if an alert does not match their own instruction. Depositories also send alerts for credits in many cases.

points.heading: Grievance escalation path
points.text: First, the investor complains to the DP. If unresolved, the investor can approach the depository. Next, the complaint can be lodged on SEBI's SCORES platform, which requires the entity to respond within prescribed timelines, currently 21 calendar days. Unresolved disputes can then go to online dispute resolution.

points.heading: Online dispute resolution
points.text: SEBI's ODR framework allows investors to file disputes against market intermediaries on the Smart ODR portal. Disputes first go to online conciliation; if that fails, to online arbitration with arbitrators empanelled by ODR institutions. The process is time-bound and largely conducted online.

points.heading: Investor protection fund
points.text: Each depository maintains an investor protection fund, financed partly from its profits and penalties, to promote investor education and protect investors against certain defaults. It complements exchange investor protection funds that compensate investors when brokers default.

points.heading: Investor charter
points.text: Depositories and DPs publish an investor charter describing services provided, timelines, rights and obligations of investors, and grievance redress mechanisms. Displaying the charter and monthly complaint data is mandatory, which makes service quality visible.

points.heading: Safe practices
points.text: Investors should never sign blank DIS, keep the DIS booklet safe, strike out unused portions of a slip, update contact details, check statements and alerts regularly, and avoid giving broad authorisations. Use DDPI only if needed and only for the specified purposes. Freezing the account is useful during long absences.

points.heading: e-Voting and other services
points.text: Depositories provide e-voting platforms so beneficial owners can vote on company resolutions online without attending meetings. They also offer online access to holdings, e-DIS and portals for nomination and contact updates.

points.heading: Investor education
points.text: Depositories conduct investor awareness programmes and publish FAQs and guides in Indian languages. Questions sometimes ask about the purpose of investor protection funds; investor education and awareness is one of their main uses.

traps: Going to SCORES before the DP. The first point of complaint is the intermediary; SCORES comes after.
Thinking ODR starts with arbitration. It starts with conciliation; arbitration follows only if conciliation fails.
Believing the CAS is sent only on request. It is sent automatically to PAN-linked investors.
Signing a blank DIS for convenience. This is the most common route for unauthorised transfers.
items.recap: CAS covers all demat and MF holdings, monthly with transactions and half-yearly otherwise. Alerts go directly to investors. Escalate DP, then depository, then SCORES, then ODR (conciliation, then arbitration). Investor protection funds support education and protection. Never sign blank DIS and keep contact details updated.

items.title: NISM VII Securities Market Overview: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII notes on the securities market: primary vs secondary segments, equity, debt, derivatives and money markets, issue types and regulators.
items.intro: The Securities Operations and Risk Management exam begins with a broad map of the market that the rest of the syllabus builds on. Questions here are conceptual: what the market does, how the primary and secondary segments differ, what kinds of issues companies make, which products trade where and which regulator oversees each part.

points.heading: Functions of the market
points.text: The securities market moves savings to productive uses (capital formation), gives investors liquidity because they can sell holdings, discovers prices through continuous trading, and spreads risk across many investors. It also improves corporate governance by forcing listed companies to disclose information regularly.

points.heading: Primary market issues
points.text: Companies raise fresh capital through an IPO (first public issue), FPO (further public issue by a listed company), rights issue (offered to existing shareholders in proportion to holdings), private placement to a small group, preferential allotment, and qualified institutions placement (QIP) to QIBs only. An offer for sale by existing shareholders does not bring money to the company.

points.heading: Secondary market
points.text: Listed securities trade on recognised stock exchanges such as NSE and BSE through an anonymous order-matching system. Trades are guaranteed by clearing corporations. Over-the-counter trades, such as many bond deals, are reported to exchange platforms for transparency and settled through clearing corporations.

points.heading: Market segments
points.text: Equity cash segment trades shares and ETFs; the equity derivatives segment trades futures and options on indices and stocks; the debt segment trades corporate bonds and G-secs; currency and interest rate derivatives trade in separate segments. Commodity derivatives also trade on exchanges under SEBI regulation.

points.heading: Money market vs capital market
points.text: The money market deals in short-term instruments of up to one year, such as treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, call money and repo. The capital market deals in long-term instruments such as equity and bonds. RBI regulates most money market instruments, while SEBI regulates capital market securities.

points.heading: Regulators
points.text: SEBI regulates the securities market and intermediaries; RBI regulates banks, money and government securities markets and foreign exchange; IRDAI regulates insurance; PFRDA regulates pensions; IFSCA regulates financial services in IFSCs such as GIFT City; MCA administers company law. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and Depositories Act are key laws besides the SEBI Act.

points.heading: Government securities vs corporate securities
points.text: Government securities are issued by RBI on behalf of the central and state governments, carry negligible credit risk and are traded mostly by institutions on the NDS-OM platform. Corporate bonds carry credit risk reflected in their ratings and spreads over G-secs. Both carry interest rate risk.

points.heading: Products in the market
points.text: Common products include equity shares, preference shares, debentures, bonds, mutual fund units, ETFs, REIT and InvIT units, warrants, sovereign gold bonds, and derivatives. Each has different risk, return and liquidity features, and operations teams must handle their settlement and corporate actions differently.

points.heading: Role of market infrastructure
points.text: Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories form the backbone. Exchanges provide trading platforms and surveillance, clearing corporations provide settlement guarantee and risk management, and depositories hold securities electronically. Their failure would affect the whole market, so SEBI regulates them as systemically important institutions.

traps: Treating an offer for sale as raising capital for the company. OFS proceeds go to the selling shareholders.
Confusing QIP with private placement to anyone. A QIP is only to qualified institutional buyers.
Assuming SEBI regulates T-bills and call money. These are money market instruments under RBI.
Thinking a rights issue is open to the public. It is offered to existing shareholders, who may renounce their entitlement.
items.recap: The market raises capital, provides liquidity and discovers prices. Primary issues: IPO, FPO, rights, private placement, preferential, QIP; OFS money goes to sellers. Secondary trading on exchanges is guaranteed by clearing corporations. SEBI regulates securities, RBI money markets and G-secs, IFSCA GIFT City. Money market is up to one year.

items.chapter: Market Participants in the Securities Market
items.title: NISM VII Securities Market Participants: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on securities market participants for NISM VII: investor categories, brokers, authorised persons, DPs, custodians, RTAs and rating agencies.
items.intro: This chapter introduces everyone who takes part in the securities market and how each is regulated. Expect questions that describe a role and ask who performs it, or that test how investors are categorised in public issues. A clear grasp of who does what makes later chapters on broking, clearing and settlement much easier.

points.heading: Investors
points.text: Investors include retail individuals, high-net-worth individuals, NRIs, HUFs, corporates, trusts, mutual funds, insurers, pension funds, banks and foreign portfolio investors. In public issues, retail individual investors bid up to ₹2 lakh, non-institutional investors bid above ₹2 lakh, and qualified institutional buyers include mutual funds, FPIs, banks, insurers and similar institutions.

points.heading: Issuers
points.text: Issuers are entities that raise money by issuing securities: companies, governments, public sector units, banks, mutual funds (through units) and infrastructure and real estate trusts. Listed issuers must follow SEBI's listing regulations on disclosure and governance.

points.heading: Stock brokers
points.text: Brokers are members of stock exchanges registered with SEBI who execute trades for clients and themselves. They may be trading members only, or trading-cum-clearing members, or professional clearing members who only clear. Brokers must keep client funds and securities segregated.

points.heading: Authorised persons
points.text: An authorised person is appointed by a broker, with exchange approval, to provide access to trading for clients. The AP acts as the broker's agent; the client relationship and contract notes remain with the broker. The older sub-broker category has been merged into the AP framework.

points.heading: Depository participants and custodians
points.text: DPs open and maintain demat accounts on behalf of depositories. Custodians hold securities and settle trades for institutional clients such as FPIs and mutual funds, handle corporate actions and maintain records. Many large banks act as both DPs and custodians.

points.heading: Clearing members and clearing banks
points.text: Clearing members settle trades with the clearing corporation for themselves and for trading members who appoint them. Clearing banks act as the funds settlement channel, debiting and crediting clearing members' accounts on pay-in and pay-out.

points.heading: Merchant bankers and RTAs
points.text: Merchant bankers manage public issues, perform due diligence and advise on takeovers. RTAs maintain shareholder records, process allotments, handle corporate actions and investor service requests for issuers. Both need SEBI registration.

points.heading: Credit rating agencies and others
points.text: Credit rating agencies assess the credit risk of debt instruments and issuers. Other SEBI-registered participants include investment advisers, research analysts, portfolio managers, mutual funds, alternative investment funds, debenture trustees and bankers to an issue. Each has its own regulations and code of conduct.

points.heading: Market infrastructure institutions
points.text: Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are MIIs. Their governing boards must include public interest directors, and they must maintain net worth and settlement guarantee funds. Brokers and DPs are members or participants of MIIs, which supervise them on SEBI's behalf.

traps: Confusing authorised persons with brokers. An AP is the broker's agent; the client remains the broker's client.
Putting HNIs among QIBs. Individuals bidding above ₹2 lakh are non-institutional investors, not QIBs.
Assuming custodians only hold securities. They also settle trades and process corporate actions for institutional clients.
Mixing up a professional clearing member with a trading member. A PCM clears and settles but does not trade on the exchange.
items.recap: Investors: retail (bids up to ₹2 lakh), NIIs (above ₹2 lakh) and QIBs (institutions). Brokers trade; APs act as brokers' agents; clearing members settle; clearing banks move funds. DPs and custodians hold securities; RTAs keep issuer records; merchant bankers manage issues. MIIs (exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories) supervise members.

items.title: NISM VII Securities Broking Operations: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII notes on broking operations: front, middle and back office, client onboarding, order types, trade life cycle, contract notes and client funds.
items.intro: This chapter looks inside a broking firm and follows a trade from client onboarding to settlement. It is practical and heavily tested: order types, what a contract note must contain and when it is issued, how client funds and securities must be handled, and the purpose of the unique client code. Think like an operations executive when answering.

points.heading: Front, middle and back office
points.text: The front office deals with clients and places orders through dealers or online platforms. The middle office handles risk management, margin monitoring and surveillance. The back office handles confirmation, contract notes, billing, settlement of funds and securities, accounting and regulatory reporting. Questions often ask which office performs a given task.

points.heading: Client onboarding
points.text: Onboarding includes KYC (PAN, identity, address, in-person or video verification), the account opening form, rights and obligations document, risk disclosure document, guidance note, tariff sheet and policies and procedures. Clients choose segments; derivatives activation needs proof of financial capacity. KYC is uploaded to a KRA.

points.heading: Unique client code
points.text: Every order must carry the client's unique client code linked to PAN, so the exchange knows exactly who traded. UCC details must be uploaded to the exchange before the client trades. This prevents brokers from shifting trades between clients and supports surveillance.

points.heading: Order types
points.text: A market order executes at the best available price. A limit order executes only at the specified price or better. A stop-loss order becomes active when a trigger price is hit. Day orders expire at the end of the day; IOC (immediate or cancel) orders execute immediately to the extent possible and cancel the rest.

points.heading: Trade life cycle
points.text: The life cycle runs: order placement, risk checks, order matching, trade confirmation, contract note issue, clearing (computing obligations), pay-in of funds and securities, pay-out and finally reconciliation and statements. Under T+1, pay-in and pay-out happen on the next trading day.

points.heading: Contract notes
points.text: A contract note is the legal record of the trade, issued within 24 hours of execution, physically or electronically with a digital signature. It contains order and trade numbers, time, quantity, price, brokerage, taxes such as STT and GST, and the client's UCC. Brokerage must be shown separately and within permitted limits.

points.heading: Client funds handling
points.text: Client money must be kept in client bank accounts, separate from the broker's own funds. Client funds are upstreamed to the clearing corporation at the end of each day, so they are not exposed to broker misuse. Unused funds must be settled back to clients at the chosen monthly or quarterly running account settlement.

points.heading: Client securities handling
points.text: Client securities must remain in the client's own demat account. Sales use the block mechanism; purchases are paid out directly. Margins in securities are taken through margin pledge, not transfer. Brokers must not use one client's securities for another client's obligations.

points.heading: Statements and reconciliation
points.text: Brokers send clients periodic statements of funds and securities, and must reconcile client balances with bank and demat records daily. Exchanges publish client balances so clients can verify their holdings with exchanges directly.

traps: Confusing stop-loss orders with limit orders. A stop-loss activates only when the trigger price is reached.
Thinking contract notes can be issued within a week. They must be issued within 24 hours of trade execution.
Assuming brokers can use one client's credit balance to fund another client's purchase. Client funds are segregated per client.
Allocating middle office tasks to the back office. Risk management and margin monitoring sit in the middle office.
items.recap: Front office takes orders, middle office manages risk, back office settles and reports. Every order carries a PAN-linked UCC. Market, limit, stop-loss, day and IOC orders behave differently. Contract notes within 24 hours, with brokerage and taxes shown. Client funds upstreamed daily and settled monthly or quarterly; client securities stay in client demat accounts.

items.title: NISM VII Margins and Risk Management: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII risk management notes: VaR, ELM and MTM margins, upfront and peak margin rules, position limits and the Core Settlement Guarantee Fund.
items.intro: Risk management is one of the most important and calculation-heavy chapters in this exam. You must know the types of margins collected in the cash segment and what each protects against, the rules on upfront collection, penalties for short collection, position limits and the settlement guarantee fund. Practise MTM and margin calculations until they are routine.

points.heading: Why margins exist
points.text: Between trade and settlement, prices can move and a party may default. The clearing corporation guarantees settlement through novation, so it must collect margins that cover likely losses. Margins are collected from clearing members, who collect from trading members and clients.

points.heading: VaR margin
points.text: Value at Risk margin covers the potential one-day loss on a position at a high confidence level, typically 99%. It is computed from the volatility of the security. Securities are grouped by liquidity and trading frequency, and less liquid securities attract higher VaR rates.

points.heading: Extreme loss margin
points.text: ELM covers losses beyond what VaR captures, for example a sudden market crash. It is charged in addition to VaR as a percentage of the gross position value, with a minimum prescribed by SEBI for equity in the cash segment (around 3.5% as of 2026; check exchange circulars).

points.heading: Mark-to-market margin
points.text: MTM is the notional loss on open positions, computed by comparing the trade price with the closing price. If a client bought 1,000 shares at ₹500 and the closing price is ₹480, the MTM loss is ₹20,000, which must be paid. MTM gains are not paid out in the cash segment before settlement.

points.heading: Upfront and peak margins
points.text: Brokers must collect VaR and ELM margins from clients upfront, before trades are executed. The clearing corporation checks margin compliance at several random intraday snapshots, so peak positions during the day are fully margined. Intraday leverage beyond collected margin is not allowed.

points.heading: Penalty for short collection
points.text: If a broker collects less margin from a client than required, the clearing corporation levies a penalty on the broker, graded by the shortfall amount and repetition. Brokers cannot pass this penalty to clients except where the client is at fault under rules. This creates a strong incentive for upfront collection.

points.heading: Position and concentration limits
points.text: Exchanges set limits on positions a client or broker can hold in particular securities, especially in derivatives, and monitor concentration to prevent any one entity from dominating a security. Market-wide position limits trigger a ban period in stock derivatives when exceeded.

points.heading: Core Settlement Guarantee Fund
points.text: Each clearing corporation maintains a Core SGF to meet settlement obligations if members default. It is funded by contributions from the clearing corporation, the stock exchange and clearing members, sized by stress tests covering the default of the largest members. The default waterfall uses the defaulter's margins first, then the SGF and other resources.
