points.heading: Broker-level controls
points.text: Brokers set their own client limits, monitor real-time exposure, use pre-trade risk checks and have square-off policies for positions where margins fall short. Policies on when and how positions will be squared off must be disclosed to clients in advance.

formulas: MTM loss = (trade price − closing price) × quantity for a long position; for a short position, (closing price − trade price) × quantity.
Total initial margin (cash segment) = (VaR % + ELM %) × position value; e.g. (12% + 3.5%) × ₹2,00,000 = ₹31,000.
traps: Thinking MTM gains are paid to the client before settlement in the cash segment. Only losses are collected.
Confusing VaR with ELM. VaR covers normal one-day risk; ELM covers extreme moves beyond VaR.
Assuming margins can be collected after the trade. VaR and ELM must be collected upfront.
Believing the Core SGF is used first in a default. The defaulter's own margins and collateral are used first.
items.recap: Margins protect the clearing corporation between trade and settlement. VaR covers one-day risk at 99%; ELM covers extreme moves; MTM collects notional losses. Collect upfront; peak positions are checked through intraday snapshots. Short collection draws penalties. Core SGF backs settlement after defaulter's margins.

items.title: NISM VII Clearing Process and Novation: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII notes on clearing: novation, multilateral netting, clearing members, custodians, clearing banks, depository interface and settlement calendars.
items.intro: Clearing determines exactly what each party must deliver and receive after a day's trading. This chapter covers novation, multilateral netting, the roles of clearing members, custodians and clearing banks, and the depository interface. Make sure you can distinguish clearing from settlement and work through a simple netting example.

points.heading: Clearing vs settlement
points.text: Clearing is the process of identifying and computing obligations: who owes how many securities and how much money. Settlement is the actual transfer of securities and funds to discharge those obligations. In exam terms: clearing calculates, settlement completes.

points.heading: Novation
points.text: The clearing corporation steps in as the counterparty to every trade: it becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. Each member therefore faces only the clearing corporation, which guarantees settlement even if the original counterparty defaults. Novation is the foundation of counterparty risk management.

points.heading: Multilateral netting
points.text: Instead of settling each trade separately, the clearing corporation nets all buys and sells of a member in each security across counterparties. If a member bought 1,000 shares and sold 700 shares of the same company in a settlement, it receives a net 300 shares. Funds are also netted, reducing liquidity needs.

points.heading: Netting at client level
points.text: Netting for delivery is done at the client level, not across clients. If client A sells 100 shares and client B buys 100 shares of the same company through the same broker, both obligations remain; the broker cannot simply net them off and keep A's shares for B.

points.heading: Clearing members
points.text: Trading members who clear their own trades are trading-cum-clearing members; those who only clear for others are professional clearing members. Clearing members maintain margin deposits and must meet net worth requirements. They receive obligation files from the clearing corporation after trading.

points.heading: Custodial trades
points.text: Institutional investors trade through brokers but settle through custodians. The custodian must confirm the trade within a deadline on trade day; once confirmed, the custodian takes on the settlement obligation. If the custodian rejects it, the obligation falls back on the broker.

points.heading: Clearing banks
points.text: Clearing members maintain clearing accounts with designated clearing banks. On pay-in, the clearing corporation debits these accounts; on pay-out, it credits them. Clearing banks therefore act as the funds settlement backbone of the clearing system.

points.heading: Depository interface
points.text: For securities, the clearing corporation sends instructions to the depositories to debit sellers' accounts (blocked shares) and credit buyers' accounts at pay-out. The interface is electronic and automated, which allows T+1 settlement.

points.heading: Settlement calendar
points.text: Exchanges publish a settlement calendar showing trade dates, pay-in and pay-out dates for each settlement. Settlement holidays, which can differ from trading holidays, shift these dates. Operations teams plan funding and deliveries around this calendar.

formulas: Net obligation = total bought − total sold, per security per client; positive means receive, negative means deliver.
traps: Using clearing and settlement as synonyms. Clearing computes obligations; settlement discharges them.
Assuming netting happens across different clients of the same broker. Delivery obligations are netted only within each client's account.
Thinking novation removes all risk. It shifts counterparty risk to the clearing corporation, which manages it through margins and the SGF.
Forgetting that unconfirmed custodial trades become the broker's obligation.
items.recap: Clearing calculates obligations; settlement completes them. Novation makes the clearing corporation the counterparty to all trades. Multilateral netting reduces obligations to net positions per security, within each client. Custodians confirm institutional trades; clearing banks move funds; depositories move securities. Follow the exchange settlement calendar.

items.title: NISM VII Settlement Process Under T+1: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII settlement notes: T+1 and optional T+0, pay-in and pay-out, direct pay-out, short delivery auctions, close-out, bad delivery and settlement holidays.
items.intro: Settlement is where trades are finally completed through the exchange of funds and securities. This chapter covers the T+1 cycle and the optional T+0 framework, pay-in and pay-out timings, what happens when a seller fails to deliver, and how holidays and corporate actions affect settlement. Expect date calculations and 'who bears the cost' questions.

points.heading: Rolling settlement
points.text: Under rolling settlement, each trading day's trades settle separately after a fixed number of days. India moved fully to T+1 for equities in January 2023. A trade on Wednesday settles on Thursday; a trade on Friday settles on the next Monday if it is a working day.

points.heading: Optional T+0
points.text: SEBI introduced an optional same-day settlement cycle for a limited list of stocks, running alongside T+1. Investors choose the cycle when placing orders, and the two cycles have separate price discovery. Most trading still happens in T+1.

points.heading: Pay-in and pay-out
points.text: On the settlement day, sellers' securities and buyers' funds move to the clearing corporation in the pay-in; the clearing corporation then releases securities to buyers and funds to sellers in the pay-out, usually within a few hours. Brokers must then pass funds and securities to clients promptly.

points.heading: Direct pay-out
points.text: Securities bought by a client are credited directly from the clearing corporation to the client's demat account, not to the broker's pool account. This removes the risk of brokers misusing purchased shares. Unpaid securities follow a separate prescribed process.

points.heading: Short delivery and auction
points.text: If a seller delivers fewer shares than sold, the clearing corporation conducts an auction to buy the shortfall for the buyer. The defaulting member pays the difference between the auction price and the original sale price, plus any penalty, so the buyer receives shares at the agreed cost.

points.heading: Close-out
points.text: If the auction fails because no one offers shares, the trade is closed out in cash. The close-out price is typically the higher of the highest price from trade date to auction day, or a fixed premium (such as 20%) over the closing price on the auction day. The defaulter bears this cost.

points.heading: Bad delivery
points.text: Bad delivery used to be common with physical certificates due to signature mismatches or damaged documents. With demat settlement, bad delivery is virtually eliminated, though deliveries can still fail due to frozen accounts or wrong instructions.

points.heading: Settlement holidays
points.text: Settlement holidays are days when banks or clearing are closed, even if exchanges might be open. Pay-in and pay-out move to the next working day. When calculating T+1 settlement dates, skip both weekends and settlement holidays.

points.heading: Corporate actions and open positions
points.text: When a stock goes ex-dividend or ex-bonus, prices are adjusted. A buyer who buys on or after the ex-date does not get the benefit. With T+1, the ex-date and record date are usually the same day, so buying the day before is necessary to receive the benefit.

traps: Counting a weekend as T+1. Friday trades settle on Monday, not Saturday.
Believing the buyer bears auction costs on a short delivery. The defaulting seller pays the difference and penalties.
Assuming T+0 has replaced T+1. T+0 is optional for selected stocks; T+1 remains the main cycle.
Thinking ex-date and record date are always several days apart. Under T+1 they usually coincide.
items.recap: T+1 is the default; T+0 is optional for listed stocks. Pay-in moves sellers' shares and buyers' funds to the clearing corporation; pay-out delivers to buyers' demat accounts directly. Short deliveries are auctioned; failed auctions are closed out at a premium. Defaulters bear costs. Skip weekends and settlement holidays when counting days.

items.title: NISM VII Investor Grievances and Arbitration: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII notes on investor grievances: escalation from broker to exchange to SCORES, Smart ODR conciliation and arbitration, and Investor Protection Fund use.
items.intro: Investors need a clear path to resolve disputes with brokers, listed companies and other intermediaries. This chapter explains the escalation ladder, SEBI's SCORES platform, the online dispute resolution mechanism and the Investor Protection Fund. Questions are often scenarios: a client has a complaint — where should they go first, and what happens next?

points.heading: First stop: the intermediary
points.text: Investors should first complain to the broker or intermediary. Every broker must have a grievance redressal mechanism, a designated email ID for complaints and an investor charter. Many complaints, such as delays in fund payout or contract note issues, are resolved at this stage.

points.heading: Exchange grievance cell
points.text: If the broker does not resolve the complaint, the investor can approach the stock exchange's investor service cell. The exchange takes up the matter with the broker and can direct corrective action. Exchanges have committees that also review claims involving default by members.

points.heading: SCORES
points.text: SEBI's SCORES platform allows online complaints against listed companies and intermediaries. The entity must resolve the complaint within 21 calendar days, and a first-level review by the designated body follows if the investor is unhappy. Complaints must be filed within a prescribed period, generally three years from the cause of action.

points.heading: Online dispute resolution
points.text: Disputes that are not resolved can be taken to the Smart ODR portal. The process begins with online conciliation by an independent conciliator. If conciliation fails within its time limit, the dispute moves to online arbitration, where an arbitrator issues an award. Both parties can participate remotely.

points.heading: Arbitration award and appeal
points.text: The arbitral award is binding, subject to the limited challenge available under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. Fees for ODR are prescribed and may vary by claim size. Investors should keep contract notes, statements and communication records to support their claim.

points.heading: Investor Protection Fund
points.text: Each exchange maintains an IPF to compensate investors whose claims are admitted after a broker is declared a defaulter. Compensation is subject to a per-investor ceiling set by the exchange. The IPF is not used to compensate trading losses due to market movements.

points.heading: What is not a valid complaint
points.text: Losses due to market price movements, dissatisfaction with investment performance, or complaints about investment advice from unregistered tipsters are not grounds for compensation against a broker. Investors who traded through unregistered entities may not get protection.

points.heading: Complaints against listed companies
points.text: Complaints about non-receipt of dividends, transfers or corporate benefits go to the company or RTA first, then to SCORES. Exchanges can also take up complaints against listed companies and may act against non-compliant companies.

points.heading: Investor education
points.text: Exchanges and depositories use part of their investor protection funds for investor awareness programmes. Investors are encouraged to verify broker registration, check alerts and statements, and avoid sharing passwords or giving blank authorisations.

traps: Going straight to arbitration. The ODR process begins with conciliation; arbitration follows only if conciliation fails.
Expecting the IPF to cover market losses. It covers admitted claims against defaulting brokers, within limits.
Assuming SCORES can be used before approaching the intermediary. The investor should first complain to the intermediary.
Thinking trades through unregistered tipsters are protected. Dealings with unregistered entities are generally outside the protection framework.
items.recap: Complain first to the broker, then the exchange, then SCORES (21-day resolution). Unresolved disputes go to Smart ODR: conciliation, then arbitration. IPF compensates admitted claims after broker default, subject to a ceiling, never market losses. Keep records. Avoid unregistered entities.

items.title: NISM VII Other Broker Services (MTF, SLB): Revision Notes
items.description: NISM VII notes on other broker services: margin trading facility, securities lending and borrowing, PMS, MF distribution, research and algo safeguards.
items.intro: Brokers today offer much more than order execution. This chapter covers margin trading, securities lending and borrowing, portfolio management, mutual fund distribution through exchange platforms, research, internet and algorithmic trading, and depository services. For each, know what permission or registration is needed and the main safeguards for clients.

points.heading: Margin trading facility
points.text: Under MTF, a broker funds part of the purchase value of eligible shares, and the client pays the rest as margin. For example, for a ₹1 lakh purchase with a 25% margin, the client pays ₹25,000 and the broker funds ₹75,000, charging interest. The purchased shares are pledged to the broker as collateral.

points.heading: MTF eligibility and safeguards
points.text: Only brokers meeting SEBI's net worth and other requirements can offer MTF, and only on eligible liquid securities. Funding must come from the broker's own funds or permitted borrowings, never from other clients' money. Clients must sign a separate MTF agreement and receive daily margin reports.

points.heading: Risk of MTF
points.text: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. If the stock price falls and margin drops below the requirement, the client gets a margin call; if not met, the broker can sell the shares. Interest costs also reduce returns, especially for longer holding periods.

points.heading: Securities lending and borrowing
points.text: SLB lets investors lend shares they hold to borrowers through the clearing corporation for a fee, for periods up to 12 months. Borrowers use SLB to cover short sales or meet delivery obligations. The clearing corporation guarantees that lent securities come back, reducing counterparty risk for lenders.

points.heading: Portfolio management
points.text: Brokers can offer PMS only after registering separately with SEBI as portfolio managers. The minimum investment per client is ₹50 lakh (as of 2026). PMS can be discretionary, non-discretionary or advisory, and the client's securities are held in a separate demat account.

points.heading: Mutual fund distribution
points.text: Brokers can distribute mutual funds through exchange platforms such as NSE's MF platform and BSE StAR MF after obtaining an ARN through AMFI and the required NISM certification. Units are held in the client's demat account or in statement form.

points.heading: Research services
points.text: Brokers that publish research reports must register as research analysts or have research services handled by registered persons. Research must be independent of investment banking and trading interests, with disclosures of conflicts.

points.heading: Internet and algorithmic trading
points.text: Internet trading requires exchange approval, secure systems, two-factor authentication and clear risk disclosures. Algorithmic trading needs exchange approval of algorithms, risk checks such as order limits and price bands, and audit trails. SEBI has extended a framework for retail algo trading via APIs with controls on brokers.

points.heading: Depository services
points.text: Many brokers are also DPs, offering demat accounts to their clients. The two roles remain distinct, with separate agreements and charges. Investors can choose a DP different from their broker if they prefer.

traps: Funding MTF positions from client money. MTF must be funded only from the broker's own funds or permitted borrowings.
Assuming a broker can offer PMS without separate registration. PMS requires SEBI registration as a portfolio manager.
Treating SLB as an unregulated private loan. It runs through the clearing corporation, which guarantees that lent securities come back.
Thinking MTF reduces risk. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
items.recap: MTF: broker funds part of purchase of eligible stocks, client pays margin, shares pledged, own funds only. SLB through clearing corporation for up to 12 months. PMS needs separate registration, minimum ₹50 lakh. MF distribution needs ARN. Research needs RA compliance. Algo and internet trading need exchange approval and risk controls.

items.title: NISM IX Capital Market for Merchant Bankers: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM IX notes on the capital market for merchant bankers: primary and secondary markets, ways to raise capital, issue intermediaries and key regulators.
items.intro: Merchant banking happens inside the capital market, so this chapter lays out the structure: how companies raise money, who the intermediaries are, and which regulators and laws apply. Questions are direct and test terms, roles and the flow of funds between investors and issuers. A clear picture here saves time in the issue management chapters.

points.heading: Primary and secondary markets
points.text: In the primary market, an issuer sells new securities and receives the money (except in an offer for sale, where proceeds go to selling shareholders). In the secondary market, investors trade existing securities among themselves on exchanges. A healthy secondary market supports the primary market by giving investors an exit.

points.heading: Ways to raise capital
points.text: Listed and unlisted companies raise equity through IPOs, FPOs, rights issues, preferential allotments, qualified institutions placements and private placements. Debt is raised through public issues or private placement of debentures and bonds. Each route has different eligibility, disclosure and pricing rules under SEBI's ICDR and NCS regulations.

points.heading: Issue intermediaries
points.text: A public issue involves lead managers (merchant bankers), registrar to the issue, bankers to the issue including sponsor banks for UPI, syndicate members and brokers who collect bids, self-certified syndicate banks for ASBA, underwriters, legal advisers, statutory auditors, monitoring agencies and credit rating agencies for debt issues.

points.heading: SEBI and its laws
points.text: SEBI regulates issuers and intermediaries under the SEBI Act, 1992, through regulations such as ICDR (issue of capital and disclosure requirements), LODR (listing obligations), SAST (takeovers), Buy-back and Merchant Bankers Regulations. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and Rules govern listing and minimum public shareholding.

points.heading: Companies Act role
points.text: The Companies Act, 2013, administered by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, governs prospectus contents, allotment, share capital, buybacks, mergers and schemes of arrangement. Many issue rules apply under both the Companies Act and SEBI regulations, and merchant bankers must ensure compliance with both.

points.heading: Stock exchanges, depositories and clearing corporations
points.text: Exchanges provide in-principle approval and listing, as well as the bidding platform for book-built issues. Depositories credit allotted shares to investors' demat accounts. Clearing corporations settle secondary market trades after listing. Issuers sign agreements with both depositories before an IPO.

points.heading: Minimum public shareholding
points.text: Listed companies must maintain public shareholding of at least 25%, with relaxations and timelines for large companies listing with lower public shareholding. Merchant bankers consider this when sizing issues and advising promoters on dilution and future offers.

points.heading: Fund flow in an IPO
points.text: Investors bid through ASBA or UPI, so money is blocked in their bank accounts. After allotment, the blocked funds for allotted shares move to the public issue account and then to the issuer's account after listing approval. Unallotted bids are unblocked. Refunds are rare because money is never transferred for unsuccessful bids.

points.heading: Investor categories
points.text: Investors in issues are QIBs (mutual funds, FPIs, banks, insurers, pension funds and similar institutions), non-institutional investors (bids above ₹2 lakh) and retail individual investors (bids up to ₹2 lakh). Employees and existing shareholders may have reservations.

traps: Assuming an offer for sale raises money for the company. OFS proceeds go to selling shareholders.
Confusing ICDR with LODR. ICDR governs issues; LODR governs continuing obligations after listing.
Treating the registrar and the banker to the issue as the same intermediary. The registrar handles allotment records; bankers handle funds.
Forgetting that the Companies Act also applies to prospectus and allotment rules alongside SEBI regulations.
items.recap: Primary market: issuer raises money (except OFS). Routes: IPO, FPO, rights, preferential, QIP, private placement, debt issues. Intermediaries: lead managers, registrar, bankers, syndicate, SCSBs, underwriters, monitoring agency. SEBI regulations (ICDR, LODR, SAST, Buy-back) work with the Companies Act and SCRR. Investors: QIB, NII, retail.

items.title: NISM IX Introduction to Merchant Banking: Revision Notes
items.description: Merchant banking basics for NISM IX: evolution in India, services such as issue management, underwriting and advisory, and the 1992 regulations.
items.intro: This chapter explains what merchant bankers do and how their role developed in India. Expect questions on the range of services, which activities need SEBI registration, the core functions of a lead manager and how merchant bankers protect investors through due diligence. Keep the distinction between regulated issue management and other advisory work clear.

points.heading: Meaning
points.text: A merchant banker is any person engaged in issue management, either by making arrangements for selling, buying or subscribing to securities, or acting as manager, consultant or adviser in relation to such issue management. The definition in the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992 makes issue management the central regulated activity.

points.heading: Evolution in India
points.text: Merchant banking in India began in the late 1960s and 1970s with banks such as Grindlays and SBI setting up merchant banking divisions. Before SEBI, issues were priced under the Controller of Capital Issues. After the 1992 reforms, free pricing and SEBI regulation made due diligence and disclosure the merchant banker's main responsibilities.

points.heading: Issue management
points.text: The lead manager structures the issue, prepares the offer document, coordinates due diligence, files documents with SEBI and exchanges, appoints and coordinates other intermediaries, markets the issue through roadshows, manages book building and oversees allotment and listing. This is the core regulated function.

points.heading: Underwriting
points.text: Merchant bankers often act as underwriters, committing to subscribe to any unsubscribed portion of an issue for a commission. Underwriting gives the issuer certainty of funds and signals confidence. Underwriting obligations must be within the underwriter's capital adequacy.

points.heading: Corporate advisory
points.text: Merchant bankers advise companies on capital structure, fundraising options, mergers, acquisitions, takeovers, buybacks, delisting and restructuring. Acting as manager to an open offer, buyback or delisting offer is regulated and requires a registered merchant banker.

points.heading: Project counselling and loan syndication
points.text: Merchant bankers may help prepare project reports, assess feasibility and arrange loans from banks and financial institutions. These activities do not by themselves require merchant banker registration, but registered entities often provide them alongside issue work.

points.heading: Coordination of intermediaries
points.text: In a public issue, the lead manager coordinates the registrar, bankers, syndicate members, legal advisers, auditors, advertising agencies and printers. The lead manager is responsible for ensuring each performs on time and that investors' interests are protected throughout.

points.heading: Investor protection role
points.text: Because investors rely on the offer document, the merchant banker's due diligence is the main safeguard against false or misleading disclosures. The lead manager must independently verify information, not merely compile what the issuer provides, and certify to SEBI that disclosures are true, fair and adequate.

points.heading: Regulatory framework
points.text: The SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992, substantially amended in December 2024, govern registration, net worth, permitted activities, code of conduct and obligations. Merchant bankers also follow ICDR, SAST, Buy-back and Delisting regulations when acting as managers. The 2024 amendments tightened eligibility and limited activities outside SEBI-regulated work.

traps: Treating loan syndication as a regulated merchant banking activity. Issue management is the core regulated activity; syndication alone does not need registration.
Thinking the lead manager just compiles issuer information. It must verify and certify disclosures through due diligence.
Assuming any adviser can manage an open offer or buyback. Only a SEBI-registered merchant banker can act as manager.
Confusing underwriting with issue management. Underwriting is a commitment to subscribe; management covers the whole process.
items.recap: Merchant banker = issue manager under SEBI's 1992 regulations (amended 2024). Core functions: issue management, underwriting, managing open offers, buybacks and delisting, plus advisory. Lead managers coordinate intermediaries, perform due diligence and certify disclosures. Project counselling and loan syndication alone do not need registration.

items.title: NISM IX Merchant Banker Registration Rules: Revision Notes
items.description: Merchant banker registration notes for NISM IX: eligibility, net worth, fit and proper test, code of conduct, compliance officer and SEBI inspection.
items.intro: This chapter deals with the rules a merchant banker must meet to enter and remain in business. It covers SEBI registration, eligibility and capital requirements, the fit and proper criteria, the code of conduct, general obligations, record keeping and SEBI's supervisory powers. Requirements change, so learn principles and the reasons behind them.

points.heading: Registration
points.text: No person can act as a merchant banker without a certificate of registration from SEBI. SEBI considers the applicant's infrastructure, experience of key personnel, past conduct, net worth and whether it is a fit and proper person. Registration is permanent unless suspended or cancelled, subject to periodic fees.

points.heading: Net worth and categories
points.text: Net worth requirements were increased substantially by the December 2024 amendments, which also replaced the old four-category structure with categories based on the activities undertaken; entities managing main-board equity issues need the highest net worth. Existing merchant bankers get a phased timeline to comply. Check the current figures on SEBI's website.

points.heading: Fit and proper person
points.text: Under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, the applicant, its principal officers and directors must have integrity, reputation and character, and must not be subject to disqualifications such as convictions, insolvency or debarment orders. This test applies at registration and continuously thereafter.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: A merchant banker must act with integrity, dignity and fairness, render the best possible advice, avoid conflicts or disclose them, not make misleading statements, maintain confidentiality, ensure adequate disclosure in offer documents and not indulge in unfair or manipulative practices. It must also cooperate with SEBI.

points.heading: Restrictions on dealings
points.text: A merchant banker cannot deal in securities of an issuer it is advising on the basis of unpublished price-sensitive information, and must disclose its holdings in the issuer. It cannot act as lead manager to an issue of an associate company, which protects independence.

points.heading: Responsibilities to the issue
points.text: A merchant banker must enter into an agreement with the issuer defining responsibilities, submit due diligence certificates, ensure proper underwriting arrangements, and report to SEBI on the issues it manages. It must not accept more lead manager assignments than it can handle properly.

points.heading: Compliance officer
points.text: Every merchant banker appoints a compliance officer who monitors compliance with laws, regulations and circulars, reports non-compliance to SEBI, and handles investor grievances. The compliance officer is a key point of contact during inspections.

points.heading: Books and records
points.text: Merchant bankers must maintain books of account, records and documents, including balance sheets, profit and loss accounts and records of issues managed, for the prescribed period (generally at least five years). SEBI must be informed where they are kept.

points.heading: Inspection and action
points.text: SEBI can inspect a merchant banker's books, records and systems, either routinely or on complaints. Defaults can lead to warnings, monetary penalties under the SEBI Act, suspension or cancellation of registration, or debarment. Enforcement depends on the seriousness and repetition of breaches.

traps: Assuming registration has to be renewed every few years. It is permanent, subject to fees and continued compliance.
Thinking fit and proper is checked only at registration. It is a continuing requirement.
Believing a merchant banker can lead-manage an associate's issue with disclosure. It is prohibited from acting as lead manager for an associate.
Ignoring the 2024 changes. The old Category I to IV structure was replaced and net worth requirements were raised.
items.recap: SEBI registration is mandatory and permanent subject to fees. Net worth and activity-based categories were overhauled in 2024. Fit and proper is a continuing test. Code of conduct: integrity, best advice, disclose conflicts, confidentiality, no misleading statements. No lead managing an associate's issue. Compliance officer, records for at least five years, SEBI inspection powers.

items.title: NISM IX Public Issue Terms and Book Building: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM IX revision notes on public issue terms: book building, price band, cut-off price, anchor investors, QIBs, RHP, green shoe option, ASBA and UPI.
items.intro: Questions in this chapter test precise vocabulary used under the SEBI ICDR Regulations. Many options differ only in a definition, so learn exactly what each term means, who each investor category includes, how price discovery works in book building and what each offer document contains. This chapter carries a large share of marks.

points.heading: Fixed price vs book building
points.text: In a fixed price issue, the price is stated upfront in the offer document. In book building, the issuer announces a price band and investors bid within it; the final price is discovered based on demand. Most Indian IPOs use book building, and demand is shown on exchange websites during the bidding period.

points.heading: Price band
points.text: The floor price is the lower end and the cap price the upper end of the band. Under ICDR, the cap must not exceed 120% of the floor, and the cap must be at least 105% of the floor (as of 2026). For example, with a floor of ₹200, the cap can be anywhere from ₹210 to ₹240.

points.heading: Cut-off price
points.text: Retail investors and employees can bid at 'cut-off', meaning they agree to buy at whatever final price is discovered within the band. Their bid amount is blocked at the cap price. QIBs and non-institutional investors cannot bid at cut-off and must specify a price.

points.heading: Investor categories
points.text: QIBs include mutual funds, FPIs (other than individuals and family offices), banks, insurers, pension and provident funds, AIFs and similar institutions. Non-institutional investors bid above ₹2 lakh; retail individual investors bid up to ₹2 lakh. Employee and shareholder reservations may also exist.

points.heading: Anchor investors
points.text: Anchor investors are QIBs who bid one working day before the issue opens, applying for at least ₹10 crore. Up to 60% of the QIB portion can go to anchors. Half the anchor shares are locked in for 30 days and the rest for 90 days after allotment (check current rules, as SEBI revised anchor reservations in 2025).

points.heading: Offer documents
points.text: The draft red herring prospectus is filed with SEBI for observations. The red herring prospectus contains all details except price and issue size and is filed with the Registrar of Companies before the issue opens. The prospectus is filed after pricing. An abridged prospectus accompanies application forms.

points.heading: Fresh issue and offer for sale
points.text: A fresh issue creates new shares and brings money to the company, diluting existing holders. An offer for sale is the sale of existing shares by promoters or shareholders, bringing no money to the company. Many IPOs combine both.

points.heading: Green shoe option
points.text: The green shoe or over-allotment option allows allotting up to 15% more shares than the issue size, with a stabilising agent using the extra proceeds to buy shares in the market if the price falls below issue price after listing. It supports post-listing price stability.

points.heading: ASBA and UPI
points.text: All public issue applications must use ASBA, which blocks funds in the investor's account. Individual bids up to the prescribed limit can use the UPI mechanism through a sponsor bank, with the investor approving the mandate in their UPI app.

points.heading: Basis of allotment
points.text: After the issue closes, the registrar, lead managers and the designated exchange finalise the basis of allotment. In retail oversubscription, the minimum bid lot is allotted to as many applicants as possible by lottery. Listing must occur within the timeline prescribed, now T+3 after issue closure.

formulas: Maximum cap price = 1.20 × floor price; minimum cap = 1.05 × floor price.
traps: Allowing QIBs or NIIs to bid at cut-off. Only retail and employee bidders can.
Getting the price band rule wrong. The cap can be at most 120% of the floor, not 120% higher.
Treating the RHP as having the final price. The RHP lacks price and size; the prospectus has them.
Confusing OFS and fresh issue. Only a fresh issue brings money to the company.
items.recap: Book building: price band with cap up to 120% of floor; final price discovered. Retail and employees can bid at cut-off. QIBs are institutions; NIIs bid above ₹2 lakh; retail up to ₹2 lakh. Anchors bid a day early, minimum ₹10 crore, up to 60% of QIB book. DRHP to SEBI, RHP without price, prospectus with price. Green shoe up to 15%.

items.title: NISM IX IPO Process and Underwriting: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM IX notes on the public issue process: ICDR eligibility, regulation 6(1) and 6(2) allocation, bidding, promoter contribution, lock-in and underwriting.
items.intro: This chapter follows a public issue from appointing intermediaries to listing. It is the most heavily weighted part of the Merchant Banking exam and mixes sequencing questions with numbers you must recall exactly: eligibility under regulation 6(1) and 6(2), allocation percentages, minimum subscription, promoter contribution and lock-in. Work through numerical examples until the figures stick.

points.heading: Sequence of steps
points.text: Typical sequence: appoint lead managers and other intermediaries; due diligence; board and shareholder approvals; file DRHP with SEBI and exchanges; obtain in-principle approval and SEBI observations; file RHP with RoC; roadshows and anchor bidding; announce price band; bid/issue period; pricing; file prospectus; basis of allotment; credit of shares, unblocking of funds; listing. Questions often scramble these steps.

points.heading: Eligibility under regulation 6(1)
points.text: A company can make an IPO under 6(1) if it meets track-record tests: net tangible assets of at least ₹3 crore in each of the preceding three full years, average operating profit of at least ₹15 crore in the preceding three years with profit in each, and net worth of at least ₹1 crore in each of the preceding three years, among other conditions (as of 2026).

points.heading: Regulation 6(2) route
points.text: A company that does not meet 6(1) tests can still do an IPO through book building if at least 75% of the net offer is allotted to QIBs. This route is used by younger, loss-making technology companies. The higher QIB share is meant to ensure informed investors drive pricing.

points.heading: Allocation percentages
points.text: Under 6(1): QIBs not more than 50% of the net offer, NIIs not less than 15% and retail not less than 35%. Under 6(2): QIBs at least 75%, NIIs not more than 15% and retail not more than 10%. Within QIB, 5% of the non-anchor portion is reserved for mutual funds. The NII portion is split one-third for bids of ₹2–10 lakh and two-thirds for bids above ₹10 lakh.

points.heading: Issue period
points.text: A public issue must stay open for at least three working days and at most ten working days. If the price band is revised, the issue must be extended by at least three working days, subject to the ten-day maximum. Revisions must be widely publicised.

points.heading: Minimum subscription
points.text: If the issue does not receive minimum subscription of 90% of the fresh issue, all application money must be unblocked or refunded within the prescribed time. Underwriting can be used to ensure this threshold is met.

points.heading: Promoter contribution and lock-in
points.text: Promoters must hold at least 20% of the post-issue capital as minimum promoter contribution, locked in for 18 months from allotment, or three years if the issue proceeds are mainly for capital expenditure. Promoter holding in excess of 20% is locked in for six months (one year in the capex case). Pre-IPO shares of other holders are generally locked in for six months.

points.heading: Underwriting
points.text: The issuer signs an underwriting agreement with the book running lead managers and syndicate members after pricing. Underwriters commit to subscribe to any shortfall in their share. An underwriter's total commitments must stay within its capacity; under 6(2) issues, the QIB requirement cannot be met by underwriters' own bids.

points.heading: Basis of allotment and listing
points.text: After closure, the registrar and lead manager finalise allotment with the designated exchange. For retail oversubscription, as many retail bidders as possible get the minimum lot through a lottery. Allotment and listing must be completed on T+3, where T is the issue closing day.

formulas: Minimum promoter contribution = 20% × post-issue paid-up capital; e.g. post-issue capital of 10 crore shares needs at least 2 crore promoter shares locked in.
Retail allocation under 6(1) ≥ 35% × net offer; e.g. net offer ₹1,000 crore gives retail at least ₹350 crore.
traps: Swapping 6(1) and 6(2) percentages. Under 6(1), QIBs are capped at 50%; under 6(2), QIBs must get at least 75%.
Forgetting the capex exception. Lock-in of minimum promoter contribution is three years when proceeds are mainly for capital expenditure.
Thinking minimum subscription is 100%. It is 90% of the fresh issue.
Assuming the issue period can be shortened after a price revision. It must be extended by at least three working days.
items.recap: Steps: intermediaries, due diligence, DRHP, SEBI observations, RHP, anchors, price band, bidding, pricing, prospectus, allotment, listing on T+3. 6(1): QIB ≤50%, NII ≥15%, retail ≥35%. 6(2): QIB ≥75%, NII ≤15%, retail ≤10%. Issue open 3–10 working days. Minimum subscription 90%. Promoters 20% locked in 18 months (3 years for capex).

items.title: NISM IX Lead Manager Due Diligence Duties: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM IX notes on lead manager duties: due diligence, due diligence certificates, monitoring agency, advertisement norms and post-issue obligations.
items.intro: The lead manager's responsibility does not stop at filing an offer document; it covers verifying disclosures, controlling publicity, monitoring the use of funds and handling post-issue matters. This chapter's scenario questions often describe a red flag during due diligence and ask what the merchant banker should do. The guiding principle is verification, not compilation.

points.heading: Meaning of due diligence
points.text: Due diligence is the independent investigation of the issuer's business, financials, legal matters, promoters, litigation, material contracts and risk factors to ensure the offer document is true, fair and adequate. The lead manager must check source documents, meet management, visit sites and consult experts where needed.

points.heading: Due diligence certificates
points.text: The lead manager submits due diligence certificates to SEBI at key stages, such as filing the draft offer document, before the issue opens and after the issue. These certify that disclosures are adequate and that the issuer has complied with applicable laws. A false certificate exposes the merchant banker to action.

points.heading: Responding to red flags
points.text: If the lead manager discovers undisclosed litigation, unusual related-party transactions, doubtful assets or inconsistent figures, it must insist on full disclosure or corrections. If the issuer refuses, the lead manager should not proceed. Signing off on known gaps is a breach of its obligations.

points.heading: Expert reliance
points.text: Lead managers may rely on statutory auditors, legal counsel and other experts for specialised matters, but they must apply professional judgement and cannot blindly accept expert reports when there are warning signs. Consent of experts named in the offer document must be obtained.

points.heading: Monitoring agency
points.text: For issues with fresh issue size above a threshold (₹100 crore as of 2026), the issuer must appoint a monitoring agency, which must be a SEBI-registered credit rating agency, to report on the use of proceeds. Reports go to the audit committee and stock exchanges, and deviations from the stated objects require shareholder approval.

points.heading: Advertisement norms
points.text: Issue advertisements must be truthful, fair and clear, must not contain promises of returns, misleading claims or information not in the offer document, and must include key risk disclosures. Publicity through the issuer's normal business advertising should not be used to promote the issue indirectly.

points.heading: Research and quiet periods
points.text: During the issue period, research reports or statements by syndicate members about the issuer must be consistent with the offer document. Communications that could influence investors outside the offer document are restricted until listing.

points.heading: Post-issue responsibilities
points.text: After the issue closes, the lead manager oversees finalisation of allotment, credit of shares, unblocking of funds, listing and trading approvals. It submits post-issue reports to SEBI and handles investor complaints, coordinating with the registrar to resolve them promptly.

points.heading: Continuing liability
points.text: Liability for misstatements in the offer document can arise under the Companies Act and SEBI regulations even after listing. Directors, promoters, experts and the lead manager may face penalties and civil liability. This is why thorough documentation of due diligence work is essential.

traps: Thinking the lead manager can simply rely on the issuer's statements. It must independently verify information.
Assuming responsibilities end at listing. Post-issue reporting and grievance handling continue afterwards.
Treating issue advertisements like normal product ads. They cannot carry information not in the offer document or misleading claims.
Believing any agency can be the monitoring agency. It must be a SEBI-registered credit rating agency.
items.recap: Due diligence means verifying, not compiling. Certificates go to SEBI at key stages. Red flags must be disclosed or the issue should not proceed. Monitoring agency (a CRA) tracks use of proceeds above the threshold. Advertisements must match the offer document and avoid return promises. Post-issue allotment, listing, reporting and grievances remain the lead manager's job.

items.title: NISM IX Mergers and SAST Takeover Code: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM IX revision notes on mergers and takeovers: schemes under the Companies Act, SAST open offer triggers, creeping acquisition, offer size and price.
items.intro: This chapter covers corporate restructuring and the Takeover Regulations, 2011. You need to know types of mergers, how schemes of arrangement are approved, and the key SAST concepts: triggers for an open offer, creeping acquisition, offer size, offer price, disclosures and the manager's role. Thresholds and timelines are tested exactly, so revise them carefully.

points.heading: Types of combinations
points.text: A horizontal merger joins competitors in the same business; a vertical merger joins firms at different stages of the value chain; a conglomerate merger joins unrelated businesses. In a reverse merger, a larger or unlisted company merges into a smaller listed one. A demerger separates a business into a new company, with shareholders getting shares in it.

points.heading: Schemes of arrangement
points.text: Mergers and demergers are done through schemes under sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013, approved by shareholders and creditors and sanctioned by the NCLT. Listed companies need stock exchange observations and SEBI's no-objection before filing with NCLT. Fast-track mergers under section 233 apply to small companies and wholly owned subsidiaries.

points.heading: Valuation and swap ratio
points.text: Swap ratios are based on valuations using methods such as net asset value, earnings and market price. If Company A is valued at ₹300 per share and B at ₹100 per share, a fair swap ratio might be one A share for three B shares. Valuation reports by registered valuers and fairness opinions by merchant bankers are required for listed companies.

points.heading: Open offer triggers
points.text: An acquirer who, with persons acting in concert, acquires 25% or more of the voting rights of a listed company must make an open offer. Acquiring control, directly or indirectly, also triggers an open offer regardless of the percentage. Indirect acquisitions through an overseas parent can trigger offers too.

points.heading: Creeping acquisition
points.text: An acquirer already holding 25% or more but less than the maximum permissible non-public shareholding can acquire up to 5% additional voting rights in a financial year without an open offer. Crossing 5% in a year triggers an offer. Gross acquisitions are counted, ignoring intermediate sales.

points.heading: Offer size
points.text: A mandatory open offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares of the target company. A voluntary offer by an acquirer holding at least 25% must be for at least 10%. If acceptances exceed the offer size, shares are accepted proportionately.

points.heading: Offer price
points.text: The offer price must be the highest of: the negotiated price under the agreement triggering the offer; the volume-weighted average price paid by the acquirer in the preceding 52 weeks; the highest price paid in the preceding 26 weeks; and, for frequently traded shares, the 60-trading-day volume-weighted average market price. This protects minority shareholders from being underpaid.

points.heading: Disclosures
points.text: Anyone acquiring 5% or more of a listed company's shares must disclose it, and further changes of 2% or more must also be disclosed, within two working days to the company and exchanges. Promoters disclose encumbrances such as pledges of their shares.

points.heading: Manager and escrow
points.text: The acquirer must appoint a SEBI-registered merchant banker, not an associate of the acquirer, as manager to the open offer. An escrow account must be created to secure the offer: 25% of the first ₹500 crore of consideration and 10% of the balance. The manager can forfeit escrow if obligations are not met.

points.heading: Competing offers and withdrawal
points.text: Another person can make a competing offer within 15 working days of the detailed public statement of the first offer. An open offer can be withdrawn only in limited cases, such as statutory approvals being refused or the acquirer's death.

formulas: Escrow = 25% × first ₹500 crore + 10% × consideration above ₹500 crore; e.g. ₹800 crore offer needs ₹125 crore + ₹30 crore = ₹155 crore.
traps: Thinking the open offer must be for 25%. The trigger is 25%; the minimum offer size is 26%.
Counting net instead of gross acquisitions for creeping limits. Gross acquisitions within the year are counted.
Choosing a single price for the offer. The offer price is the highest of several benchmarks.
Allowing an associate merchant banker to manage the offer. The manager must not be an associate of the acquirer.
items.recap: Mergers through NCLT schemes under sections 230–232; fast-track under 233. SAST: 25% or control triggers an open offer; creeping 5% a year for holders between 25% and the maximum non-public holding. Offer size at least 26% (voluntary 10%). Offer price = highest of four benchmarks. Disclose at 5% and every 2%. Escrow 25% of first ₹500 crore plus 10% above.

items.title: NISM IX Disinvestment and Share Buyback: Revision Notes
items.description: Revision notes on disinvestment and buyback for NISM IX: DIPAM methods, OFS via exchanges, CPSE ETFs, buyback limits, tender route and debt-equity cap.
items.intro: This chapter covers two ways ownership changes without a regular public issue. Disinvestment is the government selling its stake in public sector companies; buyback is a company purchasing its own shares. Expect conceptual questions on disinvestment methods and numerical questions on buyback limits, approvals and conditions under the Companies Act and SEBI Buy-back Regulations.

points.heading: Disinvestment and DIPAM
points.text: Disinvestment means the government reducing its shareholding in central public sector enterprises. The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) under the Ministry of Finance manages it. Objectives include raising resources, improving efficiency, broadening ownership and promoting market discipline.

points.heading: Methods of disinvestment
points.text: Methods include IPOs and FPOs of CPSEs, offer for sale through the stock exchange mechanism, strategic sale with transfer of management control to a buyer, exchange traded funds such as CPSE ETF and Bharat 22 ETF, buybacks by CPSEs, and minority stake sales to institutions. Strategic sales involve a bidding process and transfer of control.

points.heading: OFS through stock exchanges
points.text: Promoters of eligible listed companies, including the government, can sell shares through a separate exchange window over one or two days. A minimum 10% of the offer is reserved for retail investors, who may get a discount, and a portion for mutual funds and insurers. The seller announces a floor price in advance.

points.heading: Buyback routes
points.text: Under the SEBI Buy-back Regulations, a listed company can buy back shares through a tender offer to existing shareholders on a proportionate basis. The open market route through stock exchanges has been phased out since April 2025, so tender offers are now the main route (check current rules). Odd-lot buybacks are rare.

points.heading: Sources of buyback
points.text: Buyback can be funded only from free reserves, the securities premium account or proceeds of an issue of other securities, but not from proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares. When funded from free reserves, an amount equal to the nominal value of shares bought back is transferred to the capital redemption reserve.

points.heading: Limits and approvals
points.text: A buyback up to 10% of paid-up capital and free reserves needs only a board resolution; up to 25% needs a special resolution of shareholders. Equity shares bought back in a financial year cannot exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital. The company's post-buyback debt-equity ratio must not exceed 2:1 (with specified exceptions).

points.heading: Gaps and restrictions
points.text: No fresh buyback offer can be made within one year of the previous one. After a buyback, the company cannot issue the same kind of shares for a specified period (except bonus or conversions). Promoters must disclose their intention to participate in tender offers.

points.heading: Extinguishment
points.text: Shares bought back must be extinguished and physically destroyed (or the demat holding extinguished) within the prescribed period, generally seven days of completion. They cannot be reissued, which permanently reduces share capital.

points.heading: Worked example
points.text: A company has paid-up capital ₹100 crore and free reserves ₹400 crore. Board approval alone permits a buyback up to ₹50 crore (10% of ₹500 crore); with a special resolution, up to ₹125 crore (25%). The 2:1 debt-equity test must also hold after the buyback reduces equity.

formulas: Board-approved buyback limit = 10% × (paid-up capital + free reserves); special-resolution limit = 25% × (paid-up capital + free reserves).
traps: Confusing OFS with an IPO. An OFS through exchanges is a sale of existing shares by promoters, bringing no fresh money to the company.
Funding a buyback from a fresh issue of the same kind of shares. That is not permitted.
Applying the 25% limit only to capital. It is 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, and separately 25% of equity shares in a year.
Forgetting the one-year gap between buybacks.
items.recap: Disinvestment is managed by DIPAM via IPO/FPO, OFS through exchanges (10% retail), strategic sale and ETFs. Buyback: tender offer route, funded from free reserves, securities premium or other securities. Up to 10% with board approval, up to 25% with special resolution; post-buyback debt-equity ≤ 2:1; one-year gap; shares extinguished promptly.

items.title: NISM X-B Risk Management and Insurance: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on personal risk management: avoid, reduce, retain or transfer, risk pooling, and insurance principles like insurable interest and subrogation.
items.intro: The Investment Adviser Level 2 exam starts its insurance block by asking how an adviser should think about risk before choosing any product. This chapter covers risk identification, the four ways of handling risk, how insurance pools risk, and the legal principles that decide claims. Expect scenario questions that describe a claim and ask which principle applies.

points.heading: Identifying personal risks
points.text: Households face risks to life (premature death), health (illness, disability), property (fire, theft, accidents), liability (legal claims by others) and income (job loss). The adviser lists these risks, estimates their likely frequency and severity, and checks which ones could derail the client's goals.

points.heading: Four ways to handle risk
points.text: Avoidance means not taking the activity at all, such as not riding a motorbike. Reduction lowers frequency or severity, like installing smoke detectors. Retention means bearing small losses yourself through an emergency fund. Transfer moves the financial impact to someone else, mainly through insurance.

points.heading: Frequency-severity matrix
points.text: Low-frequency, high-severity risks (early death, major illness, house fire) should be transferred through insurance. High-frequency, low-severity risks (minor repairs, small medical bills) are cheaper to retain. High-frequency, high-severity risks should be avoided. This matrix explains why buying insurance for small, predictable losses is inefficient.

points.heading: Pooling of risk
points.text: Insurance works because many people facing similar risks pay premiums into a common pool from which the few who suffer losses are paid. The law of large numbers makes losses predictable for the insurer even though each individual loss is uncertain.

points.heading: Utmost good faith
points.text: Both parties must disclose all material facts honestly. If a proposer hides a known heart condition, the insurer may repudiate the claim. Under the Insurance Act, a life policy cannot be called in question on any ground after three years from issue, which protects policyholders from old disputes.

points.heading: Insurable interest
points.text: The insured must suffer a financial loss if the event occurs. A person has insurable interest in their own life, spouse and dependants, and in property they own. For life insurance it must exist at the time of the contract; for property insurance, at the time of loss.

points.heading: Indemnity, subrogation and contribution
points.text: Indemnity means the insured is restored to the same financial position as before the loss, not better; it applies to general insurance, not life. Subrogation lets the insurer, after paying, step into the insured's shoes to recover from a third party at fault. Contribution shares the loss among multiple insurers covering the same property.

points.heading: Proximate cause
points.text: A claim is payable only if the loss is caused by an insured peril as the dominant, effective cause. If a fire (insured) causes a wall to collapse, the collapse damage is covered; if an uninsured peril is the dominant cause, the claim may fail.

points.heading: Insurance in the financial plan
points.text: Insurance protects goals from being derailed by shocks. An adviser addresses protection before building investment portfolios: an emergency fund, adequate term life cover, health cover and key general insurance come first, and investments are then planned around them.

traps: Applying indemnity to life insurance. Life policies pay the sum assured; they are not indemnity contracts.
Insuring small, frequent losses. Retention is cheaper; insurance suits low-frequency, high-severity risks.
Getting the timing of insurable interest wrong. For life, at inception; for property, at the time of loss.
Confusing subrogation with contribution. Subrogation recovers from a third party; contribution shares between insurers.
items.recap: Identify risks, then avoid, reduce, retain or transfer them using the frequency-severity matrix. Insurance pools risk. Principles: utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity (not life), subrogation, contribution, proximate cause. Protection comes before investment in a financial plan.

items.title: NISM X-B Life Insurance Products: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B revision notes on life insurance: term, endowment, whole life, ULIPs, annuities, riders, surrender and paid-up value, assignment and MWP Act.
items.intro: Advisers must evaluate life insurance products on cost, cover and suitability. This chapter covers the main product types, policy features such as surrender and paid-up values, nomination and assignment, and protection under the Married Women's Property Act. Questions often compare two products or ask what happens when a policyholder stops paying premiums.

points.heading: Term insurance
points.text: Term plans pay the sum assured only if death occurs within the term, with no maturity benefit. They provide the highest cover per rupee of premium. A 30-year-old non-smoker can typically get ₹1 crore cover for a modest annual premium. Return-of-premium versions cost much more.

points.heading: Endowment and money-back
points.text: Endowment plans pay the sum assured plus bonuses on death or maturity. Money-back plans pay part of the sum assured at intervals during the term. Both combine insurance with low-return savings, so cover per rupee is much lower than term insurance.

points.heading: Whole life
points.text: Whole life policies cover the insured for life (often up to age 99 or 100), with premiums paid for a limited term or throughout. They suit estate planning and legacy needs but are expensive compared with term plans.

points.heading: Participating vs non-participating
points.text: Participating policies share in the insurer's surplus through bonuses (reversionary and terminal), which are not guaranteed in advance. Non-participating policies have fixed, guaranteed benefits declared at inception and no bonus.

points.heading: ULIPs
points.text: Unit linked insurance plans invest premiums in market-linked funds after deducting charges such as premium allocation, policy administration, mortality and fund management charges. They have a five-year lock-in. Investment risk is borne by the policyholder, and switching between funds is allowed.

points.heading: Annuities and pension plans
points.text: Immediate annuities convert a lump sum into a regular income starting at once; deferred annuities accumulate first and pay later. Options include life annuity, annuity with return of purchase price, joint life and increasing annuity. Annuity income is taxable as income.

points.heading: Riders
points.text: Riders add cover for a small extra premium: accidental death benefit, critical illness, waiver of premium on disability and term riders. IRDAI caps rider premiums relative to the base policy, so riders cannot dominate the contract.

points.heading: Surrender and paid-up value
points.text: If premiums stop after the policy has acquired value, the policyholder may surrender for cash or keep the policy as paid-up with a reduced sum assured. Paid-up sum assured = sum assured × premiums paid ÷ premiums payable. Surrender early in a policy often means significant loss.

points.heading: Nomination and assignment
points.text: Nomination names who receives the claim; it does not transfer ownership. Assignment transfers rights in the policy, absolutely (for example to a buyer) or conditionally (for a loan). On assignment, an existing nomination is generally cancelled except in certain cases.

points.heading: MWP Act protection
points.text: A policy taken by a married man under section 6 of the Married Women's Property Act, 1874 for his wife and/or children creates a trust; the proceeds cannot be claimed by his creditors. This is useful for business owners with personal guarantees.

formulas: Paid-up sum assured = sum assured × (number of premiums paid ÷ total premiums payable); e.g. ₹10 lakh × 6/20 = ₹3 lakh.
traps: Assuming bonuses are guaranteed in participating plans. Reversionary and terminal bonuses depend on the insurer's surplus.
Thinking ULIP investment risk is borne by the insurer. The policyholder bears it.
Treating nomination as transferring ownership. Assignment transfers ownership; nomination only names a recipient.
Recommending endowment plans for high cover needs. Term plans give far more cover per rupee.
items.recap: Term plans give the most cover per rupee; endowment, money-back and whole life mix savings with low cover. Par policies earn non-guaranteed bonuses; non-par are fixed. ULIPs carry market risk and a five-year lock-in. Paid-up value = SA × paid ÷ payable. Assignment transfers rights; MWP Act protects proceeds from creditors.

items.title: NISM X-B Health and General Insurance: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on health and general insurance: floaters, top-ups and super top-ups, deductibles, co-pay, waiting periods, no-claim bonus and motor cover.
items.intro: Non-life insurance protects a household's savings from large medical bills and property losses. This chapter covers health covers, top-ups, critical illness and personal accident policies, plus motor and home insurance. The exam often asks for claim calculations involving deductibles, co-payments and room-rent limits, so practise these until they are easy.

points.heading: Indemnity health policies
points.text: Standard hospitalisation policies reimburse actual medical expenses up to the sum insured, covering in-patient treatment, pre- and post-hospitalisation and day care procedures. They are indemnity contracts: the claim cannot exceed actual expenses. Cashless claims are settled directly with network hospitals via the TPA or insurer.

points.heading: Individual vs family floater
points.text: An individual policy gives each member their own sum insured. A family floater shares one sum insured across the family, which is cheaper but can be exhausted by one big claim. Floaters suit young families; individual covers suit older members with higher claim probability.

points.heading: Top-up vs super top-up
points.text: A top-up pays when a single claim exceeds the deductible. A super top-up pays when total claims in the policy year exceed the deductible. With a ₹3 lakh deductible and two claims of ₹2 lakh each, a top-up pays nothing, while a super top-up pays ₹1 lakh.

points.heading: Co-payment and deductibles
points.text: Co-payment means the insured bears a fixed percentage of each admissible claim. With 20% co-pay on a ₹1,50,000 claim, the insurer pays ₹1,20,000. A deductible is a fixed amount the insured bears first. Both reduce premiums but increase out-of-pocket costs.

points.heading: Room-rent limits
points.text: Some policies cap room rent, for example 1% of the sum insured per day. If a client chooses a costlier room, many associated charges are reduced proportionately, not just the room rent. This proportionate deduction is a common cause of reduced claims.

points.heading: Waiting periods
points.text: Policies have an initial waiting period (often 30 days except accidents), specific-disease waiting periods, and pre-existing disease waiting periods. IRDAI rules cap PED waiting at 36 months and introduced a moratorium after 60 months of continuous cover, after which claims cannot be contested except for fraud (as of 2026).

points.heading: Critical illness and personal accident
points.text: Critical illness policies pay a lump sum on diagnosis of listed illnesses, regardless of actual expenses; they are benefit, not indemnity, policies. Personal accident policies pay for accidental death and permanent or temporary disablement, often as a percentage of the sum insured.

points.heading: No-claim bonus and portability
points.text: A claim-free year earns a cumulative bonus, increasing the sum insured or reducing premium. Portability lets policyholders move to another insurer while keeping credit for waiting periods already served. Continuity benefits make switching less risky than it seems.

points.heading: Motor and home insurance
points.text: Third-party motor insurance is mandatory under the Motor Vehicles Act; own-damage cover is optional. Depreciation applies to parts unless a zero-depreciation add-on is bought. Home insurance covers the structure and contents against fire, natural perils and burglary, and should reflect reconstruction cost, not market value.

formulas: Insurer's payment with co-pay = admissible claim × (1 − co-pay %).
Super top-up payout = total annual claims − deductible (if positive), up to the super top-up sum insured.
traps: Confusing top-up and super top-up. Top-up looks at each claim; super top-up looks at the year's aggregate.
Thinking critical illness reimburses bills. It pays a fixed lump sum on diagnosis.
Ignoring proportionate deduction. A higher room category reduces many related charges, not only room rent.
Insuring a house at market value. Cover should be based on reconstruction cost; land is not insurable.
items.recap: Indemnity health policies reimburse actual costs; floaters share one sum insured. Top-up works per claim, super top-up on aggregate. Co-pay is a percentage; deductible is a fixed amount. PED waiting capped at 36 months with a 60-month moratorium. Critical illness pays lump sums. Third-party motor cover is compulsory.

items.title: NISM X-B Insurance Needs Analysis (HLV): Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on insurance needs analysis: human life value, needs-based method, adjusting for liabilities and assets, health and disability cover adequacy.
items.intro: An adviser must estimate how much insurance a client really needs, not sell the largest or smallest policy. This chapter covers the human life value and needs-based approaches, how liabilities, goals, existing cover and assets change the answer, and how to judge health and disability needs. Calculations dominate, so practise them step by step.

points.heading: Human life value
points.text: HLV estimates the economic value of a person to their family as the present value of future income they would contribute, net of their own consumption and taxes, until retirement. It answers: how much money would replace the earner's contribution if they died today?

points.heading: HLV worked example
points.text: A 35-year-old earns ₹15 lakh a year after tax and spends ₹4 lakh on himself, so ₹11 lakh supports the family. With 25 working years and a discount rate equal to income growth (a real rate of zero for simplicity), HLV ≈ ₹11 lakh × 25 = ₹2.75 crore. A positive real discount rate would reduce this figure.

points.heading: Needs-based approach
points.text: The needs or expense-replacement method adds up what the family will need: present value of household expenses until dependants become independent, outstanding loans, future goals such as children's education and marriage, and an emergency fund. Existing liquid assets and existing cover are then subtracted.

points.heading: Needs-based example
points.text: Family expenses need a corpus of ₹1.2 crore, home loan outstanding ₹40 lakh, children's education goal ₹30 lakh in present value. Total ₹1.9 crore. Less investments ₹25 lakh and existing cover ₹50 lakh. Additional cover needed = ₹1.15 crore.

points.heading: When HLV and needs differ
points.text: HLV focuses on the earner's income; needs analysis focuses on the family's requirements. A high earner with modest family needs may have a high HLV but low need. A single-income family with large loans may need more than HLV suggests. Advisers often use both and justify the final figure.

points.heading: Reviewing over the life cycle
points.text: Insurance needs usually peak when dependants are young and loans are high, and fall as assets build up and children become independent. Reviews are needed after marriage, childbirth, a home loan, a job change or a big salary jump.

points.heading: Health cover adequacy
points.text: Health cover should reflect city of residence, hospital preference, family size, ages and medical history. Rising medical inflation means cover that seemed adequate five years ago may be insufficient now. A base policy combined with a super top-up is a cost-effective way to raise cover.

points.heading: Disability needs
points.text: Long-term disability can be financially worse than death, because the earner's expenses continue and medical costs rise. Personal accident and disability income covers fill this gap. Group covers from employers are useful but end when the job ends.

points.heading: Typical gaps in Indian households
points.text: Common gaps include reliance on employer group cover alone, investment-oriented policies with tiny sum assured, inadequate cover for the main earner, no disability cover and no separate cover for homemakers whose services have economic value.

formulas: HLV = PV of (annual income − personal consumption − taxes) over remaining working years at a real discount rate.
Additional life cover = (PV of expenses + liabilities + goals + emergency fund) − (liquid assets + existing cover).
traps: Using gross income for HLV. Use income net of personal consumption and taxes.
Forgetting to subtract existing cover and liquid assets in needs analysis.
Assuming insurance needs rise forever. They usually peak in mid-life and fall as assets grow and dependants become independent.
Relying only on employer group health cover. It lapses on job change or retirement.
items.recap: HLV = present value of the earner's future contribution to the family. Needs-based = PV of expenses + loans + goals + emergency fund − assets − existing cover. Use both and review at life events. Health cover must track medical inflation; add disability cover. Avoid relying on group covers alone.

items.title: NISM X-B Retirement Planning Concepts: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on retirement planning concepts: retirement phases, expense estimation, inflation and longevity risk, sequence risk and starting early.
items.intro: Retirement is the longest and most expensive goal most clients have. This chapter explains how to think about retirement before choosing products: the phases of retirement, estimating expenses, the effects of inflation and longevity, sequence-of-returns risk and the power of starting early. Expect conceptual questions and simple projections.

points.heading: Phases of retirement
points.text: Retirement planning has an accumulation phase (building the corpus during working years), a transition phase around retirement, and a distribution phase in which the corpus is drawn down. Within retirement, active early years often cost more on travel, while later years cost more on health and care.

points.heading: Estimating retirement expenses
points.text: Start with current expenses, remove items that will end (children's education, EMIs, commuting), add new ones (health, travel, domestic help), and project to retirement using inflation. A family spending ₹50,000 a month today on items that continue may need about ₹1.6 lakh a month in 20 years at 6% inflation.

points.heading: Income replacement ratio
points.text: Some planners express retirement need as a percentage of pre-retirement income, often 70–80%. This is a shortcut; a detailed expense-based estimate is more reliable because it accounts for the client's actual lifestyle and obligations.

points.heading: Inflation risk
points.text: Inflation erodes purchasing power: at 6% inflation, prices double in about 12 years (rule of 72). A fixed pension that looks adequate at 60 may cover only half the same expenses at 72. Retirement income must therefore include growth assets or inflation-linked components.

points.heading: Longevity risk
points.text: Longevity risk is the risk of outliving savings. Life expectancy at 60 in India is rising, and many retirees live into their late 80s or 90s. Planning to age 85 or 90, rather than average life expectancy, reduces the chance of running out of money.

points.heading: Sequence-of-returns risk
points.text: Poor returns early in retirement, while withdrawals are happening, damage a corpus far more than the same poor returns later. Two retirees with identical average returns can end up very differently depending on the order of returns. Keeping a few years of expenses in stable assets helps manage this.

points.heading: Real rate of return
points.text: What matters is return after inflation. If a portfolio earns 8% and inflation is 6%, the real return is about 1.9% using (1.08 ÷ 1.06) − 1. Corpus calculations use real returns to capture the effect of rising expenses.

points.heading: Starting early
points.text: Compounding rewards early savers. Saving ₹10,000 a month from age 25 to 60 at 10% annual return builds roughly ₹3.8 crore, while starting at 35 produces only about ₹1.3 crore. Delaying ten years cuts the corpus by about two-thirds for the same monthly saving.

points.heading: Levers available
points.text: If the projected corpus falls short, clients can save more, invest in higher-return assets within their risk tolerance, work longer, retire later, reduce planned expenses or plan part-time income. Each lever has trade-offs that the adviser must discuss.

formulas: Real return = (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.
Future expense = current expense × (1 + inflation)^years; e.g. ₹50,000 × 1.06^20 ≈ ₹1.6 lakh a month.
traps: Using nominal returns in corpus calculations without adjusting for inflation. Use the real rate.
Planning only to average life expectancy. Plan to a conservative age such as 85–90.
Ignoring the order of returns. Losses early in retirement hurt more than the same losses later.
Assuming expenses fall sharply at retirement. Health and leisure costs often offset savings on work-related items.
items.recap: Retirement: accumulation, transition, distribution. Estimate continuing expenses and inflate them. Manage inflation, longevity and sequence risk. Use real returns: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. Starting early is the biggest lever; otherwise save more, work longer or spend less.

items.title: NISM X-B Retirement Products and Pensions: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on retirement products: EPF, EPS, VPF, PPF, NPS Tier I and II, Atal Pension Yojana, SCSS, annuities and retirement mutual funds.
items.intro: Indian retirement savers have many products, each with its own rules on contributions, lock-in, withdrawals and taxes.
