This chapter compares them so that an adviser can match products to clients. Limits and exit rules change, so focus on structure and suitability, and use exact figures only with the year in mind.

points.heading: EPF and EPS
points.text: Under the Employees' Provident Fund scheme, employee and employer each contribute 12% of basic wages plus DA. Of the employer's share, 8.33% (on wages up to ₹15,000 a month) goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme, which pays a monthly pension after ten years of service. EPF interest is declared annually by EPFO.

points.heading: Voluntary Provident Fund
points.text: Employees can contribute more than 12% to their PF account as VPF, earning the same interest rate. Interest on employee contributions above a threshold is taxable, which reduces VPF's appeal for high earners.

points.heading: Public Provident Fund
points.text: PPF is a government-backed account with a 15-year term, extendable in blocks of five years, with annual contributions between ₹500 and ₹1.5 lakh. Partial withdrawals and loans are allowed after specified years. Interest is set quarterly by the government and is tax-free.

points.heading: NPS Tier I and Tier II
points.text: The National Pension System, regulated by PFRDA, has a Tier I pension account with restrictions on withdrawal and a Tier II voluntary account with free withdrawals. Subscribers choose active or auto choice across equity, corporate bonds and government securities, with lifecycle funds reducing equity exposure with age.

points.heading: NPS exit rules
points.text: At normal exit, a part of the corpus must be used to buy an annuity and the rest can be withdrawn. PFRDA relaxed these rules in 2025, reducing the minimum annuity requirement for many non-government subscribers (check current PFRDA rules). Premature exit requires a larger annuity share.

points.heading: Atal Pension Yojana
points.text: APY targets unorganised-sector workers aged 18–40, offering a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 from age 60 depending on contribution and joining age. On the subscriber's death, the spouse gets the pension and then the nominee gets the corpus.

points.heading: Senior citizens' schemes
points.text: The Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme offers a five-year deposit for those aged 60 and above, with quarterly interest and an investment ceiling. The Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana has closed for new investment. Bank senior citizen FDs offer additional interest.

points.heading: Annuity products
points.text: Annuities from life insurers convert a corpus into lifelong income. Options include life annuity, joint life with last survivor, and return of purchase price. Annuity rates are fixed at purchase, so buying when interest rates are low locks in lower income.

points.heading: Retirement-oriented mutual funds
points.text: Retirement solution-oriented mutual fund schemes have a lock-in of five years or until retirement, whichever is earlier. They are flexible in asset allocation but offer no guaranteed income. They suit clients who want market-linked growth with built-in discipline.

traps: Assuming the full employer contribution goes to EPF. A part goes to EPS, calculated on capped wages.
Treating NPS Tier II like Tier I. Tier II is voluntary, flexible and has no retirement lock-in.
Thinking APY is open to anyone at any age. It is for ages 18–40 joining.
Believing annuity income is tax-free. It is taxable as income in the year received.
items.recap: EPF: 12% + 12%, with part of employer share to EPS. PPF: 15 years, ₹500–₹1.5 lakh a year, tax-free. NPS: Tier I locked to retirement with partial annuity at exit; Tier II flexible. APY: guaranteed pension, entry 18–40. SCSS for 60+. Annuities lock in rates. Check current limits before advising.

items.title: NISM X-B Retirement Corpus Calculation: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on retirement corpus and drawdown: first-year expense, real-rate annuity maths, SIP needed, SWPs, annuities and the bucket strategy.
items.intro: This is the most calculation-heavy part of the retirement block. You must estimate the corpus needed at retirement, the monthly saving required to build it, and a sensible way to draw it down. Questions give a client's age, expenses, inflation and return assumptions and ask for a number, so practise every step with a calculator.

points.heading: Step 1: first-year expense
points.text: Project today's continuing annual expenses to the retirement year. A client spending ₹3 lakh a year on continuing items, retiring in 25 years with 6% inflation, needs about ₹3 lakh × 1.06^25 ≈ ₹12.9 lakh in the first year of retirement.

points.heading: Step 2: real rate during retirement
points.text: During retirement, expenses keep rising with inflation while the corpus earns a return. Combine them into a real rate: with 7% return and 5% inflation, real rate = 1.07 ÷ 1.05 − 1 ≈ 1.9%. Using this rate lets you treat rising withdrawals as a flat annuity.

points.heading: Step 3: corpus as PV of an annuity
points.text: The corpus is the present value, at retirement, of the first-year expense for the retirement period at the real rate, usually as an annuity due because withdrawals start at the beginning of each year. For ₹6 lakh a year, 25 years and 2% real rate, the factor is about 19.9, giving a corpus of roughly ₹1.19 crore.

points.heading: Step 4: saving required
points.text: Subtract the future value of existing retirement savings from the target corpus and calculate the monthly SIP needed for the gap. If the gap is ₹1 crore in 20 years at 10% a year, the required SIP is roughly ₹13,000 a month. A step-up SIP that rises with salary lowers the starting amount.

points.heading: Systematic withdrawal plans
points.text: An SWP from mutual funds gives regular cash flows while the remaining units stay invested. Each withdrawal redeems units, so only the gain portion is taxed. SWPs offer flexibility and potential growth but no guarantee of lifelong income.

points.heading: Annuities
points.text: Annuities give guaranteed lifelong income, removing longevity risk, but are inflexible, taxable as income and lock in prevailing rates. A common approach is to annuitise part of the corpus to cover essential expenses and keep the rest invested for growth and flexibility.

points.heading: Bucket strategy
points.text: Split the corpus into buckets: a cash bucket for 1–3 years of expenses, an income bucket in short and medium-term debt for the next few years, and a growth bucket in equity for later years. Refill buckets periodically. This reduces the need to sell equity during market falls, managing sequence risk.

points.heading: Sustainable withdrawal rate
points.text: The well-known 4% rule comes from US data. In India, higher inflation makes a lower or flexible initial withdrawal rate more prudent. Withdrawals should be reviewed annually against portfolio performance rather than fixed rigidly.

points.heading: Multiple income sources
points.text: A retiree's income may combine EPS or other pensions, annuities, SCSS interest, rent, SWPs and dividends. The plan should sequence these to cover essential expenses with stable sources and discretionary expenses with market-linked sources.

formulas: Corpus = E × [1 − (1 + r)^−n] ÷ r × (1 + r), where E = first-year expense, r = real rate, n = retirement years.
Monthly SIP = FV × i ÷ [(1 + i)^m − 1], where i = monthly rate and m = number of months (end-of-month investment).
traps: Using the nominal return to discount retirement expenses. Use the inflation-adjusted real rate.
Treating withdrawals as starting at year end. Retirement withdrawals usually start immediately, so use an annuity due.
Assuming SWPs are guaranteed income. They depend on fund performance and can run out.
Applying the US 4% rule without adjustment. Indian inflation usually requires a more cautious rate.
items.recap: Inflate today's expenses to retirement, convert return and inflation into a real rate, and compute corpus as PV of an annuity due. Find the SIP needed for the gap. Draw down using a mix of annuities for essentials and SWPs or buckets for growth. Review withdrawal rates yearly.

items.title: NISM X-B Income Tax Fundamentals: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on income tax basics: residential status, heads of income, old vs new regime, rebate, clubbing, set-off and carry forward, and advance tax.
items.intro: Advisers must understand how individuals are taxed in order to make sensible recommendations. This chapter covers residential status, heads of income, the two tax regimes, deductions, clubbing, loss set-off and advance tax. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 with largely similar concepts and a single 'tax year', so focus on principles rather than section numbers.

points.heading: Residential status
points.text: An individual is resident in India for a year if present for 182 days or more, or 60 days in the year plus 365 days in the preceding four years (with modified rules for certain Indian citizens and visitors). Residents are taxed on global income; non-residents only on income arising or received in India.

points.heading: Heads of income
points.text: Income is computed under five heads: salaries, income from house property, profits and gains of business or profession, capital gains, and income from other sources. Each head has its own deductions and rules, and the totals are combined to compute gross total income.

points.heading: New vs old regime
points.text: The new regime is the default, with lower slab rates and few deductions; the old regime allows deductions such as provident fund, life insurance and ELSS, health insurance premiums and home loan interest. Salaried taxpayers can choose each year; those with business income have limited switching options.

points.heading: Rebate and standard deduction
points.text: Under the new regime, a rebate makes total income up to ₹12 lakh effectively tax-free for residents, and salaried individuals get a standard deduction of ₹75,000 (as of 2026; check the current Finance Act). Rebate does not apply to special-rate income such as certain capital gains.

points.heading: Surcharge and cess
points.text: Surcharge is an additional tax on high incomes, applied on tax at rates that increase with income bands. Health and education cess of 4% applies on tax plus surcharge. Marginal relief prevents the surcharge from exceeding the extra income above a threshold.

points.heading: Clubbing of income
points.text: Income from assets transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is taxed in the transferor's hands. A minor child's income is generally clubbed with the parent having higher income, with a small exemption per child, except income from the minor's own skill or manual work.

points.heading: Set-off and carry forward
points.text: Losses can be set off against income in the same year subject to rules. A house property loss can be set off against other heads up to a limit. Short-term capital loss can be set off against short or long-term gains; long-term capital loss only against long-term gains. Most unabsorbed losses carry forward for eight years if the return is filed on time.

points.heading: Advance tax
points.text: Taxpayers whose liability exceeds ₹10,000 must pay advance tax in instalments: 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March. Resident senior citizens without business income are exempt. Shortfalls attract interest.

points.heading: Filing returns
points.text: Returns must be filed by the due date, typically 31 July for non-audit individual cases. Late filing attracts fees and loss of the right to carry forward certain losses. Updated returns allow correcting omissions within a time limit, with additional tax.

traps: Assuming non-residents are taxed on global income. Only residents are taxed on worldwide income.
Setting off long-term capital loss against short-term gains. It can only be set off against long-term gains.
Applying the rebate to special-rate capital gains. The rebate generally does not cover them.
Clubbing a minor's income from their own skill. That income is not clubbed.
items.recap: Residential status decides scope of taxation. Five heads of income. New regime is the default with rebate up to ₹12 lakh and ₹75,000 standard deduction (check current year); old regime keeps deductions. Cess 4% on tax plus surcharge. Clubbing for spouse transfers and minors. LTCL only against LTCG. Advance tax 15/45/75/100.

items.title: NISM X-B Taxation of Investment Products: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on taxing investments: equity and equity fund gains, debt funds, bonds, FDs, PPF, ELSS, ULIPs, NPS, gold and property, dividends and TDS.
items.intro: Post-tax return is what clients keep, so advisers must know how each product is taxed. This chapter covers holding periods, capital gains rates, exemptions and TDS across equity, debt, insurance, retirement, gold and real estate. Rates changed in July 2024 and the Income-tax Act, 2025 took effect in April 2026, so always note the year assumed in a question.

points.heading: Listed equity and equity funds
points.text: For listed shares and equity-oriented funds, gains are long-term after 12 months. As of 2026, short-term gains are taxed at 20% and long-term gains at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year, provided STT is paid (check current rates). There is no indexation.

points.heading: Debt mutual funds
points.text: Units of specified debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates regardless of holding period. This removed the earlier long-term benefit with indexation. Advisers should compare post-tax yields of debt funds and FDs accordingly.

points.heading: Bonds and debentures
points.text: Interest is taxed at slab rates. For listed bonds, gains after 12 months are long-term at 12.5% without indexation; unlisted bonds and debentures are taxed at slab rates on gains. Tax-free bonds pay exempt interest but gains on sale are taxable.

points.heading: Bank deposits and small savings
points.text: FD and RD interest is taxed at slab rates on an accrual basis, with TDS above a threshold. PPF has exempt-exempt-exempt status: contributions (old regime), interest and maturity are all exempt. NSC interest is taxable but deemed reinvested.

points.heading: ELSS
points.text: Equity-linked savings schemes have a three-year lock-in and qualify for deduction under the old regime within the overall limit. Gains on redemption are taxed like other equity funds. Under the new regime, there is no deduction benefit.

points.heading: ULIPs and life insurance
points.text: Maturity proceeds of life policies are exempt if conditions on premium relative to sum assured are met. For ULIPs issued after February 2021 with annual premium above ₹2.5 lakh, and non-ULIP policies above ₹5 lakh premium from April 2023, maturity proceeds are taxable. Death benefits remain exempt.

points.heading: NPS
points.text: Contributions get deductions under specified provisions, including employer contributions under the new regime. At exit, the lump sum withdrawal up to the permitted limit is exempt, while annuity income is taxable as income. Tier II has no such tax benefits for most subscribers.

points.heading: Gold and real estate
points.text: Physical gold, gold funds and real estate become long-term after 24 months and are taxed at 12.5% without indexation. For property bought before 23 July 2024, resident individuals may choose the older 20% with indexation route. Sovereign gold bonds held to maturity give exempt gains.

points.heading: Dividends and TDS
points.text: Dividends are taxed at slab rates in the investor's hands, with TDS by the company or fund above a threshold. Buyback proceeds are now taxed as dividends in shareholders' hands (from October 2024). Interest TDS can be avoided by eligible investors submitting declarations.

traps: Assuming debt funds still get indexation. Units bought from April 2023 are taxed at slab rates.
Thinking all life insurance maturity proceeds are tax-free. High-premium policies lose the exemption.
Using a 36-month holding period for listed equity. It is 12 months; 24 months applies to gold, property and unlisted assets.
Treating the NPS annuity as tax-free. Only the permitted lump sum is exempt; annuity income is taxable.
items.recap: Listed equity: long-term after 12 months, STCG 20%, LTCG 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh (as of 2026). Debt funds bought from April 2023: slab rates. Gold and property: 24 months, 12.5% without indexation. PPF is EEE. ELSS: three-year lock-in. High-premium ULIPs and policies lose exemption. Dividends at slab rates.

items.title: NISM X-B Wealth and Estate Planning: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on estate planning concepts: nominee vs legal heir, joint holding, gifts, power of attorney, wills and trusts, and keeping records in order.
items.intro: Estate planning ensures that wealth reaches the intended people smoothly when someone dies or becomes unable to manage their affairs. This chapter introduces wealth management for affluent clients and the tools for transferring wealth. Questions focus on roles: who is a nominee, legal heir, executor or trustee, and which tool suits which family situation.

points.heading: Wealth management scope
points.text: Wealth management for high-net-worth clients integrates investment management, tax planning, risk management, succession and philanthropy. It goes beyond portfolio returns to protecting and transferring wealth across generations, often coordinating with lawyers and chartered accountants.

points.heading: Nominee vs legal heir
points.text: A nominee receives assets from the institution, giving it a valid discharge, but courts have held that nomination generally does not override succession law. In 2023, the Supreme Court confirmed that nominees for shares do not become absolute owners; legal heirs under a will or succession law ultimately inherit. Nomination should therefore match the will.

points.heading: Joint holding
points.text: Joint holding with 'either or survivor' mode allows the survivor to operate the account after one holder's death. It avoids freezing of accounts but does not decide ultimate ownership, which still follows the will or succession law. Joint holding is a convenience tool, not a substitute for a will.

points.heading: Gifts
points.text: Gifts during one's lifetime transfer assets immediately. In India, gifts from specified relatives are tax-free in the recipient's hands, while gifts from non-relatives above ₹50,000 in a year are taxable. Gifts of immovable property need a registered gift deed. Clubbing rules may apply to gifts to a spouse or minor child.

points.heading: Power of attorney
points.text: A power of attorney authorises another person to act on one's behalf, for example to manage bank accounts or property. A general POA covers broad acts; a specific POA covers defined acts. A POA ends on the death or, in most cases, the mental incapacity of the principal, so it cannot be used for estate transfer.

points.heading: Wills
points.text: A will states how a person's assets will be distributed after death and names an executor to carry it out. It can be changed any number of times until death; the latest valid will prevails. Without a will, assets pass under the applicable succession law, which may not match the person's wishes.

points.heading: Trusts
points.text: A trust transfers assets to trustees to be held for beneficiaries. Private trusts help with protecting assets for minors or dependants with special needs, managing family business holdings and avoiding fragmentation. They can operate during the settlor's lifetime and continue after death.

points.heading: Roles to distinguish
points.text: Executor: carries out the will. Trustee: manages trust assets for beneficiaries. Nominee: receives assets from an institution. Legal heir: entitled under succession law. Beneficiary: receives benefit under a will or trust. Exam questions often swap these roles.

points.heading: Records and documentation
points.text: Estate planning fails when families cannot find assets. A record of accounts, policies, demat holdings, property documents, loans and digital assets, kept with key contacts, saves months of effort. Updating nominations, wills and records after life events is essential for everyone, not only the very wealthy.

traps: Treating a nominee as the ultimate owner. Legal heirs or will beneficiaries usually prevail.
Assuming a power of attorney survives death. It ends on the principal's death.
Believing joint holding settles ownership. It allows operation by the survivor, but ownership follows the will or law.
Thinking estate planning is only for the rich. Every family benefits from nominations, a will and organised records.
items.recap: Wealth management integrates investment, tax, risk and succession. Nominees receive; legal heirs own. Joint holding gives access, not ownership. Gifts from relatives are tax-free; from others above ₹50,000 taxable. POA ends at death. Wills direct distribution through an executor; trusts manage assets for beneficiaries. Keep records updated.

items.title: NISM X-B Wills, Succession and Trusts Law: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on wills and succession: valid will, codicil, probate, Hindu Succession Act heirs, Muslim law limits and private trusts under the Trusts Act.
items.intro: This chapter covers the legal tools of estate planning in India. You need to know what makes a will valid, when probate is needed, how property is distributed when someone dies without a will under different personal laws, and how trusts are created. Expect distribution scenarios: a person dies intestate leaving certain relatives — who gets what?

points.heading: Valid will
points.text: A will must be made by a person of sound mind who is not a minor, voluntarily and without coercion. Under the Indian Succession Act, it must be signed by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses who see the testator sign. Registration is optional, but it adds evidential strength. Witnesses should not be beneficiaries.

points.heading: Codicil and revocation
points.text: A codicil is a document that adds to, changes or explains a will and must be executed with the same formalities. A will can be revoked by a later will, by a written declaration of revocation, or by destroying it with the intention to revoke. Under the Indian Succession Act, marriage revokes a will for some communities but not for Hindus.

points.heading: Probate and letters of administration
points.text: Probate is a court's certification of a will's validity, granted to the executor. It is mandatory for wills of Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains made in, or covering immovable property in, the former presidency towns of Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai. Letters of administration are granted when there is no executor or no will.

points.heading: Hindu Succession Act basics
points.text: When a Hindu male dies intestate, his property goes first to Class I heirs, such as sons, daughters, widow and mother, who share equally. If there are none, it passes to Class II heirs, then agnates and cognates. Daughters have been coparceners in ancestral property, equal to sons, since the 2005 amendment.

points.heading: Distribution example
points.text: A Hindu man dies intestate leaving his widow, mother, one son and one daughter. All four are Class I heirs and each gets one-fourth of his separate property. Children of a predeceased son or daughter take their parent's share together.

points.heading: Hindu female's property
points.text: Property of a Hindu woman dying intestate goes first to her sons, daughters and husband; property inherited from her parents goes back to her father's heirs if she has no children; property inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes to the husband's heirs.

points.heading: Muslim personal law
points.text: A Muslim can bequeath by will only up to one-third of the estate to non-heirs without the consent of the heirs; the rest passes under Islamic law with fixed shares. A will in favour of an heir needs the other heirs' consent. Christians and Parsis are governed by the Indian Succession Act for intestacy.

points.heading: Trusts under the Indian Trusts Act
points.text: A private trust is created when the author (settlor) transfers property to a trustee for beneficiaries with a clear intention, purpose, beneficiary and property. Trusts of immovable property need a registered instrument. Public charitable trusts are governed by state laws and tax rules.

points.heading: Types of trusts
points.text: A revocable trust can be cancelled by the settlor; an irrevocable trust cannot. In a specific trust, beneficiaries' shares are fixed; in a discretionary trust, trustees decide distributions. Trusts are used for minors, special-needs dependants, family businesses and to avoid fragmentation of assets.

traps: Thinking a will must be registered to be valid. Registration is optional; attestation by two witnesses is required.
Assuming the widow gets a larger share than children under Class I. Class I heirs share equally.
Believing a Muslim can freely will all property. Bequests are limited to one-third without heirs' consent.
Confusing probate and letters of administration. Probate validates a will with an executor; letters of administration apply when there is no executor or no will.
items.recap: Valid will: adult of sound mind, signed, attested by two witnesses; registration optional. Codicil amends. Probate mandatory in specified cases for wills in Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai. Hindu Class I heirs share equally; daughters are coparceners. Muslims can will only one-third to non-heirs. Trusts need settlor, trustee, beneficiary and property.

items.title: NISM X-B Financial Planning Case Studies: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM X-B notes on comprehensive financial planning: data gathering, analysis, goal priority, integrating insurance, tax and estate, and plan reviews.
items.intro: The final chapter of the Investment Adviser Level 2 exam ties all modules into one client plan. Case-study questions present a family's data and ask what to address first, how to resolve conflicting goals and what to change when circumstances shift. Marks depend on logical, client-centred judgement as much as on correct calculations.

points.heading: Planning process
points.text: The process is: establish the relationship and scope, gather data (quantitative and qualitative), analyse the current position, develop recommendations, present and agree on them, implement, and monitor and review. SEBI's investment adviser rules also require risk profiling and suitability assessment before advice.

points.heading: Data gathering
points.text: Collect income, expenses, assets, liabilities, insurance, investments, tax details, goals with time frames, risk tolerance and family circumstances. Qualitative data such as values, attitudes to debt and family responsibilities often explains why a plan succeeds or fails. Incomplete data leads to flawed plans.

points.heading: Analysing the current position
points.text: Build a personal balance sheet and cash flow statement. Key ratios include savings ratio (savings ÷ income), liquidity ratio (liquid assets ÷ monthly expenses), debt-to-income ratio (EMIs ÷ income) and solvency (net worth ÷ assets). These quickly reveal weaknesses.

points.heading: Order of priorities
points.text: A common sequence: build an emergency fund of several months' expenses, secure adequate term life and health cover, repay high-cost debt such as credit cards, and then invest for goals. Retirement should not be sacrificed for children's goals because children can borrow for education, but retirees cannot borrow for retirement.

points.heading: Resolving conflicting goals
points.text: When resources fall short, options include extending goal timelines, reducing goal amounts, increasing savings, improving asset allocation within risk tolerance or prioritising goals by importance. The adviser presents trade-offs clearly and lets the client decide with informed consent.

points.heading: Integration across areas
points.text: Recommendations must work together: insurance needs reflect liabilities and goals; investment allocation reflects goal horizons; tax planning should not drive poor product choices; estate planning aligns nominations with the will. A tax-saving product that fails the suitability test is not a good recommendation.

points.heading: Case example
points.text: A 38-year-old with two children, ₹20 lakh income, a ₹50 lakh home loan, only employer health cover and an endowment policy with ₹10 lakh cover. Priority: buy adequate term cover and family health cover, build an emergency fund, then restructure investments towards education and retirement goals.

points.heading: Presenting recommendations
points.text: A good plan states assumptions, explains the reasoning for each recommendation, shows the impact on goals, discloses costs and conflicts, and gives action steps with responsibilities and dates. Clear documentation protects both client and adviser.

points.heading: Monitoring and review
points.text: Plans need regular reviews, at least annually, and after life events such as job loss, inheritance, birth, divorce or a market crash. Reviews compare progress to targets, rebalance portfolios and update assumptions. A plan is a living document, not a one-time report.

formulas: Savings ratio = annual savings ÷ annual income; liquidity ratio = liquid assets ÷ monthly expenses; debt-service ratio = total EMIs ÷ monthly income.
traps: Investing before securing protection. Emergency fund and insurance come first.
Prioritising children's education over retirement without discussion. Education can be funded by loans; retirement cannot.
Recommending a product mainly for tax savings. Suitability must come first.
Treating the plan as complete after delivery. Monitoring and reviews are part of the process.
items.recap: Process: engage, gather data, analyse, recommend, implement, monitor. Use ratios to diagnose. Priority: emergency fund, insurance, costly debt, then goals. Do not sacrifice retirement for children's goals. Integrate insurance, investments, tax and estate. Present assumptions and trade-offs clearly and review at least yearly and after life events.

items.title: NISM XV Research Analyst Profession: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on the research analyst's role: sell-side, buy-side and independent analysts, the research process, key skills, users of research and ethics.
items.intro: The Research Analyst exam opens by describing what analysts do and why their independence matters. Questions test the different types of analysts, who uses research, the steps of the research process, the skills required and the ethical foundations of the profession. These ideas recur in the regulatory chapter, so build a clear picture early.

points.heading: What an analyst does
points.text: A research analyst studies economies, industries and companies, builds forecasts and valuations, and communicates conclusions as recommendations or opinions about securities. The output helps investors decide whether to buy, sell or hold, and helps markets price securities more efficiently.

points.heading: Sell-side analysts
points.text: Sell-side analysts work for brokers and investment banks and publish research for clients, often with buy, sell or hold ratings and target prices. Their research supports the broker's business, which creates potential conflicts with investment banking and trading desks that regulation seeks to control.

points.heading: Buy-side analysts
points.text: Buy-side analysts work for mutual funds, insurers, PMS and other asset managers, and their research is used internally to make investment decisions. Their work is usually not published. Success is measured by the performance of the portfolio rather than by publicity.

points.heading: Independent analysts
points.text: Independent research firms and individual analysts sell research directly to investors or institutions without investment banking ties. Their independence is a selling point, but they still need SEBI registration and must follow disclosure and conflict rules.

points.heading: Users of research
points.text: Research is used by retail and institutional investors, fund managers, company managements benchmarking peers, lenders evaluating credit, and regulators and policymakers watching sectors. Different users need different depth: a retail investor wants a clear thesis; a fund manager wants detailed models.

points.heading: Research process
points.text: Typical steps: define the question, collect data, analyse the economy, industry and company, build financial models and forecasts, value the security, form a recommendation, write the report and monitor after publication. Updating views when facts change is part of the process.

points.heading: Skills required
points.text: Analysts need accounting and finance knowledge, quantitative and modelling skills, industry understanding, scepticism, communication and writing skills, and the discipline to separate facts from opinions. Interpersonal skills help in management meetings and channel checks, but must never compromise objectivity.

points.heading: Independence and objectivity
points.text: Recommendations must be based on research, not on pressure from issuers, bankers, sales teams or personal holdings. Analysts should not let investment banking deals, brokerage revenue or their own trades influence ratings. Regulation enforces this through separation, disclosure and trading restrictions.

points.heading: Confidentiality and fair dealing
points.text: Analysts often access sensitive information. They must not use or pass on unpublished price-sensitive information, must treat all clients fairly when releasing research, and must not selectively give advance notice of rating changes to favoured clients.

traps: Assuming buy-side research is published. It is usually used internally by the asset manager.
Thinking independent analysts need no registration. Anyone providing research for consideration needs SEBI registration.
Treating management access as a reason to soften ratings. Objectivity must not depend on relationships.
Believing the process ends at publication. Analysts must monitor and update their views.
items.recap: Analysts turn data into recommendations. Sell-side publishes for broker clients; buy-side serves its own fund; independents sell research directly. Process: question, data, analysis, model, valuation, report, monitor. Independence, objectivity, confidentiality and fair dealing are the ethical core.

items.title: NISM XV Securities Market for Analysts: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on the securities market for analysts: primary and secondary markets, MIIs, indices, free-float weighting, market efficiency and regulators.
items.intro: Analysts interpret prices and volumes, so they must understand how the market itself works. This chapter covers primary and secondary markets, market infrastructure, how indices are built, settlement, liquidity and the efficient market hypothesis. Questions are mostly conceptual, with some on index construction and forms of market efficiency.

points.heading: Primary vs secondary market
points.text: The primary market issues new securities through IPOs, FPOs, rights issues, QIPs and private placements, bringing money to issuers. The secondary market provides liquidity by allowing investors to trade existing securities on exchanges, which in turn makes investors willing to buy in the primary market.

points.heading: Market participants
points.text: Participants include issuers, retail and institutional investors, FPIs, brokers, depository participants, custodians, merchant bankers, credit rating agencies, research analysts and investment advisers. Each is registered with and regulated by SEBI or other regulators.

points.heading: Market infrastructure
points.text: Stock exchanges (NSE, BSE) provide trading; clearing corporations guarantee and settle trades through novation; depositories (NSDL, CDSL) hold securities electronically. Equity trades settle on T+1. Analysts should understand these mechanics when interpreting delivery volumes and corporate action dates.

points.heading: How indices are built
points.text: Major Indian indices such as Nifty 50 and Sensex use free-float market capitalisation weighting: each stock's weight is based on the market value of shares available for trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings. A company with large promoter holding gets less weight than its full market cap suggests.

points.heading: Uses of indices
points.text: Indices measure market performance, serve as benchmarks for funds and portfolio managers, and underlie index funds, ETFs and derivatives. Sectoral and thematic indices help analysts compare sector performance. Index rebalancing can cause large flows into or out of stocks.

points.heading: Liquidity and impact cost
points.text: Liquidity means the ability to trade quickly without moving prices. Impact cost measures the cost of executing a trade of a given size relative to the ideal price, and is used in index eligibility. Low liquidity widens bid-ask spreads and makes reported prices less reliable.

points.heading: Efficient market hypothesis
points.text: In the weak form, prices reflect all past price information, so technical analysis should not earn consistent excess returns. In the semi-strong form, prices reflect all public information, so fundamental analysis of public data should not either. In the strong form, prices reflect all information, including private.

points.heading: Market efficiency in practice
points.text: Real markets are not perfectly efficient: anomalies, behavioural biases and information gaps create opportunities for skilled analysis. However, competition among analysts tends to reduce mispricing in heavily researched large caps, while small caps may be less efficiently priced.

points.heading: Regulatory structure
points.text: SEBI regulates securities markets under the SEBI Act, SCRA and Depositories Act. RBI regulates money and government securities markets. Listed companies follow SEBI's LODR regulations on disclosures, which are a primary source of information for analysts.

traps: Using total market cap for Nifty weights. Indices use free-float market cap.
Mixing up weak and semi-strong forms. Weak covers past prices; semi-strong covers all public information.
Assuming an efficient market means prices never change. Prices change quickly as new information arrives.
Thinking the issuer benefits from secondary market trades. Only primary issues raise money for the issuer.
items.recap: Primary market raises capital; secondary market provides liquidity. Exchanges trade, clearing corporations settle on T+1, depositories hold. Indices use free-float market cap weighting. Impact cost measures liquidity. EMH: weak (past prices), semi-strong (public info), strong (all info). LODR disclosures feed research.

items.chapter: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
items.title: NISM XV Equity and Debt Market Terms: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on market terminology: face value, book value, EPS, P/E, earnings and dividend yield, payout, market cap, coupon, YTM, duration and spreads.
items.intro: This chapter is about the vocabulary and simple formulas analysts use every day. You must be able to compute and interpret each measure, see how corporate actions change per-share figures, and understand how bond prices, coupons and yields relate. Many questions are quick calculations, so precision matters more than speed.

points.heading: Face value, book value and market price
points.text: Face value is the nominal value printed on a share, such as ₹10. Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding. Market price is what the share trades at. A share with ₹10 face value, ₹150 book value and ₹600 price trades at four times book.

points.heading: EPS and P/E
points.text: Earnings per share = net profit attributable to equity shareholders ÷ weighted average shares. P/E = market price ÷ EPS. If profit is ₹200 crore and there are 10 crore shares, EPS is ₹20; at a price of ₹400, P/E is 20. Earnings yield is the inverse: EPS ÷ price = 5%.

points.heading: Dividends
points.text: Dividend per share is the cash dividend declared per share. Dividend yield = DPS ÷ market price. Payout ratio = DPS ÷ EPS; retention ratio = 1 − payout. A company with EPS ₹20 paying ₹6 has a 30% payout and retains 70%. Dividends are declared as a percentage of face value in India, which confuses beginners.

points.heading: Market capitalisation and EV
points.text: Market cap = shares outstanding × market price. Enterprise value = market cap + debt + minority interest + preference capital − cash and equivalents. EV represents the value of the whole business to all capital providers and is used with EBITDA.

points.heading: Corporate actions and per-share data
points.text: A 1:1 bonus doubles shares and halves EPS, price and book value per share, leaving totals unchanged. A split from ₹10 to ₹2 face value multiplies shares by five. Analysts must adjust historical per-share data for such actions to keep comparisons valid.

points.heading: Bond basics
points.text: Face value is the amount repaid at maturity; coupon is the annual interest rate on face value; current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price. A ₹100 bond with 8% coupon priced at ₹95 has current yield of 8.42%. YTM is the internal rate of return if held to maturity.

points.heading: Price-yield relationship
points.text: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. When market yields rise above the coupon, the bond trades at a discount; when they fall below, at a premium. A bond trades at par only when its YTM equals its coupon.

points.heading: Duration
points.text: Modified duration estimates the percentage price change for a 1% change in yield. A bond with modified duration 5 falls about 5% if yields rise by 1%. Longer maturity and lower coupons increase duration and interest rate risk.

points.heading: Credit ratings and spreads
points.text: Ratings from agencies like CRISIL, ICRA and CARE indicate default risk, from AAA (highest safety) down to D (default). The credit spread is the extra yield over a G-sec of similar maturity. Spreads widen when credit risk rises or markets become risk-averse.

formulas: % bond price change ≈ − modified duration × change in yield (in % points).
P/B = market price ÷ book value per share; earnings yield = EPS ÷ price.
traps: Confusing payout ratio with dividend yield. Payout uses EPS; yield uses market price.
Forgetting to adjust EPS history for bonus issues and splits.
Assuming a high coupon bond always trades at a premium. It trades at a premium only if market yield is below the coupon.
Computing current yield on face value. Current yield uses the market price.
items.recap: EPS = profit ÷ shares; P/E = price ÷ EPS; earnings yield is its inverse. Payout = DPS ÷ EPS; dividend yield = DPS ÷ price. EV = market cap + debt − cash. Bonus and splits change per-share data, not totals. Bond prices move inversely to yields; current yield = coupon ÷ price; modified duration estimates price sensitivity.

items.title: NISM XV Fundamentals of Research: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on research methods: fundamental, technical and quantitative approaches, top-down vs bottom-up, data sources, models and behavioural biases.
items.intro: This chapter explains how an analyst actually carries out research. It covers the main approaches, the choice between top-down and bottom-up methods, primary and secondary data sources, building financial models, testing assumptions and the behavioural traps that undermine good research. Questions are mostly conceptual but often framed as practical situations.

points.heading: Fundamental analysis
points.text: Fundamental analysis estimates a security's intrinsic value from the economy, industry and company: earnings, cash flows, balance sheet strength, management and competitive position. If the market price is below estimated value, the analyst may recommend buying, expecting the gap to close over time.

points.heading: Technical analysis
points.text: Technical analysis studies price and volume patterns, trends, support and resistance and indicators such as moving averages and RSI to predict price movements. It assumes prices reflect all information and that patterns repeat. It is used mostly for timing rather than valuation.

points.heading: Quantitative analysis
points.text: Quantitative analysts use statistical models and large data sets to identify factors such as value, momentum, quality and low volatility that explain returns. Quant research is systematic and rule-based, which reduces emotional bias but depends on the robustness of historical relationships.

points.heading: Top-down vs bottom-up
points.text: Top-down research starts with the economy, moves to sectors likely to benefit, then picks the best companies within them. Bottom-up research starts with individual companies' strengths regardless of the macro view. Many analysts combine both to check consistency.

points.heading: Primary data
points.text: Primary data is collected first-hand for the research: management meetings, plant visits, channel checks with dealers and distributors, customer surveys and expert interviews. It provides insight not yet in published numbers, but must not cross into unpublished price-sensitive information.

points.heading: Secondary data
points.text: Secondary data comes from existing sources: annual reports, quarterly results, exchange filings, industry association data, government statistics, RBI publications and databases. It is cheaper and verifiable but may be dated or not tailored to the question.

points.heading: Building a model
points.text: A financial model links revenue drivers (volume, price, market share) to costs, margins, capital expenditure, working capital and financing, producing forecast income statements, balance sheets and cash flows. Good models are transparent, internally consistent and easy to update.

points.heading: Testing assumptions
points.text: Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time, such as raw material cost, to see the effect on earnings or value. Scenario analysis changes several inputs together to build bull, base and bear cases. Both show how robust the thesis is.

points.heading: Behavioural pitfalls
points.text: Analysts are prone to confirmation bias (seeking evidence that supports their view), anchoring (sticking to an initial estimate), overconfidence, herding with consensus and the sunk-cost effect after a wrong call. Checklists, peer review and pre-defined exit criteria help counter these.

traps: Treating technical analysis as a valuation tool. It is mainly used for timing based on price and volume patterns.
Confusing top-down with bottom-up. Top-down starts with the economy; bottom-up starts with the company.
Thinking channel checks allow use of insider information. Primary research must not involve UPSI.
Mixing sensitivity and scenario analysis. Sensitivity changes one variable; scenarios change several together.
items.recap: Fundamental (value), technical (timing) and quantitative (factors) approaches. Top-down starts with the economy, bottom-up with companies. Primary data is first-hand; secondary data is published. Models link drivers to statements. Use sensitivity and scenario analysis. Guard against confirmation, anchoring, overconfidence and herding.

items.title: NISM XV Economic Analysis for Research: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on economic analysis: GDP components, CPI and WPI, monetary and fiscal policy, balance of payments, the rupee, PMI and business cycles.
items.intro: Macroeconomic conditions set the backdrop for all sectors and companies. This chapter covers GDP, inflation, interest rates, fiscal policy, external balances, currency movements and business cycles, and how analysts translate these into sector views. Expect questions on indicator interpretation and on how policy changes transmit to markets.

points.heading: GDP and its components
points.text: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced in a period. By expenditure, GDP = private consumption + investment + government spending + net exports. In India, private consumption is the largest component, so rural and urban demand trends matter greatly for consumer sectors.

points.heading: Inflation measures
points.text: CPI measures retail price changes and is RBI's target indicator; WPI tracks wholesale prices. RBI's inflation target is 4% with a tolerance band of 2% to 6% (as of 2026). High inflation squeezes margins and real incomes; falling inflation usually supports lower rates and higher valuations.

points.heading: Monetary policy
points.text: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate. Rate cuts lower borrowing costs, support demand and benefit rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, autos and real estate. Rate hikes do the opposite. Liquidity tools such as CRR changes and open market operations also affect market rates.

points.heading: Fiscal policy
points.text: Government spending, taxation and borrowing make up fiscal policy. The fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Higher deficits increase government borrowing, which can push up bond yields and crowd out private investment, while capital spending on infrastructure supports cement, steel and capital goods.

points.heading: Balance of payments
points.text: The current account records trade in goods and services, remittances and income; the capital account records investment and loans. India usually runs a current account deficit, financed by capital inflows such as FDI and FPI. A widening deficit can pressure the rupee.

points.heading: Exchange rates
points.text: A weaker rupee helps exporters such as IT services and pharmaceuticals, and hurts importers such as oil marketing companies and firms with foreign-currency debt. Analysts assess each company's net currency exposure rather than assuming uniform effects.

points.heading: High-frequency indicators
points.text: The Purchasing Managers' Index above 50 signals expansion and below 50 contraction. The Index of Industrial Production tracks factory output. GST collections, auto sales, power demand, credit growth and core sector data help analysts spot turning points before GDP data is released.

points.heading: Business cycle and sectors
points.text: In expansion, cyclicals such as autos, metals, capital goods and banks tend to do well. In slowdowns, defensives such as FMCG, pharma and utilities hold up better. Analysts map their view of the cycle to sector allocation, adjusting for valuations already in prices.

points.heading: Interest rates and valuations
points.text: Lower interest rates reduce the discount rate used in valuations, increasing the present value of future earnings, especially for long-duration growth stocks. Rising rates compress valuation multiples. This is why equity markets often react sharply to monetary policy surprises.

formulas: GDP (expenditure) = C + I + G + (X − M).
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
traps: Treating WPI as RBI's target. RBI targets CPI inflation.
Reading PMI of 49 as growth. Below 50 signals contraction.
Assuming a weaker rupee helps every company. Importers and firms with foreign debt lose.
Including borrowings in receipts when computing fiscal deficit. Borrowings are excluded.
items.recap: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M). RBI targets CPI at 4% (2–6% band). Rate cuts help rate-sensitives; hikes compress valuations. Fiscal deficit excludes borrowings. Current account deficit pressures the rupee; a weak rupee helps exporters. PMI above 50 = expansion. Cyclicals lead in expansion, defensives in slowdowns.

items.title: NISM XV Industry Analysis Frameworks: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on industry analysis: Porter's five forces, concentration and HHI, industry life cycle, SWOT and PESTLE, cost structure and pricing power.
items.intro: Even a well-managed company struggles in a structurally poor industry. This chapter covers frameworks that analysts use to judge industry attractiveness: structure and concentration, Porter's five forces, life cycle stages, regulation, demand drivers and cost structures. Questions ask you to apply frameworks to scenarios or interpret concentration data.

points.heading: Industry structure
points.text: Structures range from perfect competition (many sellers, no pricing power) through monopolistic competition and oligopoly (few large players) to monopoly. Indian telecom and cement have oligopolistic features; many textile segments are fragmented. Concentrated industries often have better pricing power and margins.

points.heading: Measuring concentration
points.text: The concentration ratio CR4 adds the market shares of the four largest firms. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index sums the squares of all firms' market shares. Four firms with 25% each give HHI = 4 × 625 = 2,500, indicating high concentration. A higher HHI implies less competition.

points.heading: Porter's five forces
points.text: Industry profitability depends on threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat of substitutes and rivalry among existing firms. Strong forces erode profits. For example, airlines face intense rivalry, powerful suppliers (aircraft makers, fuel) and price-sensitive buyers.

points.heading: Barriers to entry
points.text: High capital requirements, regulatory licences, economies of scale, brand loyalty, distribution networks and switching costs protect incumbents. Banking licences and spectrum in telecom are regulatory barriers; brand and distribution protect FMCG leaders.

points.heading: Industry life cycle
points.text: Stages: pioneering (high growth, many failures), expansion or growth (rapid growth, improving profits), maturity or stabilisation (slower growth, consolidation, steady cash flows) and decline (shrinking demand). Valuation approaches differ: growth stage focuses on revenue scaling, mature stage on cash flows and dividends.

points.heading: SWOT and PESTLE
points.text: SWOT lists internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors. Both are checklists to ensure nothing important is missed, not substitutes for numbers.

points.heading: Cost structure and operating leverage
points.text: Industries with high fixed costs, such as steel, cement and telecom, have high operating leverage: profits rise sharply with volume growth and fall sharply in downturns. Industries with variable costs show more stable margins. Analysts track capacity utilisation for such industries.

points.heading: Demand drivers and metrics
points.text: Each industry has key metrics: average revenue per user in telecom, same-store sales growth in retail, net interest margin in banking, realisation per tonne in cement and order book in capital goods. Knowing the metrics helps identify what really drives earnings.

points.heading: Regulation
points.text: Regulated industries such as power, banking, telecom and pharmaceuticals face price controls, licensing and compliance costs, and policy risk. Regulatory changes can quickly alter industry economics, so analysts monitor policy announcements and regulators' consultation papers.

formulas: HHI = Σ (market share of each firm in %)²; e.g. shares of 40, 30, 20, 10 give 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000.
traps: Adding market shares for HHI. HHI uses the sum of squared market shares.
Assuming a fast-growing industry is always attractive. Intense rivalry or low entry barriers can destroy returns.
Confusing SWOT's internal and external elements. Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.
Ignoring operating leverage. High fixed-cost industries have volatile profits.
items.recap: Assess industry structure and concentration (CR4, HHI as sum of squared shares). Porter's five forces: entrants, suppliers, buyers, substitutes, rivalry. Life cycle: pioneering, growth, maturity, decline. SWOT is internal plus external; PESTLE scans the environment. High fixed costs mean high operating leverage. Learn industry metrics.

items.title: NISM XV Company Business and Governance: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on qualitative company analysis: business model, moats, management quality, capital allocation, governance red flags, pledging and ESG.
items.intro: Numbers tell what a company has done; qualitative analysis helps judge whether it can keep doing it. This chapter covers business models, competitive advantages, management quality, capital allocation and corporate governance, including promoter behaviour and ESG. Expect scenario questions in which you must spot a governance red flag despite attractive financials.

points.heading: Business model
points.text: Understand how the company makes money: what it sells, to whom, at what price, through which channels and with what cost structure. A subscription software firm with recurring revenue has very different economics from a project-based engineering firm with lumpy order inflows.

points.heading: Competitive advantages or moats
points.text: Durable advantages include brand strength (pricing power in FMCG), network effects (exchanges, payment platforms), switching costs (enterprise software, banking relationships), cost advantages (scale in cement or steel) and regulatory licences. Moats allow returns on capital to stay above the cost of capital for long periods.

points.heading: Management quality
points.text: Assess track record in executing plans, honesty in communication, consistency between guidance and results, depth of the second line of management and succession planning. Management that blames external factors for every miss or frequently changes strategy deserves caution.

points.heading: Capital allocation
points.text: Good managements reinvest in high-return projects, avoid value-destroying acquisitions, return surplus cash through dividends or buybacks and keep leverage sensible. Repeated equity dilution at low prices or diversification into unrelated businesses are warning signs.

points.heading: Board and independence
points.text: An effective board has genuinely independent directors with relevant expertise, an independent audit committee and transparent remuneration. SEBI's LODR rules set minimum independence requirements, but analysts look beyond compliance to substance.

points.heading: Related-party transactions
points.text: Large or unusual dealings with promoter-group entities, such as purchases at above-market prices, loans to group firms or royalty payments to a promoter entity, can transfer value away from minority shareholders. Analysts read RPT disclosures and shareholder approvals carefully.

points.heading: Promoter pledging
points.text: When promoters pledge a large share of their holdings for loans, a fall in share price can trigger margin calls and forced selling, leading to sharp price declines and even change of control. Rising pledge levels are a red flag about promoter finances.

points.heading: Other governance red flags
points.text: Frequent auditor resignations, qualified audit opinions, delayed results, complex group structures, aggressive accounting, high management turnover and regulatory actions all signal risk. An attractive valuation does not compensate for poor governance.

points.heading: ESG considerations
points.text: Environmental, social and governance factors affect long-term risk and cost of capital. Top listed companies publish a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. Analysts look at emissions, safety records, labour practices, data privacy and governance, especially in sectors exposed to regulation or reputational risk.

traps: Valuing a company with weak governance at the same multiple as peers. Governance risk warrants a discount or avoidance.
Treating high growth as proof of a moat. Moats show up in sustained high returns on capital.
Ignoring rising promoter pledging. It can force selling and price crashes.
Assuming legal compliance means good governance. Substance matters beyond minimum rules.
items.recap: Understand the business model and moat (brand, network, switching costs, cost, licences). Judge management by track record, candour and capital allocation. Watch boards, related-party transactions, pledging, auditor changes and accounting quality. ESG affects risk and cost of capital. Good financials do not cancel governance red flags.

items.title: NISM XV Financial Statement Analysis: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on financial analysis: three statements, profitability, efficiency, liquidity and leverage ratios, DuPont, cash conversion and red flags.
items.intro: Financial statement analysis is the core quantitative skill for a research analyst and carries many marks. You need to compute ratios from raw data, interpret trends, break ROE into its drivers using DuPont, judge the quality of earnings and link numbers back to the business. Practise with real annual reports to make the ratios intuitive.

points.heading: Three statements
points.text: The income statement shows revenue, expenses and profit for a period. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. The cash flow statement splits cash movements into operating, investing and financing activities. Profit can be manipulated more easily than cash, so analysts compare the two.

points.heading: Profitability ratios
points.text: Gross margin, EBITDA margin and net profit margin measure profit per rupee of sales. Return on equity = net profit ÷ average equity; return on capital employed = EBIT ÷ capital employed. A company earning 25% ROCE in a business with 12% cost of capital creates value.

points.heading: Efficiency ratios
points.text: Asset turnover = sales ÷ total assets. Inventory days, receivable days and payable days show how quickly working capital moves. A retailer with low margins can still earn high returns through high asset turnover.

points.heading: Working capital cycle
points.text: Cash conversion cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days. A company with 60 inventory days, 45 receivable days and 30 payable days has a 75-day cycle, meaning cash is tied up for 75 days. Lengthening cycles absorb cash even when profits rise.

points.heading: Liquidity ratios
points.text: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio excludes inventory. Very low ratios signal stress; very high ratios may indicate idle cash or slow-moving inventory. Industry norms matter: FMCG firms often run negative working capital.

points.heading: Leverage and coverage
points.text: Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity. Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest expense. A coverage of 1.5 leaves little room if profits dip. Net debt to EBITDA shows how many years of operating profit would repay debt.

points.heading: DuPont analysis
points.text: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (assets ÷ equity). Two companies with 18% ROE may differ: one with high margins, another with high leverage. Leverage-driven ROE is riskier, so DuPont shows the quality of returns.

points.heading: Quality of earnings
points.text: Compare cash flow from operations with net profit over several years; persistent shortfalls suggest aggressive revenue recognition or rising receivables. Watch one-time gains, capitalised expenses, changes in depreciation policy and large other income. High-quality earnings are recurring and cash-backed.

points.heading: Accounting red flags
points.text: Receivables growing faster than sales, frequent restatements, contingent liabilities that are large relative to net worth, complex subsidiaries and loans to related parties are warning signs. Read notes to accounts and the auditor's report, not just headline numbers.

points.heading: Trends and peers
points.text: A single ratio means little alone. Analysts compare ratios over five or more years and against peers in the same industry, and link changes to business events such as a new plant, a price war or an acquisition.

formulas: ROE = (net profit ÷ sales) × (sales ÷ assets) × (assets ÷ equity).
Cash conversion cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.
Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest expense.
traps: Using year-end equity when average equity is required, or mixing profit before and after tax in ratios.
Treating rising profit with falling operating cash flow as healthy. It may indicate poor earnings quality.
Assuming high ROE is always good. DuPont may reveal it is driven by leverage.
Comparing ratios across unrelated industries. Benchmarks differ by business model.
items.recap: Read all three statements; cash confirms profit. Profitability: margins, ROE, ROCE. Efficiency: turnover and working capital days; CCC = inventory + receivable − payable days. Liquidity: current and quick ratios. Leverage: D/E, interest coverage. DuPont splits ROE into margin, turnover and leverage. Look for trends, peers and red flags.

items.title: NISM XV Corporate Valuation Methods: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on valuation: FCFF and FCFE DCF, dividend discount model, WACC, terminal value, P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, PEG and sum-of-the-parts.
items.intro: Valuation turns analysis into a target price. This chapter covers absolute methods (discounted cash flow and dividend discount models), relative valuation using multiples, sum-of-the-parts, cost of capital and terminal value. Questions are numerical and conceptual: compute a value, or identify which method suits which company and why a multiple is high or low.

points.heading: Free cash flow to firm
points.text: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in working capital. Discounting FCFF at WACC gives enterprise value; subtracting net debt gives equity value. FCFF is preferred when leverage is expected to change.

points.heading: Free cash flow to equity
points.text: FCFE = FCFF − interest × (1 − tax rate) + net borrowing. Discounting FCFE at the cost of equity gives equity value directly. It suits companies with stable leverage, such as many mature businesses.

points.heading: Cost of capital
points.text: Cost of equity is usually estimated with CAPM: risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium. WACC = weight of equity × cost of equity + weight of debt × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate). For example, 60% equity at 13% and 40% debt at 9% pre-tax with 25% tax gives WACC = 7.8% + 2.7% = 10.5%.

points.heading: Terminal value
points.text: Most DCF value often comes from the terminal value. Using the Gordon growth formula, TV = FCF in year n+1 ÷ (discount rate − long-term growth). Small changes in growth or discount rate swing value sharply, so analysts run sensitivity tables and keep long-term growth below nominal GDP growth.

points.heading: Dividend discount model
points.text: For stable dividend payers, value = D1 ÷ (r − g). If next year's dividend is ₹10, required return 12% and growth 7%, value = 10 ÷ 0.05 = ₹200. The model fails when growth is close to or above the required return, and suits utilities or mature banks better than growth companies.

points.heading: P/E and P/B
points.text: P/E compares price with earnings and suits companies with stable positive profits. P/B compares price with book value and suits banks and financial companies whose assets are marked close to market. A justified P/B rises with ROE relative to cost of equity.

points.heading: EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales
points.text: EV/EBITDA neutralises differences in capital structure and depreciation policies, making it useful for capital-intensive sectors such as telecom, cement and power. EV/Sales is used for early-stage or loss-making companies, with caution, since sales do not guarantee profits.

points.heading: PEG ratio
points.text: PEG = P/E ÷ expected earnings growth rate (in %). A stock with P/E 30 and 20% growth has PEG 1.5. PEG helps compare growth stocks, but depends heavily on the growth estimate.

points.heading: Sum of the parts
points.text: For conglomerates and holding companies, analysts value each business separately, using the most suitable method for each, add listed investments at market value (often with a holding company discount), and subtract net debt at the parent. This is common for Indian diversified groups.

points.heading: What drives multiples
points.text: Higher growth, higher return on capital and lower risk justify higher multiples. A company growing fast but earning below its cost of capital destroys value as it grows, so a high multiple is not justified.

formulas: FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC; FCFE = FCFF − interest(1 − t) + net borrowing.
WACC = We × Ke + Wd × Kd × (1 − t).
Terminal value = FCF(n+1) ÷ (r − g); value per share (DDM) = D1 ÷ (r − g).
traps: Discounting FCFF at the cost of equity. FCFF uses WACC; FCFE uses cost of equity.
Applying DDM when growth exceeds the discount rate. The formula breaks down.
Using P/E for loss-making companies. Use EV/Sales or other measures instead.
Forgetting to subtract net debt when moving from enterprise value to equity value.
items.recap: FCFF at WACC gives EV; FCFE at cost of equity gives equity value. WACC uses after-tax cost of debt. Terminal value dominates DCF, so test sensitivity. DDM: D1 ÷ (r − g). P/B for banks, EV/EBITDA for capital-intensive firms, PEG for growth stocks, SOTP for conglomerates. Growth, ROCE and risk drive multiples.

items.title: NISM XV Risk and Return Fundamentals: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on risk and return: holding period and annualised returns, expected return, standard deviation, correlation, beta, CAPM, Sharpe and Treynor.
items.intro: Analysts must measure returns correctly and understand which risks investors are paid to bear. This chapter covers return calculations, expected return from scenarios, variance and standard deviation, covariance and correlation, beta, diversification, CAPM and risk-adjusted performance measures. Most questions are calculations, so learn the formulas well.

points.heading: Holding period return
points.text: HPR = (ending price − beginning price + income) ÷ beginning price. Buying at ₹200, receiving a ₹5 dividend and selling at ₹230 gives HPR = 35 ÷ 200 = 17.5%. For multi-year periods, annualise using CAGR = (ending ÷ beginning)^(1/n) − 1.

points.heading: Expected return
points.text: Expected return is the probability-weighted average of possible outcomes. If a stock has 30% chance of 20%, 50% chance of 10% and 20% chance of −10%, expected return = 6% + 5% − 2% = 9%.

points.heading: Variance and standard deviation
points.text: Variance measures dispersion of returns around the mean; standard deviation is its square root and is expressed in the same units as returns. A higher standard deviation means a wider range of likely outcomes and higher total risk.

points.heading: Covariance and correlation
points.text: Covariance shows whether two assets' returns move together. Correlation standardises covariance to a range of −1 to +1. Combining assets with low or negative correlation reduces portfolio risk without proportionately reducing return; this is the basis of diversification.

points.heading: Systematic vs unsystematic risk
points.text: Unsystematic risk is specific to a company or industry, such as a plant fire or management change, and can be diversified away. Systematic risk arises from market-wide factors such as interest rates and economic cycles and cannot be diversified away.

points.heading: Beta
points.text: Beta measures a stock's sensitivity to market movements: covariance of stock with market ÷ variance of market. A beta of 1.3 means the stock tends to move 1.3% for a 1% market move. Defensive stocks have betas below 1; cyclical stocks often above 1.

points.heading: CAPM
points.text: Expected return = risk-free rate + beta × (market return − risk-free rate). With a risk-free rate of 7%, market return of 12% and beta 1.2, expected return = 7% + 1.2 × 5% = 13%. CAPM says only systematic risk is rewarded because unsystematic risk can be diversified.

points.heading: Sharpe and Treynor ratios
points.text: Sharpe ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation, measuring excess return per unit of total risk. Treynor ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ beta, measuring excess return per unit of systematic risk. Sharpe suits undiversified portfolios; Treynor suits well-diversified ones.

points.heading: Jensen's alpha
points.text: Alpha = actual return − CAPM expected return. A portfolio returning 15% when CAPM predicts 13% has alpha of 2%, suggesting value added by the manager after adjusting for market risk.

formulas: CAPM: E(R) = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf).
Beta = Cov(stock, market) ÷ Var(market).
Two-asset variance = w1²σ1² + w2²σ2² + 2w1w2ρσ1σ2.
traps: Thinking diversification removes all risk. It removes only unsystematic risk.
Using standard deviation in Treynor. Treynor uses beta; Sharpe uses standard deviation.
Adding variances of two assets to get portfolio variance. Covariance terms must be included.
Assuming a beta of 0 means no risk. It means no market risk; the stock may still be volatile.
items.recap: HPR includes income; annualise with CAGR. Expected return is probability-weighted. SD measures total risk; correlation drives diversification. Only systematic risk (beta) is priced under CAPM: Rf + β(Rm − Rf). Sharpe uses SD, Treynor uses beta, Jensen's alpha is actual minus CAPM return.

items.chapter: Qualities of a Good Research Report
items.title: NISM XV Qualities of a Research Report: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on good research reports: clear thesis, accurate data, rating and target price with time frame, key risks, disclosures, plain language.
items.intro: A research report is only useful if readers can understand it, trust it and act on it. This chapter covers the essential sections of a report, what makes the thesis credible, mandatory disclosures and presentation standards. Questions often ask what must be included, or which statement in a report would be misleading or non-compliant.

points.heading: Clear investment thesis
points.text: The report should state upfront why the stock is a buy, sell or hold, in a few key arguments backed by evidence. For example: 'Market share gains in two-wheelers and margin recovery from lower steel costs should lift EPS by 25% over two years'. Readers should not have to hunt for the conclusion.

points.heading: Accurate, sourced data
points.text: Data must be accurate, current and sourced: company filings, industry data, government statistics or the analyst's own estimates clearly labelled as such. Errors in basic numbers destroy credibility, and misleading data can violate regulations.

points.heading: Sound valuation
points.text: The report should explain the valuation method, key assumptions (growth, margins, discount rate) and how the target price is derived. Sensitivity of the target to key assumptions helps readers judge reliability. Valuation should be consistent with the thesis and the forecasts.

points.heading: Rating, target price and time frame
points.text: A clear rating with a target price and the time frame (for example, 12 months) must be stated, along with the rating definitions used by the firm. Ratings should be consistent: a 'buy' with a target below the current price would confuse readers.

points.heading: Key risks
points.text: Every report must explain the main risks to the thesis, such as raw material price spikes, regulatory changes, execution delays or competitive pressure. Highlighting risks shows balance and helps readers judge the recommendation.

points.heading: Mandatory disclosures
points.text: SEBI rules require disclosure of the analyst's and firm's financial interest in the company, holdings of 1% or more, material conflicts of interest, compensation received from the subject company in the past twelve months, whether the firm managed an issue for it, and whether the analyst served as an officer or director. Disclosures must be prominent, not hidden.

points.heading: Fact vs opinion
points.text: Reports must clearly distinguish facts (reported revenue, regulatory decisions) from opinions and forecasts (expected growth, target price). Presenting opinions as certainties, or implying assured returns, is misleading.

points.heading: Plain language and structure
points.text: A good report uses simple, precise language, avoids unnecessary jargon, puts key messages first and uses charts and tables to support points. Consistent formatting across reports helps readers find information quickly.

points.heading: Timeliness and consistency
points.text: Research should be updated promptly after results, major events or rating changes. Contradictions between a firm's reports, or between written and verbal views, damage trust. Reports should be distributed fairly to all clients simultaneously.

traps: Hiding disclosures in tiny print or omitting them. Disclosures are mandatory and must be clear.
Giving a target price without a time frame or method. Both are expected.
Presenting forecasts as facts. Opinions must be identified as such.
Leaving out risks to appear confident. Key risks are an essential section.
items.recap: A good report has a clear thesis, accurate sourced data, transparent valuation, a rating with target price and time frame, key risks and mandatory disclosures (holdings ≥1%, conflicts, compensation, past issue management). Separate fact from opinion, write plainly, update promptly and distribute fairly.

items.title: NISM XV Research Analyst Regulations: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XV notes on the RA Regulations, 2014 as amended: registration, qualifications, client obligations, fee limits, trading restrictions and RAASB oversight.
items.intro: This chapter covers the rules that govern research analysts in India. Expect questions on who must register, qualification and certification, separation from investment banking, disclosure duties, trading restrictions, record keeping and the role of the Research Analyst Administration and Supervisory Body. Requirements were substantially amended in December 2024, so focus on principles and check current figures.

points.heading: Who must register
points.text: Any person who prepares and publishes research reports or makes buy, sell or hold recommendations on securities for consideration must register with SEBI under the SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014. Certain persons are exempt, such as those making recommendations only through public media in limited circumstances, subject to conditions.

points.heading: Qualification and certification
points.text: Individual RAs and the persons associated with research must have the prescribed educational qualification and must pass NISM Series XV certification, keeping it current through recertification or continuing education. The 2024 amendments relaxed the education requirement to graduation in any discipline (check current rules).

points.heading: Financial requirements
