points.text: The 2024 amendments replaced net worth requirements with a deposit maintained with a bank based on the number of clients. This is meant to make the profession accessible while still providing some financial assurance.

points.heading: Fees and client terms
points.text: For individual and HUF clients, SEBI caps fees per family per year (around ₹1.5 lakh as of 2026, indexed) and limits advance fee collection to a specified period. RAs must sign written terms with clients, disclose fees clearly and must never promise assured returns.

points.heading: Separation from investment banking
points.text: Research must be independent of investment banking and other business activities. Research analysts cannot report to investment banking, cannot participate in pitches or roadshows for deals, and their compensation cannot be linked to specific banking or brokerage transactions.

points.heading: Trading restrictions
points.text: An RA and its associates cannot trade in securities they cover from 30 days before to 5 days after publishing a report, and cannot trade against their own recommendation. Exceptions exist for emergencies with compliance approval.

points.heading: Disclosures
points.text: Research reports must disclose financial interests, holdings of 1% or more at the end of the preceding month, material conflicts, compensation from the subject company in the previous 12 months, whether the entity managed an issue for it, and whether the analyst has served as an officer, director or employee. Use of artificial intelligence tools in research must also be disclosed.

points.heading: Records and compliance
points.text: RAs must maintain records of research reports, the basis of recommendations, client agreements and communications for the prescribed period, generally five years. They must appoint a compliance officer where applicable and submit to annual compliance audits.

points.heading: RAASB and SEBI oversight
points.text: BSE has been recognised as the Research Analyst Administration and Supervisory Body. It handles enrolment, monitoring, inspections and grievance handling for RAs, while SEBI retains regulatory and enforcement powers. Investors can complain through SCORES.

points.heading: Related regulations
points.text: RAs must also comply with the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, which ban trading on unpublished price-sensitive information, and the PFUTP Regulations, which prohibit fraudulent and manipulative practices, such as publishing misleading reports to profit from price moves.

traps: Assuming free recommendations on social media are never regulated. Paid recommendations and finfluencer activity are covered and scrutinised.
Thinking the trading blackout is only after publication. It runs 30 days before to 5 days after.
Linking analyst compensation to banking deals. This is prohibited.
Confusing RAASB with SEBI. BSE as RAASB supervises; SEBI regulates and enforces.
items.recap: Anyone giving research for consideration registers under the RA Regulations, 2014 (amended 2024). Need qualification and NISM XV. Deposit replaced net worth. Fee caps and written terms for individual clients. Separate from investment banking. No trading 30 days before to 5 days after a report. Disclose holdings ≥1%, conflicts and AI use. BSE is RAASB.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Investment Basics for PMS: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on investment basics: saving vs investing vs speculation, asset classes, risk-return trade-off, compounding, inflation and real returns.
items.intro: The PMS Distributors exam opens with the basics of investing that every client conversation depends on. This chapter covers how investing differs from saving and speculation, the main asset classes, the risk-return trade-off, time value of money, compounding and real returns. The key message for a distributor: recommendations start from the client's goals, horizon and risk profile.

points.heading: Saving, investing and speculation
points.text: Saving is setting aside income, often in safe and liquid forms such as bank deposits. Investing is committing money to assets expected to grow or produce income over time, accepting some risk. Speculation is taking high risks for short-term gains, often based on price movements rather than fundamentals.

points.heading: Asset classes
points.text: Equity offers ownership and long-term growth with high volatility. Debt offers regular income with lower volatility but interest rate and credit risk. Real estate offers rental income and appreciation but is illiquid and lumpy. Gold is a hedge against crises and currency weakness. Cash offers liquidity and safety but low returns. Alternatives include private equity, hedge strategies and structured products.

points.heading: Risk-return trade-off
points.text: Higher expected returns come with higher risk. Over long periods Indian equities have outperformed fixed deposits, but with sharp falls along the way. A client who cannot tolerate a 30% temporary loss should not hold a portfolio that is 100% small-cap equity, whatever its past return.

points.heading: Time value of money
points.text: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow because it can be invested. Future value = present value × (1 + r)^n. ₹10 lakh invested at 10% a year grows to about ₹25.9 lakh in 10 years. Present value works in reverse, discounting future amounts.

points.heading: Power of compounding
points.text: Compounding means earning returns on past returns. The rule of 72 gives the approximate doubling time: at 12% a year, money doubles in about 6 years; at 8%, about 9 years. Longer holding periods magnify the effect, which is why early and patient investing matters.

points.heading: Inflation and real returns
points.text: Inflation reduces purchasing power. A fixed deposit earning 7% when inflation is 6% gives a real return of only about 1%, and less after tax. Investors seeking to grow wealth need assets whose returns beat inflation after tax over their horizon.

points.heading: Liquidity and horizon
points.text: Liquidity is how quickly an asset can be converted to cash without loss. Matching liquidity to needs is essential: money needed within a year should not be in volatile or locked assets. PMS portfolios suit investors with long horizons and surplus funds, since they hold equity-heavy, concentrated portfolios.

points.heading: Goal-based investing
points.text: Investments should be linked to specific goals with amounts and dates: retirement, children's education, a home. Each goal's horizon and importance determine the right asset mix. A distributor who starts with a product rather than the goal risks mis-selling.

points.heading: Risk profiling
points.text: Risk profile combines risk capacity (financial ability to bear losses, based on income, wealth, dependants and horizon) and risk tolerance (psychological willingness). A wealthy client with low tolerance should still not be pushed into aggressive strategies.

formulas: Future value = PV × (1 + r)^n; rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return %.
traps: Treating speculation as investing. Speculation chases short-term price moves with high risk.
Comparing nominal returns without inflation and tax. Real post-tax returns matter.
Using the rule of 72 incorrectly: divide 72 by the rate to get years, not the reverse.
Equating high wealth with high risk tolerance. Capacity and tolerance must both be assessed.
items.recap: Saving preserves, investing grows with risk, speculation gambles on short-term moves. Know each asset class's risk, return and liquidity. Higher return needs higher risk. FV = PV × (1 + r)^n; rule of 72 for doubling. Real return ≈ nominal minus inflation. Start every recommendation from goals, horizon and risk profile.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Securities Market Structure: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on India's securities market structure for PMS distributors: exchanges, clearing, depositories, brokers, custodians and T+1 settlement.
items.intro: PMS clients often ask how their securities are held and how trades are executed. This chapter explains the structure of Indian securities markets, the intermediaries involved, how trades flow from order to settlement, and the investor protection mechanisms. A distributor who can explain this clearly builds trust and avoids misunderstandings about custody.

points.heading: Primary and secondary markets
points.text: Primary market issues bring fresh capital to companies through IPOs, FPOs, rights issues and private placements. Secondary markets, mainly NSE and BSE, let investors trade existing securities. PMS portfolios mostly operate in the secondary market but may also apply in IPOs.

points.heading: Equity and debt segments
points.text: The equity segment trades shares, ETFs and REIT and InvIT units. The debt segment trades government securities and corporate bonds, though much bond trading is over the counter and reported to exchanges. Derivatives segments trade futures and options.

points.heading: Market infrastructure
points.text: Stock exchanges match orders; clearing corporations become counterparty to every trade through novation and guarantee settlement; depositories (NSDL and CDSL) hold securities electronically in demat accounts maintained through DPs. Together they reduce counterparty and custody risk.

points.heading: Brokers and custodians
points.text: Brokers execute trades on exchanges for clients, including portfolio managers. Custodians safeguard securities, settle trades and handle corporate actions for institutional clients. A portfolio manager must appoint a custodian, which keeps client securities separate from the manager's own assets.

points.heading: How a PMS trade flows
points.text: The portfolio manager places an order through a broker; the exchange matches it; the clearing corporation computes obligations; the custodian settles on the client's behalf; securities are credited to the client's demat account. Contract notes and statements record each step.

points.heading: T+1 settlement
points.text: Indian equity trades settle on the next trading day after the trade. Faster settlement reduces risk and frees capital quickly. An optional same-day settlement exists for a limited set of stocks.

points.heading: Dematerialisation
points.text: Securities are held in electronic form in demat accounts, eliminating risks of forgery, loss and bad delivery. For PMS clients, holdings sit in a demat account in the client's own name, which they can verify through depository statements.

points.heading: SEBI's role
points.text: SEBI regulates exchanges, intermediaries, listed companies and portfolio managers to protect investors and develop the market. It frames rules on disclosure, conduct, settlement, margins and grievance redress.

points.heading: Investor protection
points.text: Protections include segregation of client assets, clearing corporation guarantees, investor protection funds at exchanges, the SCORES complaint system, online dispute resolution, and regular statements from depositories that let investors verify holdings independently.

traps: Thinking PMS securities are held in the portfolio manager's name. They are held in the client's own demat account.
Confusing custodian and broker. Brokers execute; custodians hold and settle.
Assuming clearing corporations only record trades. They guarantee settlement through novation.
Using T+2 as the current cycle. Indian equities settle on T+1.
items.recap: Exchanges match, clearing corporations guarantee and settle, depositories hold in demat form. Brokers execute; custodians safeguard and settle for portfolio managers. PMS holdings stay in the client's own demat account. Settlement is T+1. SEBI regulates, and investors are protected through segregation, guarantees, IPFs, SCORES and ODR.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Investing in Stocks: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on equity investing: shareholder rights, return sources, fundamental analysis, P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, ROE, technical basics and styles.
items.intro: Most PMS strategies are equity-focused, so distributors must understand how stocks are analysed and selected. This chapter covers shareholder rights, sources of equity returns, fundamental analysis from economy to company, key ratios, technical analysis basics and investment styles. Learn which ratio suits which kind of company and how to explain a manager's style to clients.

points.heading: Shareholder rights
points.text: Equity shareholders own part of the company and are entitled to vote on key matters, receive dividends when declared, receive bonus and rights entitlements, inspect certain records and share residual assets on liquidation after creditors. Their liability is limited to the amount invested.

points.heading: Sources of return
points.text: Equity returns come from dividends and capital appreciation. Capital appreciation is driven by earnings growth and changes in the valuation multiple. If earnings grow 15% a year and the P/E stays constant, the share price should rise about 15% a year, plus dividends.

points.heading: Economy-industry-company
points.text: Fundamental analysis looks at the economy (growth, inflation, rates), the industry (structure, competition, cycle) and the company (business model, management, financials). A PMS manager's investment approach often emphasises one layer, such as sector rotation or bottom-up stock picking.

points.heading: Valuation ratios
points.text: P/E = price ÷ EPS suits stable earners. P/B = price ÷ book value per share suits banks and financials. EV/EBITDA suits capital-intensive businesses and allows comparison across different debt levels. Dividend yield = DPS ÷ price suits mature, cash-generating companies such as utilities.

points.heading: Financial metrics
points.text: ROE measures profit relative to shareholders' equity; consistently high ROE with low debt suggests a strong business. Debt-to-equity measures leverage. Operating and net margins show pricing power and cost control. Sales and earnings growth show momentum. Cash flow from operations confirms profit quality.

points.heading: Technical analysis basics
points.text: Technical analysis studies price charts, trends, support and resistance, moving averages and volume to time entries and exits. Some PMS strategies use momentum or trend signals. Technical analysis does not assess business value and is used mostly for timing.

points.heading: Growth vs value
points.text: Growth investing targets companies with high earnings growth, often at higher valuations. Value investing buys companies trading below their intrinsic value, often at low P/E or P/B. Quality investing focuses on high ROE and strong balance sheets. Styles go in and out of favour over market cycles.

points.heading: Market-cap styles
points.text: Large caps are established companies with lower volatility and higher liquidity. Mid and small caps offer higher growth potential but higher volatility and lower liquidity. In SEBI's classification, large caps are the top 100 companies by market capitalisation, mid caps 101–250 and small caps beyond 250.

points.heading: Concentration in PMS
points.text: PMS portfolios are often concentrated in 15–30 stocks, unlike diversified mutual funds. Concentration can boost returns when picks work but increases volatility and stock-specific risk. Distributors must explain this clearly to clients.

traps: Using P/E for banks without considering P/B. Book value is central for financial companies.
Assuming dividends are the main source of equity returns. Earnings growth and re-rating usually dominate.
Confusing growth with quality. Growth is about earnings expansion; quality is about returns on capital and balance sheet strength.
Ignoring liquidity risk in small caps, especially in concentrated portfolios.
items.recap: Shareholders own, vote and get dividends with limited liability. Returns = dividends + earnings growth + re-rating. Use economy-industry-company analysis. P/E for stable earners, P/B for banks, EV/EBITDA for capital-intensive firms, dividend yield for mature companies. Know growth, value and quality styles and SEBI's market-cap buckets. PMS concentration raises stock-specific risk.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Fixed Income for PMS Distributors: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on fixed income: coupon, YTM, current yield, price-yield link, duration, ratings, Indian issuers, and rate, credit and liquidity risk.
items.intro: Some PMS strategies invest in debt or use it to balance equity. This chapter covers bond features, yields, the price-yield relationship, duration and convexity, credit ratings, the main Indian issuers and the risks involved. Distributors should be able to explain to clients, in plain words, why bond prices fall when interest rates rise.

points.heading: Bond features
points.text: A bond has a face value (usually ₹1,000 or ₹1 lakh for corporate bonds, ₹100 for G-secs), a coupon rate paid on face value, a maturity date and an issuer. Some bonds are zero-coupon, issued at a discount and redeemed at face value. Others have call or put options or floating coupons.

points.heading: Yields
points.text: Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price. Yield to maturity is the discount rate that equates the present value of all cash flows to the price, assuming coupons are reinvested at the same rate. A ₹100 bond with ₹9 coupon priced at ₹104 has current yield of 8.65% and a YTM lower than the coupon.

points.heading: Price-yield relationship
points.text: When market interest rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall until their yield matches the market. When rates fall, prices rise. This inverse relationship is the core of interest rate risk.

points.heading: Duration
points.text: Modified duration measures how much a bond's price changes for a 1% change in yield. A portfolio with duration of 4 years loses about 4% if yields rise by 1% and gains about 4% if they fall by 1%. Longer maturities and lower coupons mean higher duration.

points.heading: Convexity
points.text: Convexity measures how duration changes as yields change. Bonds with positive convexity gain more when yields fall than they lose when yields rise by the same amount. Duration alone is an approximation; convexity improves it for large rate moves.

points.heading: Credit ratings and spreads
points.text: Ratings from agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings indicate default risk. AAA is the highest safety; BBB- is the lowest investment grade. Lower-rated bonds pay higher yields, called credit spreads, to compensate for higher default risk. Downgrades cause price falls.

points.heading: Indian issuers
points.text: Central government securities and treasury bills carry sovereign risk; state development loans are issued by states; PSU bonds and corporate bonds carry issuer credit risk; commercial paper and certificates of deposit are short-term money market instruments. Each differs in yield, liquidity and risk.

points.heading: Other risks
points.text: Reinvestment risk arises when coupons must be reinvested at lower rates. Liquidity risk arises because many corporate bonds trade infrequently, making it hard to sell without a price discount. Inflation risk erodes real returns on fixed coupons.

points.heading: Explaining to clients
points.text: A simple explanation: if new bonds pay 8% but yours pays 7%, a buyer will pay less for your bond so that their effective return reaches 8%. Hence rising rates hurt existing bondholders, and longer bonds are hurt more.

formulas: Price change % ≈ − modified duration × change in yield (% points) + ½ × convexity × (change in yield)².
traps: Thinking higher rates increase existing bond prices. Prices fall when yields rise.
Assuming a bond priced above par has a YTM above its coupon. Premium bonds have YTM below coupon.
Treating all bonds as safe. Corporate bonds carry credit and liquidity risk.
Ignoring reinvestment risk in YTM. YTM assumes coupons are reinvested at the same yield.
items.recap: Bonds pay coupons on face value; current yield = coupon ÷ price; YTM is the full return to maturity. Prices fall when yields rise. Modified duration estimates percentage price change per 1% yield change; convexity refines it. Ratings and spreads reflect credit risk. Know G-secs, SDLs, PSU and corporate bonds, CPs and CDs.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Derivatives for PMS: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on derivatives: forwards, futures, options and swaps, margins and MTM, cost of carry, option terms, hedging uses and PMS limits.
items.intro: Portfolio managers use derivatives to hedge and rebalance, not to take leveraged bets on clients' money. This chapter introduces forwards, futures, options and swaps, their pricing basics, margins and mark-to-market, option terminology and simple strategies. Focus on hedging uses and on being able to explain derivative risks to clients clearly.

points.heading: Types of derivatives
points.text: A forward is a customised OTC agreement to buy or sell an asset at a future date at a fixed price. A future is a standardised exchange-traded forward with daily settlement. An option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a strike price. A swap exchanges cash flows, such as fixed for floating interest.

points.heading: Futures mechanics
points.text: Futures trade in fixed lot sizes with standard expiry dates. Traders deposit initial margin, and gains or losses are settled daily through mark-to-market. A 1% move in a Nifty futures contract with notional value ₹15 lakh means a ₹15,000 daily gain or loss.

points.heading: Cost of carry
points.text: The theoretical futures price = spot price × (1 + cost of carry), where carry is the financing cost minus income such as dividends. If Nifty is at 24,000 and annual carry is 7%, the one-month futures price should be about 24,000 × (1 + 0.07/12) ≈ 24,140.

points.heading: Option terms
points.text: The premium is the price paid for an option. A call is in the money when spot exceeds strike; a put is in the money when strike exceeds spot. Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount; time value is premium minus intrinsic value, which decays as expiry approaches.

points.heading: Option example
points.text: A call with strike ₹1,000 bought at ₹40 premium. If the stock is at ₹1,070 on expiry, intrinsic value is ₹70 and profit is ₹30 per share. If the stock ends at ₹980, the call expires worthless and the loss is limited to ₹40 premium.

points.heading: Hedging uses in PMS
points.text: A manager worried about a market fall can sell index futures or buy index puts against an equity portfolio, protecting value without selling stocks and incurring taxes or transaction costs. Futures can also be used to quickly adjust exposure while rebalancing between stocks.

points.heading: Basic strategies
points.text: A protective put (own stock plus buy put) caps downside. A covered call (own stock plus sell call) earns premium but caps upside. Collars combine both. These strategies change the risk-return profile rather than eliminate risk.

points.heading: Leverage and risk
points.text: Derivatives require only a margin, so small price moves cause large percentage gains or losses relative to the money deposited. Option sellers face potentially large losses. Counterparty risk exists in OTC derivatives but is reduced by clearing corporations on exchanges.

points.heading: PMS limits
points.text: SEBI rules allow portfolio managers to use derivatives for hedging and portfolio rebalancing within prescribed limits, and do not permit leveraging client portfolios. Disclosure documents must state derivatives use, and distributors must explain the related risks to clients.

formulas: Futures fair value ≈ spot × (1 + r × t) − expected dividends; option premium = intrinsic value + time value.
traps: Confusing the obligation of a futures buyer with an option buyer's right. Option buyers can walk away; futures buyers cannot.
Thinking time value increases near expiry. It decays as expiry approaches.
Assuming PMS can use derivatives to leverage portfolios. They are allowed only for hedging and rebalancing within limits.
Believing hedging removes all risk. It reduces specific risks, at a cost.
items.recap: Forwards are OTC, futures are standardised with daily MTM, options give rights for a premium, swaps exchange cash flows. Futures price ≈ spot × (1 + carry). Call ITM when spot > strike; put ITM when strike > spot. Time value decays. PMS uses derivatives for hedging and rebalancing only, never leverage.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Collective Investment Vehicles: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes comparing mutual funds, ETFs, AIF categories, PMS, REITs, InvITs and SIFs on structure, minimum ticket, liquidity, costs and taxation.
items.intro: Clients considering PMS will compare it with other managed products, so distributors must know the alternatives well. This chapter compares mutual funds, ETFs, alternative investment funds, PMS, REITs, InvITs and the newer Specialised Investment Funds on structure, regulator, minimum investment, liquidity, transparency, costs and taxation. Expect comparison and positioning questions.

points.heading: Mutual funds
points.text: Mutual funds pool money from many investors into a trust managed by an AMC, regulated by SEBI. Open-ended schemes allow daily purchase and redemption at NAV; close-ended schemes have fixed maturities and list on exchanges. Minimum investment can be as low as ₹100 to ₹500, with high transparency and capped expense ratios.

points.heading: ETFs and index funds
points.text: ETFs track an index and trade on exchanges throughout the day; index funds track an index but are bought and redeemed at NAV. Both are passive, low-cost options. They suit clients who want market returns without manager selection risk.

points.heading: Alternative investment funds
points.text: AIFs are privately pooled vehicles with a minimum investment of ₹1 crore per investor (lower for employees and certain cases). Category I invests in start-ups, SMEs and infrastructure; Category II includes private equity and debt funds without leverage; Category III uses complex strategies, including leverage and derivatives, such as hedge funds.

points.heading: PMS
points.text: PMS offers a separately managed portfolio in the client's own name with a minimum investment of ₹50 lakh (as of 2026). It provides customisation and direct ownership of securities, but higher concentration, higher minimums and fee structures that can include performance fees.

points.heading: Specialised Investment Funds
points.text: SIFs, introduced by SEBI in 2025, are offered by eligible mutual fund houses with a minimum investment of ₹10 lakh per investor. They allow strategies such as long-short equity with limited derivative exposure, sitting between mutual funds and PMS or AIFs in risk and flexibility.

points.heading: REITs and InvITs
points.text: Real Estate Investment Trusts own income-producing commercial property; Infrastructure Investment Trusts own infrastructure assets like roads and power lines. Both distribute most of their cash flows to unitholders and trade on exchanges. They give access to real assets with smaller amounts than direct ownership.

points.heading: Transparency and liquidity
points.text: Mutual funds disclose portfolios monthly and allow daily liquidity in open-ended schemes. PMS clients see their own holdings directly and can exit, though exit loads may apply in early years. AIFs have lock-ins and limited liquidity. REITs and InvITs are liquid only to the extent of exchange volumes.

points.heading: Taxation differences
points.text: Mutual funds are pass-through vehicles: investors pay tax only on redemption or dividends. In PMS, each transaction in the portfolio is taxed in the client's hands. Category I and II AIFs have pass-through status for most income; Category III is generally taxed at the fund level. These differences affect post-tax returns.

points.heading: Positioning PMS
points.text: PMS suits clients with large investible surplus, long horizons, tolerance for concentration and volatility, and a preference for customised portfolios or direct ownership. For smaller investors or those wanting high liquidity and low cost, mutual funds are usually more suitable.

traps: Assuming PMS minimum is the same as AIF. PMS is ₹50 lakh; AIF is ₹1 crore (as of 2026).
Treating mutual funds and PMS as taxed alike. MF gains are taxed on redemption; PMS trades are taxed each time in the client's hands.
Thinking Category III AIFs are low risk. They can use leverage and complex strategies.
Positioning PMS for every wealthy client. Suitability depends on horizon, risk appetite and needs.
items.recap: Mutual funds: low minimum, daily liquidity, high transparency, pass-through tax. ETFs and index funds are passive. AIFs: ₹1 crore minimum, three categories. PMS: ₹50 lakh, own demat account, customised, trade-by-trade taxation. SIFs: ₹10 lakh, between MFs and PMS. REITs and InvITs give exchange-traded real-asset exposure.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Role of Portfolio Managers: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on the role of portfolio managers: discretionary, non-discretionary and advisory PMS, fiduciary duty, minimum ticket and principal officer.
items.intro: This chapter defines who a portfolio manager is under the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020, the types of services offered and the duties owed to clients. Expect questions on who takes decisions in each service type, the minimum investment, the principal officer's role, the distributor's role and which clients PMS suits.

points.heading: Definition
points.text: A portfolio manager is a body corporate that, under a contract with a client, advises, directs or undertakes the management or administration of the client's portfolio of securities or funds. Only SEBI-registered entities can offer portfolio management services.

points.heading: Discretionary PMS
points.text: In discretionary PMS, the portfolio manager decides what to buy and sell, and when, within the agreed investment approach, without seeking the client's approval for each transaction. Most PMS assets in India are discretionary. The client relies heavily on the manager's skill and integrity.

points.heading: Non-discretionary PMS
points.text: In non-discretionary PMS, the portfolio manager recommends transactions but executes them only after the client approves. The client keeps control over decisions, while the manager handles execution, reporting and administration.

points.heading: Advisory PMS
points.text: In advisory PMS, the portfolio manager only gives advice; the client decides and executes trades through their own arrangements. The manager is responsible for the quality of advice but not for execution.

points.heading: Minimum investment
points.text: The minimum investment per client is ₹50 lakh (as of 2026), which can be brought in as cash, securities or a combination. Securities brought in are valued at market price on the date of transfer. Large value accredited investors may agree to different terms.

points.heading: Fiduciary duty
points.text: A portfolio manager acts in a fiduciary capacity, putting the client's interests first. It must manage the portfolio in line with the agreement and disclosure document, avoid conflicts or disclose them, ensure best execution and keep client assets segregated from its own.

points.heading: Principal officer
points.text: The principal officer is responsible for decisions on managing client portfolios and for the overall activities of the portfolio manager. SEBI prescribes qualifications, experience and NISM certification for the principal officer and for employees involved in decision-making.

points.heading: Role of the distributor
points.text: Distributors introduce clients to portfolio managers, explain products, help with documentation and service clients over time. They must be registered with APMI (Association of Portfolio Managers in India) and hold NISM Series XXI-A certification. They cannot manage portfolios or promise returns.

points.heading: Suitable clients and uses
points.text: PMS suits high-net-worth investors with long horizons who want direct ownership, customisation and a focused strategy. It can be used for concentrated equity portfolios, debt or multi-asset strategies, or for specific needs like tax-efficient transition of existing holdings.

traps: Assuming the client approves each trade in discretionary PMS. The manager decides within the agreed approach.
Treating advisory PMS as including execution. The client executes trades in advisory PMS.
Thinking the minimum can only be met with cash. Securities can be contributed at market value.
Believing a distributor can make investment decisions. Distributors only introduce and service clients.
items.recap: Portfolio manager: SEBI-registered body corporate managing client portfolios under contract. Discretionary: manager decides. Non-discretionary: client approves. Advisory: advice only. Minimum ₹50 lakh in cash or securities. Fiduciary duty and segregation of assets. Principal officer leads decisions. Distributors: APMI-registered, NISM XXI-A certified, no decisions.

items.title: NISM XXI-A PMS Operations and Fees: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on PMS operations: disclosure document, client agreement, demat and bank accounts, fees with high-water mark, exit load and reporting.
items.intro: Operational rules make PMS transparent and protect clients. This chapter covers the disclosure document, client agreement, KYC and account set-up, custody, fees and charges, reporting, audit, direct onboarding and account closure. Fee calculations, especially performance fees with a high-water mark, are frequently tested, so practise with numbers.

points.heading: Disclosure document
points.text: The disclosure document describes the portfolio manager, its investment approaches, risks, fees, performance and conflicts of interest. It is filed with SEBI, certified by an independent chartered accountant and given to the prospective client before signing the agreement. It must be updated when material changes occur.

points.heading: Client agreement
points.text: The agreement sets out the service type, investment approach, fees, rights and obligations, reporting and termination terms. It must follow SEBI's minimum contents, and any additional clauses cannot dilute client protections. Clients sign it after reviewing the disclosure document.

points.heading: Accounts and custody
points.text: Each client's funds and securities are held in a separate bank account and demat account in the client's name, or a pooled bank account with clear segregation under specified conditions. A custodian holds the securities and settles trades. Client assets cannot be mixed with the portfolio manager's own.

points.heading: Fees and expenses
points.text: Fees can include a fixed management fee, a performance-based fee, or a hybrid. Operating expenses other than brokerage are capped as a percentage of average daily AUM. All fees and expenses are charged as per the agreement and shown in client reports, with an illustration of fee calculation in the disclosure document.

points.heading: High-water mark
points.text: Performance fees are charged only on gains above the highest net asset value on which a fee was earlier charged. If a portfolio rises from ₹50 lakh to ₹60 lakh (fee charged), falls to ₹55 lakh and then rises to ₹65 lakh, the next performance fee applies only to the ₹5 lakh above ₹60 lakh.

points.heading: Exit load
points.text: Portfolio managers may charge an exit load if the client exits early: up to 3% in the first year, 2% in the second year and 1% in the third year, with no exit load after three years (as of 2026; check SEBI circulars). Partial withdrawals are permitted subject to the minimum investment rules.

points.heading: Direct onboarding
points.text: Portfolio managers must offer a direct option, where clients join without a distributor and pay no distribution commission. Distributors are paid only through trail commissions, not upfront fees, which reduces incentives for churning.

points.heading: Reporting and audit
points.text: Clients receive periodic reports, at least quarterly, covering holdings, transactions, fees, performance and benchmark comparison. Client accounts are audited annually by an independent chartered accountant, and the portfolio manager reports to SEBI regularly.

points.heading: Account closure
points.text: On termination, the portfolio manager settles the account, returning funds and transferring securities to the client's own demat account after deducting due fees and charges. Securities can be transferred in kind, avoiding forced sales and immediate tax on gains.

formulas: Performance fee base = closing value − max(high-water mark, hurdle-adjusted value), only if positive.
traps: Charging performance fees on every gain. Fees apply only above the high-water mark.
Assuming the disclosure document is given after signing. It is given before the agreement.
Thinking distributors can take upfront commissions. Only trail commissions are allowed.
Believing exit loads can apply indefinitely. They are allowed only within the first three years, on a declining scale.
items.recap: Disclosure document before agreement, filed with SEBI and certified by a CA. Separate demat and bank accounts in client's name; custodian holds securities. Fees: fixed, performance or hybrid; performance fee only above the high-water mark; operating expenses capped. Exit load at most 3/2/1% in years 1–3. Direct option available; trail-only commissions. At least quarterly reporting.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Portfolio Management Process: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on the portfolio management process: client profiling, investment policy, strategic and tactical allocation, selection, rebalancing.
items.intro: The portfolio management process is a disciplined cycle rather than a set of stock tips. This chapter covers understanding the client, writing an investment policy, setting strategic and tactical asset allocation, selecting securities, executing, monitoring, rebalancing and reviewing. Questions often present a client scenario and ask which step or constraint is most relevant.

points.heading: Understanding the client
points.text: The process begins with the client's objectives (return needs, goals), risk profile (capacity and tolerance) and constraints. A 45-year-old business owner with surplus funds and a 15-year horizon may accept high equity exposure; a retired client relying on portfolio income needs stability.

points.heading: Constraints
points.text: Constraints include liquidity needs (cash required in the near term), time horizon, tax position, legal and regulatory factors (such as restrictions on certain holdings) and unique circumstances (ethical preferences, concentrated employer stock). Ignoring a constraint can make an otherwise good portfolio unsuitable.

points.heading: Investment policy statement
points.text: An IPS documents objectives, risk tolerance, constraints, asset allocation ranges, benchmarks, rebalancing rules and review frequency. It guides decisions, prevents emotional deviations and provides a basis for evaluating the manager's performance.

points.heading: Strategic asset allocation
points.text: Strategic allocation sets the long-term mix of asset classes, such as 70% equity, 25% debt, 5% gold, based on the client's profile. It is the largest driver of long-run portfolio returns and volatility, more than individual security selection.

points.heading: Tactical asset allocation
points.text: Tactical allocation makes temporary deviations from the strategic mix to take advantage of market conditions, for example raising equity to 75% when valuations are attractive. It must stay within the ranges set in the IPS.

points.heading: Security selection
points.text: Within each asset class, the manager selects securities using its investment approach: growth, value, quality, momentum, thematic or a combination. For a PMS, the disclosure document describes this approach, and the distributor should explain it accurately.

points.heading: Execution
points.text: Execution involves placing orders efficiently, minimising transaction costs and market impact, and following best execution obligations. For large orders in less liquid stocks, the manager may spread purchases over several days.

points.heading: Monitoring and rebalancing
points.text: The manager monitors the portfolio against objectives and market changes. Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to target weights when market moves cause drift: if equity rises to 80% against a 70% target, some equity is sold and debt bought. Rebalancing enforces discipline of selling high and buying low.

points.heading: Reviewing the plan
points.text: Client circumstances change through events like retirement, inheritance, health issues or business sale. The IPS and asset allocation should be reviewed periodically and after such events. A portfolio that suited the client five years ago may no longer be appropriate.

traps: Starting with stock selection before understanding the client. Profiling and constraints come first.
Confusing strategic with tactical allocation. Strategic is long-term; tactical is a temporary tilt within ranges.
Ignoring liquidity constraints. Near-term cash needs must be met before seeking returns.
Treating rebalancing as optional. It keeps risk aligned with the client's profile.
items.recap: Understand objectives, risk and constraints (liquidity, horizon, tax, legal, unique). Document them in an IPS. Strategic allocation drives long-run results; tactical tilts stay within ranges. Select securities per the stated approach, execute efficiently, monitor and rebalance, and review after life events.

items.chapter: Performance Measurement and Evaluation of Portfolio Managers
items.title: NISM XXI-A PMS Performance Measurement: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on PMS performance: TWRR vs money-weighted return, annualising, Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha, information ratio and APMI benchmarks.
items.intro: Clients compare portfolio managers mainly on reported performance, so the way returns are calculated matters. This chapter covers holding period and annualised returns, time-weighted versus money-weighted returns, risk measures, risk-adjusted ratios and SEBI's standardised benchmarking framework for PMS. Calculations are common, and TWRR is a favourite topic.

points.heading: Holding period and annualised returns
points.text: Holding period return measures total return over a period. To compare periods of different length, annualise: a 50% gain over three years is (1.5)^(1/3) − 1 ≈ 14.5% a year. Returns for periods under one year should not be annualised in client reports.

points.heading: Time-weighted return
points.text: TWRR breaks the period into sub-periods between cash flows, computes each sub-period return and links them geometrically. It removes the effect of the timing and size of client deposits and withdrawals, so it reflects only the manager's decisions. SEBI mandates TWRR for PMS performance reporting.

points.heading: TWRR example
points.text: If a portfolio returns 20% in the first half-year, then the client adds money, and the portfolio returns −10% in the second half, TWRR = 1.20 × 0.90 − 1 = 8% for the year, regardless of how much money was added mid-year.

points.heading: Money-weighted return
points.text: MWRR is the internal rate of return of all cash flows, reflecting the investor's actual experience including timing. If the client added a large amount just before the −10% half, the MWRR would be lower than 8%. MWRR is useful for clients but unfair for judging managers who do not control cash flows.

points.heading: Risk measures
points.text: Standard deviation measures total volatility. Beta measures sensitivity to the market. Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns, showing how far the manager deviates from the benchmark.

points.heading: Sharpe and Treynor ratios
points.text: Sharpe = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation. Treynor = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ beta. A PMS with 18% return, 7% risk-free rate and 22% standard deviation has a Sharpe ratio of 0.5. Concentrated PMS portfolios are better judged by Sharpe because they carry significant unsystematic risk.

points.heading: Jensen's alpha and information ratio
points.text: Jensen's alpha = actual return − [Rf + β(Rm − Rf)], showing return beyond what market risk explains. Information ratio = (portfolio return − benchmark return) ÷ tracking error, showing how consistently the manager beats the benchmark per unit of active risk.

points.heading: Benchmarking framework
points.text: SEBI requires portfolio managers to report performance of each investment approach against a common benchmark for its strategy category (equity, debt, hybrid, multi-asset), chosen from benchmarks notified by APMI. Performance data is published on APMI's platform, allowing like-for-like comparison.

points.heading: Interpreting performance
points.text: Past performance does not indicate future results. Distributors should present returns net of fees and expenses, over consistent periods, alongside the benchmark and risk measures, and avoid selective time periods that flatter performance.

formulas: Information ratio = (Rp − Rb) ÷ tracking error; Sharpe = (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp.
traps: Using MWRR to judge a manager. TWRR removes client cash flow effects and is mandated for PMS.
Annualising returns for periods under a year in client reports.
Comparing a PMS against an unrelated benchmark. Use the prescribed strategy benchmark.
Quoting gross returns. Present returns net of fees and expenses.
items.recap: Annualise with (1 + HPR)^(1/n) − 1. TWRR links sub-period returns and removes client cash flow effects; SEBI mandates it. MWRR is the IRR of the investor's flows. Sharpe uses SD; Treynor uses beta; alpha is excess over CAPM; information ratio is active return ÷ tracking error. Compare with APMI-notified strategy benchmarks, net of fees.

items.title: NISM XXI-A Taxation of PMS Investments: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on PMS taxation: trade-by-trade taxation in the client's hands, capital gains on equity and debt, dividends, STT, fees, losses and NRIs.
items.intro: Because PMS securities are held in the client's own name, every transaction has tax consequences for the client, unlike in a mutual fund. This chapter covers how capital gains, dividends and interest are taxed, the role of STT, the treatment of PMS fees, set-off of losses and issues for non-resident clients. Rates change with Budgets, so learn the principles.

points.heading: Taxed in the client's hands
points.text: Each purchase and sale in a PMS account is the client's own transaction. Gains and losses are computed per security using purchase cost and holding period, and reported in the client's return. High portfolio turnover can therefore create frequent short-term gains and a higher tax bill.

points.heading: Listed equity gains
points.text: For listed shares held over 12 months, long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% above an annual exemption of ₹1.25 lakh; short-term gains are taxed at 20% (as of 2026, with STT paid; check current rates). Gains on mutual fund units held in PMS follow the rules for that type of fund.

points.heading: Debt instruments
points.text: Interest on bonds is taxed at slab rates. Gains on listed bonds held over 12 months are long-term at 12.5% without indexation, while unlisted bonds and specified debt funds are taxed at slab rates regardless of holding period. Debt PMS strategies should be evaluated on post-tax yield.

points.heading: Dividends
points.text: Dividends received in the PMS account are taxable in the client's hands at slab rates, with TDS deducted by the company above the threshold. For high-income clients, high dividend yield strategies may be less tax-efficient than growth strategies.

points.heading: STT and transaction costs
points.text: Securities transaction tax is charged on equity trades on exchanges. STT is not deductible when computing capital gains, but brokerage and other transfer costs are generally included in cost or deducted from sale value.

points.heading: Treatment of PMS fees
points.text: Whether management and performance fees can be deducted against capital gains has been debated, with tax authorities and tribunals taking different views. Clients should consult their tax adviser. Distributors must not give tax advice beyond general principles.

points.heading: Set-off and carry forward
points.text: Short-term capital losses can be set off against both short and long-term gains; long-term losses only against long-term gains. Unabsorbed capital losses can be carried forward for eight years if the return is filed on time. PMS statements help clients track realised gains and losses.

points.heading: Business income risk
points.text: Very frequent trading may lead tax authorities to treat gains as business income rather than capital gains. CBDT guidance allows taxpayers to choose capital gains treatment for listed shares held over 12 months, applied consistently.

points.heading: Non-resident clients
points.text: NRIs can invest through PMS via the portfolio investment route, with tax deducted at source on capital gains and dividends at applicable rates. Double taxation avoidance agreements may reduce tax, subject to documentation such as a tax residency certificate.

traps: Assuming PMS is taxed like a mutual fund. Every trade is taxed in the client's hands.
Deducting STT from capital gains. STT is not deductible.
Setting off long-term losses against short-term gains. Long-term losses offset only long-term gains.
Promising tax benefits on PMS fees. Treatment is debated; refer clients to tax advisers.
items.recap: PMS gains and income are taxed trade by trade in the client's hands. Listed equity: STCG 20%, LTCG 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh (as of 2026). Debt interest at slab rates. Dividends at slab rates with TDS. STT not deductible. Loss set-off rules apply with eight-year carry forward. Fee deductibility is debated. NRIs face TDS and DTAA rules.

items.chapter: Regulatory, Governance and Ethical Aspects of Portfolio Managers
items.title: NISM XXI-A PMS Regulation and Ethics: Revision Notes
items.description: NISM XXI-A notes on PMS regulation and ethics: registration, net worth, code of conduct, conflicts, associate limits, distributor duties and grievances.
items.intro: This chapter covers the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020 and the conduct expected of portfolio managers and their distributors. Expect scenario questions on what a distributor should or should not do, along with questions on registration, net worth, investment restrictions, conflicts of interest and grievance redress. Ethical selling is the theme throughout.

points.heading: Registration and net worth
points.text: A portfolio manager must be a body corporate registered with SEBI, with net worth of at least ₹5 crore (as of 2026), adequate infrastructure and qualified key personnel. Registration is permanent subject to compliance and fees, and SEBI can suspend or cancel it for violations.

points.heading: Key personnel
points.text: The principal officer must meet prescribed qualification and experience criteria and hold NISM certification for portfolio managers. A separate compliance officer monitors compliance with laws and handles regulatory reporting. Employees involved in decision-making also need certification.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: Portfolio managers must act with integrity, fairness and in the clients' best interest, maintain high standards of service, avoid conflicts or disclose them, protect client confidentiality, keep client assets separate and never make misleading statements about performance.

points.heading: Investment restrictions
points.text: Client funds can be invested in unlisted securities only within prescribed limits (25% of AUM, with flexibility for certain accredited investor arrangements). Investments in securities of associates and related parties are capped, with an overall limit of 30% of client AUM. Leverage of client portfolios is not permitted.

points.heading: Conflict of interest
points.text: Managers must disclose conflicts, such as investments in group companies or commissions from intermediaries. They cannot favour one client over another in allocation of trades, and cannot use client portfolios to support group company securities.

points.heading: Distributor obligations
points.text: Distributors must be registered with APMI and certified. They must explain the strategy, risks, fees and lock-ins honestly, disclose all commissions received, assess whether PMS is appropriate for the client and never assure returns. They must not handle client cash or securities.

points.heading: Prevention of mis-selling
points.text: Mis-selling includes recommending PMS to a client who cannot bear its risks, making false performance claims, hiding fees, encouraging churning between products for commissions and misrepresenting tax benefits. Trail-only commissions and direct plans were introduced to reduce such incentives.

points.heading: Grievance redress
points.text: Clients should first approach the portfolio manager, which must resolve complaints within prescribed timelines. If unresolved, they can complain on SCORES and then use SEBI's online dispute resolution mechanism with conciliation and arbitration.

points.heading: Penalties
points.text: Violations can lead to warnings, monetary penalties, suspension or cancellation of registration, and prosecution under the SEBI Act. Distributors who violate norms can lose their APMI registration and face action.

traps: Allowing a distributor to collect client cheques in their own name. Distributors must not handle client funds.
Assuming PMS can invest freely in group companies. Associate investments are capped.
Thinking it is acceptable to quote expected returns. Assurance of returns is prohibited.
Skipping the portfolio manager and going straight to SCORES. Complaints start with the entity.
items.recap: Portfolio managers: body corporate, SEBI registration, net worth ₹5 crore (as of 2026), qualified principal officer and compliance officer. Unlisted and associate investments capped; no leverage. Code of conduct: integrity, client first, disclose conflicts. Distributors: APMI-registered, disclose commissions, assess appropriateness, no assured returns, no handling client money. Grievances: entity, SCORES, ODR.
